channel.title: Japan Specialty Traveler
channel.description: Recent content on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Abeno Harukas: Japan's Tallest Skyscraper View — Guide
item.description: Abeno Harukas, rising 300 metres above Tennoji, was Japan’s tallest building on its completion in 2014 and remains among the very tallest. It is a vertical city — a department store, a hotel, an art museum and offices stacked in one tower — but for visitors the draw is Harukas 300, the observation complex on the top three floors. Floor-to-ceiling glass wraps a full circuit 300 metres up, with an open-air atrium at its heart, giving a genuinely commanding view over Osaka, out to Kobe, Awaji and, on clear days, the mountains beyond.

item.title: Amerikamura: Osaka's Youth and Street-Culture Quarter — Guide
item.description: Amerikamura, universally shortened to Amemura, is the centre of youth and street culture in Osaka, a dense grid of lanes just west of the Shinsaibashi shopping arcade. It grew from the 1970s as a place selling imported American clothing and records, and today it is packed with vintage and streetwear boutiques, sneaker shops, record stores, tattoo studios, cafes and cheap eats, its walls covered in murals and graffiti. Its heart is Sankaku (Triangle) Park, a paved plaza where young people gather, and a small replica Statue of Liberty perched on a building is its quirky landmark.

item.title: Arashiyama Monkey Park: Wild Macaques and a City View — Guide
item.description: The Iwatayama Monkey Park sits on a hilltop above the Arashiyama district, home to a troop of more than a hundred wild Japanese macaques who roam freely across the open summit. Unlike a zoo, here the monkeys are unpenned and the visitors are the ones enclosed: you can buy food and hand it to the macaques through the mesh of a feeding hut, watching them up close while they stay wild and free outside.

item.title: Bitchu Matsuyama Castle: Japan's Highest Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Bitchu Matsuyama is unique: of Japan’s twelve surviving original castle keeps, it is the only one still standing on a mountain top, at 430 metres above the town of Takahashi. Built and rebuilt from the 13th century onwards, the present keep dates from 1683 and has never been reconstructed — you climb to a genuinely old wooden building, small and weathered, set among massive stone ramparts and rock outcrops that follow the ridge.

item.title: Bunraku: Osaka's Grand Puppet Theatre — Guide
item.description: Bunraku, the classical puppet theatre of Japan, was born in Osaka and remains most at home here, performed at the National Bunraku Theatre near Nipponbashi. It is an art of astonishing subtlety: each half-life-size puppet is operated by three black-robed handlers in full view of the audience, one controlling the head and right arm, one the left arm, one the feet, their movements so unified that the figures seem to breathe.

item.title: Calligraphy in Kyoto: A Shodo Brush Experience — Guide
item.description: Shodo, the way of writing, is one of Japan’s most revered arts, and a calligraphy experience in Kyoto is a quiet, meditative counterpoint to sightseeing. Guided by a teacher in a studio, machiya or temple, you begin by grinding an ink stick against a stone with water — a slow ritual that settles the mind — before learning to hold the brush and form the strokes of a character in the correct order and rhythm.

item.title: Den Den Town: Osaka's Electronics and Anime District — Guide
item.description: Den Den Town, in the Nipponbashi district south of Namba, is Osaka’s centre for electronics, anime and otaku culture — the city’s counterpart to Tokyo’s Akihabara. Once a strip of radio and electrical-parts shops, it has evolved into blocks packed with anime and manga stores, retro and current video games, figures, trading cards, hobby and model shops, alongside maid cafes and specialist retailers of every niche. It is less polished and less crowded than Akihabara but rewarding for collectors, and each spring the streets host the Nipponbashi Street Festa, one of Japan’s largest cosplay events.

item.title: Fushimi Sake District: Kyoto's Historic Brewing Quarter — Guide
item.description: Fushimi, in the south of Kyoto, is one of the three greatest sake-brewing centres in Japan, rivalled only by Nada in Kobe. Its fame rests on its water: the soft, mineral-rich springs here give a sake traditionally regarded as gentler and rounder than most. Dozens of breweries, some four centuries old, cluster along willow-lined canals of black-timbered storehouses, and several open their doors for tastings and tours. The Gekkeikan Okura Sake Museum tells the story with old tools and a tasting, and in spring pleasure boats drift along the canal past the storehouses — an atmospheric and grown-up counterpoint to the temples.

item.title: Ginkakuji, the Silver Pavilion: Restraint and Raked Sand — Guide
item.description: Ginkakuji, the Silver Pavilion, is the quieter, more contemplative counterpart to the golden Kinkakuji across the city. Built in 1482 as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa and converted to a Zen temple on his death, it was never actually clad in silver — its beauty lies instead in restraint. The dark wooden pavilion overlooks a refined garden of moss, a still pond and, most famously, a great cone of raked white sand and a silvery ‘sea’ meant to reflect the moon.

item.title: Gozan no Okuribi: Kyoto's Great Bonfire Farewell — Guide
item.description: Gozan no Okuribi, popularly called Daimonji, is one of Kyoto’s most solemn and spectacular annual events, held on the night of 16 August to close the Obon festival, when the spirits of ancestors are believed to return to the other world. On five mountains encircling the city, huge bonfires are lit in the shape of characters and forms — most famously the giant character for ‘great’, dai, blazing on Mount Nyoigatake above the eastern hills — each ignited in turn over the course of an hour.

item.title: HEP Five Ferris Wheel: The Red Wheel Over Umeda — Guide
item.description: The HEP Five Ferris wheel is one of Umeda’s most recognisable sights: a vivid red wheel that appears to grow straight out of the roof of the HEP Five shopping mall in the busy Umeda district. Riders board from the seventh floor and rise to 106 metres above street level, the enclosed gondolas giving a close, unusual view directly over the shops, stations and towers of northern Osaka rather than a distant panorama.

item.title: Hiroshima Castle: The Rebuilt Carp Castle — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima Castle, nicknamed the Carp Castle, was originally built in the 1590s by the warlord Mori Terumoto as the seat of his domain, a striking black-walled keep on the delta plain. The original survived until 1945, when it was destroyed by the atomic bomb; the present five-storey keep is a faithful concrete reconstruction of 1958, its dark timber-look exterior rising from a broad moat and stone base. Inside is a well-presented museum of the castle’s history and samurai culture, and the top floor gives a view over the rebuilt city.

item.title: Hiroshima Flower Festival: Golden Week on Peace Boulevard — Guide
item.description: The Hiroshima Flower Festival, held over three days of Golden Week each May, is the city’s largest annual celebration and draws well over a million people. Begun in 1977, it fills the broad Peace Boulevard with flower-decked floats, marching bands, dance teams and stages of music running from the city centre toward the Peace Park, culminating in a huge floral monument. Its founding spirit was explicitly one of peace and recovery, and the effect is striking: the same city that mourns each August turns bright, loud and joyful in spring, and the festival is free and open to everyone.

item.title: Hiroshima Lantern Floating: The Evening of 6 August — Guide
item.description: Every year on the evening of 6 August, after the morning’s memorial ceremony, Hiroshima marks the anniversary of the atomic bombing with toro nagashi, the floating of paper lanterns. Thousands of lanterns, each carrying a handwritten message of peace or remembrance for the dead, are set on the Motoyasu River and drift slowly past the illuminated A-Bomb Dome as darkness falls. It draws people from all over the world and locals whose families were lost that day, and the atmosphere is quiet and profoundly moving rather than festive.

item.title: Hiroshima Okonomiyaki Cooking Class: Build Your Own — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima okonomiyaki looks simple and is deceptively hard: the layering, the timing and above all the flip of a tall, loose stack take real skill, which is exactly what makes a cooking class here so satisfying. In a small group around a teppan griddle, an instructor walks you through spreading the thin crepe, piling on the cabbage and pork, steaming it down, frying the noodles alongside and finally combining and flipping the whole thing without collapse, before finishing with sauce, seaweed and bonito flakes.

item.title: Hiroshima Oysters: Japan's Great Oyster Coast — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima is Japan’s oyster capital, growing the great majority of the country’s crop on rafts strung across the calm, nutrient-rich waters of the Seto Inland Sea. The oysters here are famously plump and creamy, and locals eat them in every conceivable way: grilled in the half shell over charcoal at stalls on Miyajima, deep-fried as kaki-fry, simmered in a miso hotpot called doteni, folded into rice, or simply raw with lemon.

item.title: Hiroshima Paper Crane Workshop: Folding for Peace — Guide
item.description: The folded paper crane, orizuru, is the worldwide symbol of the wish for peace, and that meaning was born in Hiroshima. It comes from the story of Sadako Sasaki, a girl who developed leukaemia from the bomb’s radiation and set out to fold a thousand cranes in the hope of recovery before she died aged twelve; the Children’s Peace Monument in the Peace Park, hung with millions of cranes sent from around the world, is dedicated to her and all child victims.

item.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum: Bearing Witness — Guide
item.description: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, at the southern end of the Peace Park, is one of the most important and affecting museums in the world. Extensively renewed in 2019, it presents the atomic bombing of 6 August 1945 not through statistics but through the human beings who lived and died that day: a child’s scorched tricycle, a stopped watch, tattered school uniforms, photographs of the ruined city and the personal testimonies of survivors, the hibakusha.

item.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park: A Place of Remembrance — Guide
item.description: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park occupies the open ground near the point where the atomic bomb detonated on 6 August 1945, once a busy commercial district reduced to ash in an instant. Rather than rebuild, the city made it a place of memory and a plea for peace. At its edge stands the A-Bomb Dome, a UNESCO World Heritage Site preserved as a ruin exactly as the blast left it, its skeletal frame one of the most powerful anti-war images in the world.

item.title: Hiroshima Ramen & Tsukemen: The City's Noodle Bowls — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima has two distinct noodle traditions of its own. Hiroshima ramen is a relatively gentle, comforting bowl: a soy-based broth built on pork bones, less heavy than Hakata tonkotsu, with soft straight noodles, chashu pork, bean sprouts and spring onion. Quite different is Hiroshima tsukemen, a local speciality unrelated to the Tokyo dipping-noodle style: chilled noodles served with raw cabbage and cucumber alongside a cold, intensely spicy chilli-and-sesame dipping sauce, ordered by heat level from mild to genuinely punishing.

item.title: Hiroshima Sake Festival: Saijo's Great October Tasting — Guide
item.description: The Sake Festival, held in Saijo over a weekend each October, is one of the largest sake events in Japan and turns the whole brewery town into a celebration. Its centrepiece is a huge tasting hall where, for a single ticket, visitors can sample from hundreds of labels gathered from breweries the length of the country — an extraordinary opportunity to compare regional styles side by side. Outside, Saijo’s own historic breweries open their courtyards, food stalls fill the streets between the red-brick chimneys, and stages host music.

item.title: Hiroshima Winter Illuminations: Lights on Peace Boulevard — Guide
item.description: Through the winter months, Hiroshima strings its broad Peace Boulevard and the adjacent Heiwa-odori park with elaborate illuminations, in an annual display long known to locals as Dreamination. Themed light sculptures, arches and tunnels of glowing bulbs line the avenue for several hundred metres, turning an ordinary walk into a cheerful evening outing that draws couples, families and photographers from across the city. It is free to walk, runs nightly for several weeks over the coldest part of the year, and offers a warm, bright counterpoint to a city that otherwise feels quiet in winter.

item.title: Hiroshima-style Okonomiyaki: Layered, Not Mixed — Guide
item.description: Okonomiyaki is Hiroshima’s proudest food, and locals will tell you firmly that theirs is the original and superior version. Unlike the Osaka style, where everything is mixed into a batter, Hiroshima okonomiyaki is built in layers: a thin crepe is spread on the griddle, then piled high with shredded cabbage, bean sprouts and pork belly, pressed down as it steams, and finally set on a nest of fried soba or udon noodles and topped with a fried egg and a slick of sweet-savoury sauce.

item.title: Hiruzen Yakisoba: Miso-Sauced Noodles of the Highlands — Guide
item.description: Hiruzen yakisoba is a distinct regional take on Japan’s ubiquitous fried noodles. Instead of the usual dark Worcestershire-style sauce, cooks in the Hiruzen highlands use a rich miso-based sauce blended with garlic, apple and other fruit, giving a sweeter, deeper, slightly nutty flavour. The other signature is the protein: kashiwa, chewy parent chicken rather than pork, along with plenty of local cabbage. Each family and restaurant has its own sauce recipe, and the dish became nationally famous after winning the B-1 Grand Prix, Japan’s contest for regional comfort food, in 2011.

item.title: Hozenji Yokocho: The Moss-Covered Lantern Alley — Guide
item.description: Hozenji Yokocho is a pair of narrow, stone-paved lanes tucked just south of the roar of Dotonbori, and stepping into them is like stepping back a century. Lined with tiny, atmospheric restaurants and bars behind lantern-lit facades, the alleys lead to Hozenji Temple, whose small Fudo Myo-o statue is famous for being completely covered in soft green moss — the result of generations of worshippers ladling water over it as they pray for success in love and business.

item.title: Keage Incline: The Cherry-Blossom Railway Slope — Guide
item.description: The Keage Incline is a short stretch of disused railway slope near Nanzenji, built as part of the ingenious Lake Biwa Canal that once carried boats between the lake and Kyoto by hauling them up and down this ramp on rail cradles. Long out of use, its rusting twin tracks have become one of the city’s loveliest walks: some ninety cherry trees line the slope, and in early April they arch overhead into a tunnel of blossom above the old rails, drawing photographers and strollers.

item.title: Kema Sakuranomiya Park: Osaka's Great Riverside Cherry Avenue — Guide
item.description: Kema Sakuranomiya Park stretches for several kilometres along both banks of the Okawa river north of central Osaka, and in early April it becomes one of the city’s most spectacular places to see cherry blossom. Nearly five thousand trees form near-continuous tunnels of pink along the water, best appreciated on a slow walk from Sakuranomiya Station toward the old Mint Bureau, whose private cherry avenue opens to the public for a famous week each spring.

item.title: Kibidango: Momotaro's Millet Dumplings — Guide
item.description: Kibidango are small, soft, faintly sweet mochi dumplings dusted in powder, and in Okayama they carry a story: in the tale of Momotaro, the Peach Boy, it is kibidango that the hero gives to a dog, a monkey and a pheasant to win them as companions on his journey to defeat the demons. Since the Kibi Plain west of Okayama is widely held to be the origin of that legend, the dumplings have become the prefecture’s defining souvenir.

item.title: Kibitsu Shrine: The 400-Metre Corridor and the Momotaro Legend — Guide
item.description: Kibitsu Shrine, on the Kibi Plain west of Okayama city, is one of the most distinctive shrines in western Japan. Its main hall, rebuilt in 1425 and designated a National Treasure, has a rare twin-gabled roof form found nowhere else, called kibitsu-zukuri. From it, a covered wooden corridor runs some 400 metres along the contour of the hillside, rising and falling through the trees in a receding perspective that is unforgettable.

item.title: Kishiwada Danjiri Matsuri: The Runaway-Float Festival — Guide
item.description: The Kishiwada Danjiri Matsuri, held each September in the coastal city of Kishiwada, is the most exhilarating and famously reckless festival in Osaka. Teams of hundreds haul danjiri — massive, intricately carved wooden floats weighing several tonnes — through the town not in stately procession but at a flat-out run, the great skill and danger coming at the corners, where the pullers whip the float around a sharp turn without slowing while a leader dances on the roof.

item.title: Korakuen Garden: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens — Guide
item.description: Korakuen, completed in 1700 for the lord of Okayama, is counted among the three great gardens of Japan alongside Kenrokuen and Kairakuen. What sets it apart is its openness: where most Japanese strolling gardens are dense and enclosed, Korakuen spreads wide lawns, ponds and streams across a river island, giving it a rare feeling of light and space. Paths wind past a working tea plantation and small rice field, teahouses, a grove of plum and cherry, and a hill you can climb for the full view — all composed around the borrowed scenery of Okayama Castle’s black keep rising beyond the garden wall.

item.title: Kurama Fire Festival: Torches and Flame in the Mountains — Guide
item.description: The Kurama Fire Festival, held on the night of 22 October in the mountain village of Kurama north of Kyoto, is one of the most dramatic and primal festivals in the region. As night falls, watch-fires are lit along the narrow main street and villagers, from children to grown men, parade enormous flaming pine torches — some several metres long and weighing over 80 kilograms — up through the village to Yuki Shrine, shouting as they go.

item.title: Kurashiki Bikan Historic Quarter: The Willow Canal — Guide
item.description: The Bikan Historic Quarter in Kurashiki is among the most beautiful preserved townscapes in Japan. In the Edo period Kurashiki was a shogunate-controlled rice-trading town, and its merchants built rows of kura — storehouses with white plastered walls and distinctive black lattice tiling — along a canal used to move goods. That canal survives, lined with weeping willows and crossed by stone bridges, and the storehouses have become museums, cafes, craft shops and inns.

item.title: Kure: Yamato Museum & the Iron Whale — Guide
item.description: Kure, a deep natural harbour east of Hiroshima, was one of the great naval bases of imperial Japan and the shipyard that built the Yamato, the largest battleship ever constructed. The Yamato Museum tells that story through a spectacular 26-metre, 1:10 scale model of the ship, alongside a Zero fighter, a human torpedo and exhibits that deal frankly with the war, the city’s bombing and postwar shipbuilding. Directly opposite stands the Iron Whale Museum, where a real decommissioned submarine sits beached on land and can be entered and walked through — an unusual and memorable pairing.

item.title: Kyo-Wagashi: Kyoto's Seasonal Sweets — Guide
item.description: Kyo-wagashi are the refined traditional sweets of Kyoto, developed alongside the tea ceremony and elevated here into an edible art form. Made largely from sweet bean paste, glutinous rice, agar and sugar, they are prized less for sweetness than for beauty: each is shaped and coloured to evoke a season — a pink petal in spring, a cool cube of kingyoku in summer, a russet maple leaf in autumn. Served with a bowl of bitter matcha, a single wagashi is a small ceremony in itself.

item.title: Kyoto Aquarium: River to Sea in Umekoji Park — Guide
item.description: The Kyoto Aquarium, opened in 2012 in Umekoji Park near Kyoto Station, is unusual for a large aquarium in being entirely inland, and it makes a virtue of it: the visit begins not with the sea but with the rivers of Kyoto, starring the giant Japanese salamander, a strange and ancient amphibian native to the region’s waterways. From there it moves through jellyfish tanks, a large open penguin and seal zone, a big tank recreating the seas off Kyoto, and a dolphin stadium with regular shows.

item.title: Kyoto Cherry Blossom Season: Where and When for Sakura — Guide
item.description: Cherry blossom season transforms Kyoto into one of the most beautiful cities on earth for a fleeting week or two, usually in late March and early April. The old capital is arguably the finest place in Japan to see sakura, precisely because the blossom is set against temples, pagodas, canals and traditional streets rather than modern buildings. The Philosopher’s Path, the Okazaki canal, Maruyama Park’s weeping cherry, the grounds of Ninnaji and Daigoji, and the riverbanks all become famous scenes, many floodlit at night.

item.title: Kyoto Railway Museum: Steam Trains to Shinkansen — Guide
item.description: The Kyoto Railway Museum, opened in 2016 just west of Kyoto Station, is one of the best railway museums in Japan and a superb outing for families and enthusiasts alike. It displays 53 real trains spanning the whole history of Japanese rail, from black steam locomotives through classic express carriages to an early shinkansen bullet train, many of which you can board. A highlight is the preserved roundhouse and turntable, where working steam locomotives are still kept, and you can ride a genuine steam train on a short line.

item.title: Kyoto Setsubun: Driving Out Demons in Early February — Guide
item.description: Setsubun, held around 3 February, marks the eve of spring in the old lunar calendar and is celebrated across Japan with mame-maki, the throwing of roasted soybeans to drive out bad fortune, shouting ‘oni wa soto, fuku wa uchi’ — demons out, luck in. Kyoto keeps the day with particular richness: its major shrines and temples host their own ceremonies, from costumed oni demons chased away with beans at Yoshida and Rozanji, to bean-throwing led by geiko and maiko at Yasaka Shrine, to fire rituals and huge crowds scrambling for thrown packets of beans and prizes.

item.title: Kyoto Tower: The City's Only Skyscraper View — Guide
item.description: Kyoto Tower, completed in 1964 and standing 131 metres directly across from Kyoto Station, is the tallest structure in a city that otherwise keeps deliberately low to protect its skyline. Its slender white form, said to evoke a lighthouse or a candle, is a divisive landmark but an unbeatable viewpoint: because Kyoto has no other tall buildings, the observation deck at 100 metres gives a genuinely uninterrupted 360-degree panorama over the whole basin, the grid of the old city, the scattered pagodas and temple roofs, and the mountains that ring it on three sides.

item.title: Mamakari: Okayama's Vinegar-Pickled Little Fish — Guide
item.description: Mamakari is a small silvery fish of the Seto Inland Sea, a kind of sardine or shad, and one of Okayama’s most characteristic foods. It is usually filleted and cured in vinegar, giving a bright, sharp, oily bite eaten as sashimi-style sushi, with rice, or as a drinking snack. The name is a local joke: mama means cooked rice and kari means to borrow, because the fish is so good with rice that you finish your own bowl and have to borrow more from the neighbours.

item.title: Maruyama Park: Kyoto's Favourite Cherry-Blossom Park — Guide
item.description: Maruyama Park, tucked behind Yasaka Shrine at the foot of the Higashiyama hills, is the most popular public park in Kyoto and its most famous spot for hanami. Laid out in the Meiji era, it is a gentle landscape of ponds, streams, stone lanterns and winding paths, with tea houses and restaurants around its edges. At its heart stands a huge shidarezakura, a weeping cherry tree, which in early April is floodlit after dark and surrounded by revellers and food stalls in one of the city’s great cherry-blossom scenes.

item.title: Mazda Zoom-Zoom Stadium: A Carp Baseball Night — Guide
item.description: Mazda Zoom-Zoom Stadium, opened in 2009, is the home of the Hiroshima Toyo Carp and one of the best places in Japan to experience baseball. Uniquely, the Carp are community-owned rather than backed by a single corporate giant, and the bond with the city is fierce: the stands fill with a sea of red, fans chant continuously through their team’s at-bats, and the atmosphere is famously warm and family-friendly. The ballpark itself is an American-style open stadium with wide concourses, a variety of quirky seating including sofa and lie-down seats, and excellent food, including Hiroshima okonomiyaki.

item.title: Mihara Castle & the Suigun Road: A Sea-Castle Ruin — Guide
item.description: Mihara Castle was built in the 1560s by Kobayakawa Takakage on islets in the sea, a naval stronghold so surrounded by water it was nicknamed the ‘floating castle’. Land reclamation has long since left it inland, and its keep is gone, but substantial stone ramparts and a moat survive — remarkably, right against Mihara’s shinkansen station, whose platforms were built over part of the site, making this possibly the most accessible castle ruin in Japan.

item.title: Miyajima & Itsukushima Shrine: The Floating Torii — Guide
item.description: Miyajima, officially Itsukushima, is a small sacred island in the Seto Inland Sea just off Hiroshima and one of the most beautiful places in Japan. Its centrepiece is Itsukushima Shrine, a vermilion complex built out over the water on wooden piles so that at high tide it appears to float, and its huge O-torii gate, standing offshore, rises straight from the sea — one of the country’s three most celebrated views and a World Heritage Site.

item.title: Miyajima Autumn Foliage: Momijidani in Flame — Guide
item.description: Miyajima is famous for its maples — the island’s signature sweet, momiji manju, is even shaped like a maple leaf — and each autumn Momijidani, the ‘maple valley’ behind Itsukushima Shrine, becomes one of the most beautiful places in western Japan. Hundreds of maple trees, planted over centuries, turn brilliant shades of red, orange and gold in November, framing a small park of stone bridges, a mountain stream and the lower station of the Mount Misen ropeway.

item.title: Miyako Odori: Gion's Geiko and Maiko Spring Dances — Guide
item.description: The Miyako Odori, the ‘Dances of the Old Capital’, is the great annual public performance of the geiko and maiko of Gion Kobu, held throughout April since 1872. For a few weeks each spring, the geisha who normally perform only in private teahouses take to a theatre stage in a lavish, tightly choreographed production, with rows of maiko in matching seasonal kimono dancing to live traditional music, backed by painted scenery that changes with the seasons of the year.

item.title: Momiji Manju: Miyajima's Maple-Leaf Cakes — Guide
item.description: Momiji manju are little cakes baked in the shape of a maple leaf, a nod to the maples of Momijidani, and they are the definitive souvenir of Hiroshima. Created on Miyajima over a century ago, they are made from a light castella-style sponge batter poured into leaf-shaped moulds and filled traditionally with sweet red bean paste, though modern fillings run to custard, chocolate, matcha and cheese. On Miyajima you can watch them being made on rotating griddles and eat them still warm, which is a completely different experience from the boxed ones — and several shops sell them battered and deep-fried on a stick as age-momiji.

item.title: Mount Misen: Miyajima's Sacred Summit — Guide
item.description: Mount Misen, the 535-metre peak that rises behind Itsukushima Shrine, is the sacred heart of Miyajima and the island’s finest walk. Revered for over a thousand years and covered in primeval forest, its trails climb through temples and past a hall holding a flame said to have burned continuously since the monk Kukai lit it in the ninth century — the same flame used to light the Flame of Peace in Hiroshima.

item.title: Mozu Tombs: The Giant Keyhole Kofun of Sakai — Guide
item.description: The Mozu Tombs in Sakai are a group of giant burial mounds built in the fifth century for the rulers of early Japan, inscribed together with the nearby Furuichi group as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The greatest of them, the Daisen Kofun, is traditionally attributed to Emperor Nintoku: a keyhole-shaped mound 486 metres long, ringed by moats, its scale rivalling the Great Pyramid and the tomb of the First Emperor of China.

item.title: Nagai Park & Botanical Garden: Osaka's Southern Green Lung — Guide
item.description: Nagai Park is one of Osaka’s largest green spaces, a broad expanse in the south of the city built around sports stadiums, wide lawns and, at its heart, the Nagai Botanical Garden. The garden lays out themed zones — a large pond, seasonal flower fields, a rose garden and collections of trees — alongside the Osaka Museum of Natural History, whose dinosaur and whale skeletons make the pairing a strong family destination.

item.title: Namba Parks: The Terraced Rooftop Garden of Namba — Guide
item.description: Namba Parks is a shopping and office complex built above the old Nankai stadium site next to Namba Station, but it is far more interesting than that suggests. Designed by the American architect Jon Jerde to resemble a natural canyon, its floors step back as they rise, and across their setbacks climbs Parks Garden — a continuous rooftop park of some eight levels, planted with hundreds of species of trees, shrubs and flowers, with lawns, streams and quiet corners.

item.title: Naniwa Yodogawa Fireworks: Osaka's Great Summer Hanabi — Guide
item.description: The Naniwa Yodogawa Fireworks Festival is one of the biggest and best-loved summer events in Osaka, staged on a single night in high summer over the broad Yodogawa river in the north of the city. Run largely on public donations, it sends tens of thousands of shells into the sky in a tightly choreographed programme, the wide river giving space for huge low bursts reflected in the water and a finale that fills the whole sky.

item.title: Nishin Soba: Kyoto's Herring Noodle Bowl — Guide
item.description: Nishin soba is one of Kyoto’s most distinctive comfort foods: a bowl of hot soba noodles in a light broth, topped with a whole fillet of migaki-nishin, dried Pacific herring slowly simmered in soy, sugar and sake until sweet, soft and glossy. It is a dish born of geography — landlocked Kyoto relied on preserved fish carried down from Hokkaido, and the humble dried herring was transformed into something rich and warming.

item.title: Ohara & Sanzen-in: Kyoto's Tranquil Mountain Temple Village — Guide
item.description: Ohara is a quiet farming valley in the mountains an hour north of central Kyoto, a world away from the crowds and a favourite escape for those wanting the old, rural Kyoto. Its centrepiece is Sanzen-in, a serene monzeki temple set among cedar and maple, whose most famous view is a garden of deep green moss dotted with small, smiling stone jizo figures half-hidden in the undergrowth. In autumn the maples turn the whole valley to fire.

item.title: Ohara Museum of Art: Japan's First Western Art Museum — Guide
item.description: The Ohara Museum of Art, standing behind a striking neoclassical portico on the Kurashiki canal, was the first museum in Japan dedicated to Western art. It was founded in 1930 by the industrialist Ohara Magosaburo to house the collection assembled in Europe by the painter Kojima Torajiro, and it remains extraordinary for a provincial city: El Greco’s Annunciation is its most famous work, alongside pieces by Monet, Gauguin, Matisse, Renoir and Picasso.

item.title: Okayama Barazushi: The Feast Hidden Under Rice — Guide
item.description: Barazushi, also called Okayama-zushi, is the prefecture’s great festive dish: a wide bowl or lacquer box of vinegared rice scattered with a lavish topping of Seto Inland Sea seafood — prawns, mamakari, octopus, conger eel — alongside vegetables, shiitake, egg and lotus root. The story told locally is that a 17th-century lord of Okayama decreed frugal meals of one soup and one dish, so townspeople hid a feast of ingredients underneath the rice and served it as a single humble bowl.

item.title: Okayama Castle: The Black Crow Castle — Guide
item.description: Okayama Castle is known as Ujo, the Crow Castle, for the striking black lacquered boards that clad its walls — a deliberate contrast to the white ‘White Heron’ castle at Himeji. Originally completed in 1597 by Ukita Hideie, it stood on the bank of the Asahi River, which served as its natural moat, until the keep was destroyed in a wartime air raid in 1945. The present keep is a 1966 reconstruction, extensively renewed in 2022, housing a well-presented museum of the castle and its lords, with a top-floor view over the river to Korakuen garden directly opposite.

item.title: Okayama White Peaches & Muscat Grapes: The Fruit Kingdom — Guide
item.description: Okayama’s mild, dry climate and long sunshine hours have made it Japan’s ‘Fruit Kingdom’, and two products define it. The hakuto white peach is grown in paper bags to keep the skin pale and the flesh almost white, producing an intensely perfumed, delicate fruit so soft it is often eaten with a spoon. The Muscat of Alexandria, cultivated in greenhouses here since the Meiji era, yields huge, pale-green, seeded grapes with a distinctive floral aroma, alongside the newer seedless Shine Muscat.

item.title: Onomichi Temple Walk & Cat Alley: A Hillside Town — Guide
item.description: Onomichi is a charming old port town on the Seto Inland Sea, built on a steep hillside laced with narrow lanes, stone stairways and cats, looking out over a channel busy with ships. Its signature experience is the Temple Walk, a marked trail linking some twenty-five temples along the slope, threading between old wooden houses, hidden shrines and viewpoints over the sea and islands. Along the way runs the famous Cat Alley (Neko no Hosomichi), decorated with painted cat stones and home to real strays, cafes and craft shops.

item.title: Osaka Autumn Foliage: Minoo Falls and the Momiji Trail — Guide
item.description: For autumn colour, Osakans head north to Minoo (Mino-o), a wooded valley on the edge of the city that turns brilliant with maples each November. A gentle, paved riverside trail runs about three kilometres up the gorge from Minoo Station to the Minoo Waterfall, a 33-metre fall framed by fiery leaves at the head of the valley — one of the most rewarding easy walks in the Osaka area. Along the way, shops sell the local speciality of momiji tempura, whole maple leaves battered and deep-fried into a sweet, crisp snack.

item.title: Osaka Butaman: The City's Beloved Pork Bun — Guide
item.description: In Osaka the steamed pork bun is called butaman rather than the nikuman used elsewhere, and it is a genuine local institution. The most famous version comes from 551 Horai, an Osaka chain founded in 1945 whose bright counters, with their steaming towers of bamboo baskets, form queues at stations and department stores across the city. The bun is large and fluffy, filled with coarsely chopped pork and onion, and eaten piping hot with a dab of the hot mustard that comes with it — a cheap, satisfying snack that locals also carry home by the boxful.

item.title: Osaka Conveyor-Belt Sushi: Kaitenzushi Done Right — Guide
item.description: Conveyor-belt sushi, kaitenzushi, is one of the most approachable meals in Osaka and a favourite with families and travellers alike. Plates of sushi circle the room on a belt while a touch-screen at your seat lets you order anything made fresh to arrive on an express lane; you take what you want, and the bill is tallied from the stacked plates, colour-coded by price. Osaka, obsessed with cheap and cheerful eating, does this exceptionally well, from bargain nationwide chains to specialist counters using good fish from the nearby markets — a low-stress, no-reservation meal at almost any hour.

item.title: Osaka Okonomiyaki Cooking Class: Grill Your Own — Guide
item.description: Okonomiyaki, the hearty savoury pancake of cabbage, batter and toppings grilled on a hot iron plate, is Osaka’s defining home-style dish, and a cooking class is one of the most enjoyable ways to get under the skin of the city’s food culture. In a small group around a teppan, an instructor walks you through mixing the batter, grilling and the all-important flip, then eating what you’ve made hot off the plate, usually finished with sauce, mayonnaise, bonito flakes and seaweed.

item.title: Osaka Sake & Izakaya Tasting: A Night of Drinking Osaka — Guide
item.description: Osaka takes drinking as seriously as eating, and a night in its izakaya and sake bars is one of the warmest experiences the city offers. The options run from tachinomi standing bars crammed under railway arches around Umeda and Namba, where a few hundred yen buys a glass and a skewer, to specialist sake bars pouring flights from breweries across the Kansai region and English-friendly guided tastings that walk you through junmai, ginjo and the differences between them.

item.title: Osaka Spring Grand Sumo Tournament: The Haru Basho — Guide
item.description: The Spring Grand Sumo Tournament, the Haru Basho, is one of only six professional sumo tournaments held each year, and its March run makes Osaka one of the best places outside Tokyo to see the sport live. Over fifteen days at the Edion Arena (Osaka Prefectural Gymnasium) in Namba, wrestlers fight daily to build a winning record, the action climbing from lower divisions in the quiet morning to the top-division makuuchi bouts, ring-entering ceremonies and title race in the charged late afternoon.

item.title: Osaka Tenmangu: Shrine of Scholars and the Tenjin Festival — Guide
item.description: Osaka Tenmangu enshrines Sugawara no Michizane, the ninth-century scholar-official deified as Tenjin, the god of learning, and it has drawn students praying for examination success for over a thousand years. Founded in 949, the shrine sits at the head of one of the longest shopping arcades in Japan and is the spiritual home of the Tenjin Matsuri, held each July — one of the three great festivals of Japan, in which sacred palanquins are carried to the river and paraded on a flotilla of boats beneath fireworks.

item.title: Pontocho: Kyoto's Atmospheric Dining Alley — Guide
item.description: Pontocho is a single narrow lane, running for several hundred metres between Shijo and Sanjo alongside the Kamo River, and it is the most atmospheric place to eat and drink in Kyoto. Barely two metres wide and closed to cars, it is lined on both sides with wooden machiya houses turned into restaurants and bars, hung with lanterns and the crest of the district, a stylised plover. The range runs from exclusive kaiseki restaurants with summer platforms out over the river to tiny standing bars and yakitori counters.

item.title: Ryoanji: Japan's Most Famous Zen Rock Garden — Guide
item.description: Ryoanji is home to the most famous karesansui, or dry landscape garden, in Japan. Created around the late fifteenth century, it consists of nothing but fifteen rocks set in low moss beds within a rectangle of raked white gravel, enclosed by a low earthen wall. Its fame rests on an enigma: the stones are arranged so that from any vantage point on the viewing veranda, at least one is always hidden behind another.

item.title: Saijo Sake District: Brick Chimneys and Brewery Streets — Guide
item.description: Saijo, in Higashihiroshima, is one of the three most important sake-brewing towns in Japan, alongside Nada in Kobe and Fushimi in Kyoto. What makes it exceptional for visitors is its compactness: within a few minutes' walk of the station stand around half a dozen historic breweries, their white plastered walls, black-tiled roofs and tall red-brick chimneys forming an unmistakable townscape. Most open their doors to visitors with free or inexpensive tastings, wells of the soft local water you can drink from, and shops selling their own labels.

item.title: Sandankyo Gorge: A Ravine Walk in Hiroshima's Mountains — Guide
item.description: Sandankyo is a long, dramatic ravine carved into the mountains of northern Hiroshima, designated a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and one of the finest gorge walks in western Japan. A well-made trail follows the river for some sixteen kilometres between sheer rock walls, past deep emerald pools, rapids, cliffs and a series of waterfalls, with atmospheric highlights like Kurobuchi, where a small boat ferries walkers across a still, dark pool between the cliffs.

item.title: Sanjusangendo: The Hall of 1,001 Kannon — Guide
item.description: Sanjusangendo is one of Kyoto’s most quietly overwhelming sights: a long, narrow wooden hall, at 120 metres the longest in Japan, filled with a thousand and one statues of Kannon, the Buddhist deity of compassion. Rank upon rank of gilded, thousand-armed figures stand in tiered rows to either side of a great seated central Kannon, each face subtly different, backed by twenty-eight guardian deities and the thunder and wind gods carved with astonishing dynamism.

item.title: Seiryuji Temple & Its Giant Daibutsu — Guide
item.description: Seiryuji sits on the wooded slopes of western Hiroshima, well away from the tourist trail, and its landmark is a huge bronze Daibutsu, a Great Buddha seated serenely on the hillside and gazing out over the city and the delta below. The temple grounds climb the slope through halls, statuary and quiet corners, with views that open up as you ascend, and the whole place sees a fraction of the visitors of the central sights.

item.title: Seto Inland Sea Island Cruise: Sailing Between the Islands — Guide
item.description: The Seto Inland Sea, the sheltered water between Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, is one of Japan’s most beautiful landscapes and was its first designated national park. Strewn with hundreds of green, steeply rising islands and famously calm, it has been a highway for a thousand years, and the best way to appreciate it is simply to get on a boat. Options range from local ferries linking island ports for a few hundred yen, to sightseeing cruises from Hiroshima and Onomichi, to overnight luxury cruise ships.

item.title: Shimanami Kaido Cycling: Island-Hopping by Bike — Guide
item.description: The Shimanami Kaido is the finest cycling route in Japan and one of the best anywhere: a roughly 70-kilometre course running from Onomichi in Hiroshima across six islands of the Seto Inland Sea to Imabari in Shikoku. Uniquely, every bridge on the route carries a dedicated, separated cycle lane with gentle spiral approach ramps, so riders cross high above the sea in complete safety. Between the bridges the route rolls through fishing villages, citrus groves and quiet island roads, with a blue line painted on the tarmac guiding you the whole way.

item.title: Shitennoji: Japan's Oldest Official Temple — Guide
item.description: Shitennoji claims to be the oldest officially administered temple in Japan, founded in 593 by Prince Shotoku, the statesman who did more than anyone to establish Buddhism in the country. Fires and war have destroyed its buildings many times, but each rebuilding has faithfully followed the original sixth-century plan: a rigidly symmetrical line of inner gate, five-storey pagoda and golden hall enclosed by a cloister, the earliest temple layout in Japan.

item.title: Shukkeien Garden: A Miniature Landscape in the City — Guide
item.description: Shukkeien, whose name means ‘shrunken-scenery garden’, is a beautiful traditional strolling garden in the middle of Hiroshima, laid out in 1620 for the local lord. As its name suggests, it miniaturises whole landscapes — mountains, valleys, forests and a central pond dotted with islets — into a compact space that unfolds scene by scene as you follow the path around the water. An arched rainbow bridge crosses the pond, tea houses sit among the maples and cherries, and carp fill the water.

item.title: Tempozan Harbor Village: Ferris Wheel and Aquarium — Guide
item.description: Tempozan is Osaka’s waterfront leisure district, built around the bay at the mouth of the Aji river and easily reached from the city centre. Its two landmarks dominate: the Osaka Aquarium Kaiyukan, one of the largest aquariums in the world, whose central tank recreates the Pacific with whale sharks and rays; and the Tempozan Ferris Wheel, a 112-metre giant that was among the world’s tallest when built and glows in colour after dark.

item.title: Tennoji Park & Keitakuen Garden: Green Heart of the South — Guide
item.description: Tennoji Park spreads beneath the towers of Abeno Harukas, a large and varied green space at the junction of the Tennoji and Shinsekai districts. Its jewel is Keitakuen, a circular strolling garden designed in the early twentieth century around a central pond, once the private garden of the Sumitomo family and a masterpiece of the period. The park also holds Osaka’s zoo, the city art museum and, at its northern edge, a modern lawn plaza lined with cafes and lit in the evening — making it a place equally suited to garden lovers, families and anyone wanting to sit down between sights.

item.title: Tenryuji: Arashiyama's Great Zen Temple and Borrowed-Scenery Garden — Guide
item.description: Tenryuji is the most important temple in Arashiyama and one of Kyoto’s five great Zen temples, founded in 1339. While its wooden halls have burned and been rebuilt many times, its garden survives from the fourteenth century essentially unchanged — a masterpiece by the monk-designer Muso Soseki. Centred on a pond, it uses the technique of shakkei, ‘borrowed scenery’, drawing the wooded slopes of the Arashiyama hills into the composition so that garden and mountain read as one.

item.title: The Kamo River: Kyoto's Riverside Promenade — Guide
item.description: The Kamogawa, the Kamo River, runs north to south through the middle of Kyoto and is the city’s best-loved outdoor space, a long ribbon of grassy banks, paths and stepping-stone crossings threading the centre. Locals come here to jog, cycle, picnic, play music and simply sit — famously in evenly spaced couples along the water at Shijo. In summer, restaurants along the west bank at Pontocho and Kiyamachi build kawadoko, wooden dining platforms out over the river, for open-air meals in the evening cool.

item.title: Toji: Kyoto's Tallest Pagoda and Great Flea Market — Guide
item.description: Toji, ‘the East Temple’, was founded in 796 when Kyoto became the capital and given to the great monk Kukai, who made it a centre of esoteric Shingon Buddhism. Its five-story pagoda, rebuilt in 1644, rises 55 metres and is the tallest wooden tower in Japan, a landmark visible from the shinkansen and an emblem of the city. Inside its Lecture Hall stands a three-dimensional mandala of twenty-one carved deities arranged by Kukai himself.

item.title: Tomonoura: A Timeless Inland Sea Port Town — Guide
item.description: Tomonoura, on a headland south of Fukuyama, is one of the best-preserved old harbour towns on the Seto Inland Sea, so little changed that walking its lanes feels like stepping into the Edo period. Ships once waited here for the tide to turn, and the town grew wealthy on that trade, leaving a rare survival: the original stone-built harbour with its curved jetty, a squat stone lighthouse, warehouses and temples, and streets of wooden merchant houses.

item.title: Tsuruhashi: Osaka's Korea Town and Yakiniku Warren — Guide
item.description: Tsuruhashi is the heart of Osaka’s Korean community and one of the most sensory food districts in Japan. The moment you leave the station you are in a dense warren of covered lanes packed with yakiniku grills, kimchi vendors, Korean grocers and stalls of tteok and jeon, the air permanently thick with charcoal smoke. The area grew from a postwar black market around a large Zainichi Korean population, and it remains the best place in western Japan to eat grilled meat: hundreds of restaurants, from cramped smoky counters to polished specialists, packed into a few blocks.

item.title: Tsutenkaku Tower: The Heart of Retro Shinsekai — Guide
item.description: Tsutenkaku is the symbol of old, down-to-earth Osaka. The current tower dates from 1956, a rebuild of a 1912 original that mimicked the Eiffel Tower, and it rises above Shinsekai, a district frozen in a cheerfully retro version of the early twentieth century. Its observation decks give views across the south of the city, and enshrined near the top is Billiken, an American-born good-luck figure whose feet visitors rub for fortune.

item.title: Utsubo Park Rose Garden: A Green Oasis in the Business District — Guide
item.description: Utsubo Park is a slim, tree-lined green space threaded through the office towers of western Osaka, a favourite lunchtime escape for the district’s workers and a genuinely lovely city park. Its centrepiece is a rose garden of many hundreds of bushes, laid out formally around fountains, which comes into full bloom twice a year in a wash of colour and fragrance. The rest of the park mixes lawns, a tennis centre and broad tree-lined promenades, and it makes an easy, calm stop between the shops of nearby Shinsaibashi and the harbour.

item.title: Wagashi Making Class in Kyoto: Shape Your Own Sweets — Guide
item.description: A wagashi-making class is one of the most rewarding hands-on experiences in Kyoto, a direct way into the city’s refined sweet-making tradition. Under the guidance of a confectioner, you learn to shape nerikiri — a smooth, pliable dough of sweet white-bean paste — by hand and with simple tools into the seasonal flowers, leaves and motifs that define kyo-wagashi. It is finer and more meditative work than it looks, demanding a gentle touch, and at the end you sit and eat the two or three sweets you have made with a bowl of matcha.

item.title: Yasaka Shrine: Gion's Lantern-Lit Guardian Shrine — Guide
item.description: Yasaka Shrine, sometimes called Gion-san, sits at the eastern end of Shijo street where it meets the Gion district and the slopes of Higashiyama. Founded over 1,300 years ago, it is one of Kyoto’s most popular shrines, its bright vermilion gate and main hall always open and free to enter, day or night. After dark its central dance stage glows with hundreds of paper lanterns donated by local businesses, and its grounds flow directly into Maruyama Park behind.

item.title: Zen Meditation in Kyoto: A Zazen Experience — Guide
item.description: As the historic centre of Rinzai Zen, Kyoto is the best place in Japan to try zazen, the seated meditation at the heart of Zen practice. A number of temples run sessions open to visitors, some in English, in which a monk guides you in the posture, breathing and stillness of zazen in a quiet hall, often followed by a short dharma talk and a bowl of tea. In the traditional style, an attendant may walk the hall with the keisaku, a flat wooden stick used to strike the shoulders — not as punishment but, on request, to restore focus.

item.title: Adventure World: Pandas, Safari and Marine Shows in Shirahama — Guide
item.description: Adventure World, just outside Shirahama, is Wakayama’s biggest family attraction, combining a zoo, a safari park and a marine park on one large site. Its greatest fame comes from its giant pandas: the park has run one of the world’s most successful panda breeding programmes outside China, and is one of only a couple of places in Japan where visitors can see them. Beyond the pandas, a safari zone can be toured by bus, tram or on foot past lions, rhinos and giraffes, while the marine section stages dolphin and orca performances, making for a full and varied family day.

item.title: Akashi Kaikyo Bridge: The World's Longest Suspension Span — Guide
item.description: The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge leaps nearly four kilometres from the Kobe shore to Awaji Island, crossing one of Japan’s fiercest tidal straits on a central span of 1,991 metres — for many years the longest suspension span in the world. Completed in 1998 after a decade of work, it survived the 1995 Kobe earthquake mid-construction, which shifted its towers and lengthened the span by nearly a metre. From the shore it is simply enormous, best seen lit at night; for those who want more, a maintenance walkway beneath the deck and a guided tour to the top of the 297-metre tower are open to visitors.

item.title: Akashi Sea Bream: Japan's Most Prized Tai — Guide
item.description: Akashi-dai, the sea bream caught in the strait between Kobe and Awaji Island, is regarded as the finest in Japan and priced accordingly. The reason is the water: the Akashi Strait funnels enormous tidal flows between the Inland Sea and Osaka Bay, and fish that spend their lives swimming against that current develop dense, firm, well-muscled flesh with a clean sweetness. Restaurants around Akashi serve it every way — sashimi cut thin enough to see the plate through, salt-grilled whole, simmered with soy, and as tai-meshi, rice cooked with the fish and its broth.

item.title: Akashi-yaki: The Egg-Rich Octopus Dumpling — Guide
item.description: Akashi-yaki looks like takoyaki but is a different dish entirely, and locals call it tamagoyaki rather than by its tourist name. The batter is heavy on egg and light on flour, giving a dumpling so soft it barely holds together; inside is a piece of octopus from the Akashi Strait, famous for its firm texture from fighting the tidal currents. Crucially, it is not sauced — each piece is dipped into a bowl of hot dashi broth instead, which makes it lighter and more delicate than its Osaka cousin.

item.title: Arima Onsen: Japan's Oldest Hot Spring, Behind Kobe — Guide
item.description: Arima Onsen lies in a wooded valley behind Mount Rokko, barely half an hour from central Kobe yet feeling like a mountain village. It is one of Japan’s three most ancient hot springs, mentioned in eighth-century chronicles and patronised by emperors and by the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and it is famous for two entirely different waters rising side by side: kinsen, the ‘gold water’, heavily iron-rich and salty, which oxidises to a rust-brown on contact with air, and ginsen, the clear ‘silver water’ carrying carbonate and radium.

item.title: Awaji Hanasajiki: Hillside Flower Fields Above the Sea — Guide
item.description: Hanasajiki — the name means ‘flower balcony’ — is a hillside park on the northern tip of Awaji Island, planted with vast single-colour blocks of flowers that change through the year: rape blossom and poppies in spring, salvia and marigolds in summer, and a famous sweep of cosmos in autumn. The slope faces north-east toward Osaka Bay, so the flowers are seen against sea and sky rather than a backdrop of trees, and paths run right through the plantings.

item.title: Awaji Island Onions: Japan's Sweetest — Guide
item.description: Awaji Island’s onions are a genuine local obsession. The island’s mild maritime climate, long sunshine hours and well-drained sandy soil, combined with a slow curing period hanging in open-sided sheds, produce onions with unusually high sugar and low pungency — sweet enough that Japanese cooks eat them raw in salads where other onions would be too harsh. You will see the drying sheds all over the island, roadside stands selling nets of them for a few hundred yen, and restaurants building whole menus around them: onion burgers, whole roasted onions, onion soup and, inevitably, onion ice cream.

item.title: Caves of the Kii Peninsula: Limestone Caverns and Sea Caves — Guide
item.description: Beneath the mountains and cliffs of the Kii Peninsula lies a hidden world of caves, formed by water working through limestone inland and by the Pacific carving into the coast. The best-known is the sea cave beneath Sandanbeki at Shirahama, reached by lift down through the cliff to a cavern where waves surge in and which local legend links to a hideout of the medieval Kumano navy. Elsewhere, show caves and limestone caverns hung with stalactites offer cool, otherworldly walks, and guided caving tours let more adventurous visitors explore beyond the lit paths.

item.title: Daimonzaka: The Moss-Covered Pilgrim Stairway to Nachi — Guide
item.description: Daimonzaka is the single most beautiful short section of the entire Kumano Kodo: a 600-metre stairway of moss-covered stone steps climbing through a corridor of towering cedars, some of them 800 years old, toward Kumano Nachi Taisha and the falls. Two giant cedars known as the ‘husband and wife trees’ frame the entrance, and the green light filtering down through the canopy gives the climb an unmistakably sacred atmosphere. Taking only about 30 minutes, it lets any visitor walk a genuine stretch of World Heritage pilgrim path — and local shops even rent Heian-period pilgrim costumes for the walk.

item.title: Hashigui-iwa: The Bridge-Pillar Rocks of Kushimoto — Guide
item.description: Hashigui-iwa, on the coast at Kushimoto near the southern tip of Honshu, is one of Wakayama’s most striking natural sights: a line of roughly 40 rock pillars marching some 850 metres out into the sea toward Oshima island, looking uncannily like the surviving piers of a great bridge. Legend credits Kobo Daishi with attempting to build a bridge here in a single night; geology credits softer rock eroding away around harder intrusions.

item.title: Himeji Castle: Japan's Finest Surviving Castle — Guide
item.description: Himeji Castle is the greatest surviving castle in Japan and one of the finest in the world: completed in its present form in 1609, it escaped the fires, sieges, demolition orders and wartime bombing that destroyed almost every other Japanese castle, and stands today entirely original. Its brilliant white plastered walls and layered gables earned it the nickname Shirasagi-jo, the White Heron Castle, and its defensive design — a spiralling maze of gates, walled lanes and dead ends climbing to the six-storey keep — is as impressive as its beauty.

item.title: Himeji Yukata Festival: The Season's First Summer Robes — Guide
item.description: The Himeji Yukata Festival, held over three nights each June, is one of the oldest and largest summer events in western Japan and traditionally the first occasion of the year for wearing a yukata. It began in the eighteenth century, when a newly arrived lord dedicated a shrine and, so the story goes, told townspeople who had no formal dress to come in their light cotton robes instead. Today several hundred thousand people fill the streets below Himeji Castle over three evenings, among hundreds of food stalls, shrine rites and lantern-lit lanes.

item.title: Hydrangea Season in Wakayama: Blue Blooms in the Rains — Guide
item.description: June, the rainy season, is hydrangea (ajisai) season in Japan, and Wakayama’s shrines, temples and hillside gardens fill with thousands of blooms in shifting blues, purples, pinks and whites. Hydrangeas are the flower of the rains — they look their best when wet, the colours deepening and the heavy heads bowing under raindrops — so this is one of the few times when a grey, drizzly day genuinely improves the view.

item.title: Hyogo Prefectural Museum of Art: Tadao Ando on the Waterfront — Guide
item.description: The Hyogo Prefectural Museum of Art is the largest art museum in western Japan and as much an architectural destination as an art one: its building, completed in 2002 by Tadao Ando, is a monumental composition of raw concrete, glass volumes and open external stairways stepping down to the Kobe waterfront, built as part of the city’s cultural recovery after the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake. The collection spans modern Japanese and Western sculpture, prints and painting, and even without a ticket the terraces, stairways and sea-facing spaces are free to explore.

item.title: Hyogo's Museum of Nature and Human Activities — Guide
item.description: The Museum of Nature and Human Activities in Sanda is one of the largest natural history museums in western Japan, built around research collections rather than spectacle. Its halls run from minerals and fossils through the ecology of the Seto Inland Sea to the human shaping of the Hyogo landscape, and its most celebrated subject is close to home: the discovery of the sauropod dinosaur Tambatitanis in the Tamba hills, whose excavation and reconstruction the museum has led.

item.title: Katsuura Tuna: Japan's Great Fresh-Tuna Port — Guide
item.description: Nachikatsuura is Japan’s leading port for fresh, never-frozen tuna, landing more of it than anywhere else in the country thanks to a fleet that uses longlines rather than nets, bringing the fish in whole and undamaged. On most mornings the market floor fills with rows of gleaming tuna as buyers inspect and bid, and visitors can watch the whole auction free from a dedicated gallery above — a genuine working market rather than a show.

item.title: Kinosaki Onsen: The Willow-Lined Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Kinosaki Onsen, on the Sea of Japan coast of northern Hyogo, is the most complete and atmospheric hot spring town in the country. A willow-lined canal runs through its centre, crossed by little stone bridges and flanked by wooden inns, and the whole town is built around a single idea: guests stay in a ryokan but bathe out in the town, wandering between seven public bathhouses in yukata and clattering wooden geta.

item.title: Kinosaki Winter Crab: Matsuba Snow Crab Feasts — Guide
item.description: Between November and March, the hot spring town of Kinosaki turns into one of Japan’s great eating destinations. The Sea of Japan just to the north yields matsuba-gani, the male snow crab landed at nearby ports and tagged by port of origin, and the town’s ryokan build entire multi-course dinners around a single crab: sashimi of translucent raw legs, legs grilled over charcoal until the shell blisters, whole boiled crab, a simmering hotpot, and finally rice porridge cooked in the broth.

item.title: Kishu Ume: Japan's Finest Plums and Umeboshi — Guide
item.description: Wakayama produces the majority of Japan’s ume (Japanese plum), and its Nanko-ume variety, grown above all around Minabe, is considered the finest in the country — large, thin-skinned and fleshy, making umeboshi of exceptional quality. The plum orchards blanket the hills behind the coast, and in February the Minabe-Bairin grove erupts into what locals call ‘a million plum blossoms’, filling the valley with white flowers and scent. Beyond the blossoms, the region offers umeboshi tastings of every degree of saltiness and sweetness, plum wine, and factory visits explaining the long pickling process.

item.title: Kobe Beef: The World's Most Famous Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Kobe beef is the most famous wagyu on earth, and unusually for a global brand it is tightly defined: only carcasses from purebred Tajima cattle, born, raised and slaughtered in Hyogo Prefecture and meeting strict marbling and weight grades, may carry the name — a few thousand animals a year. The Tajima breed from northern Hyogo is the source of that quality, its meat threaded with exceptionally fine marbling that melts at low temperature.

item.title: Kobe Harborland: The Waterfront Heart of the Port City — Guide
item.description: Kobe Harborland is the city’s waterfront playground, a redeveloped stretch of the old docks where shopping centres, restaurants and a lit Ferris wheel line the quays. Across the water in adjoining Meriken Park stand the city’s icons: the lattice-framed red Port Tower and the white steel sails of the Maritime Museum, alongside a preserved section of quay left buckled by the 1995 earthquake as a memorial. Come at dusk, when the towers, ships and mall lights double in the harbour water — it is deservedly rated among Japan’s best night views.

item.title: Kobe Luminarie: Lights of Remembrance — Guide
item.description: Kobe Luminarie is not simply a Christmas illumination. It was created in the winter of 1995, months after the Great Hanshin earthquake killed more than six thousand people and levelled much of the city, as a memorial to the dead and a signal that Kobe would recover. Designed by Italian artists and using techniques from the illuminated festivals of southern Italy, it raises vast arcades and a cathedral-like frontage of hand-painted lightwork over the streets near the old foreign settlement.

item.title: Kobe Matsuri: The City's Great Port Parade — Guide
item.description: Kobe Matsuri is the city’s largest annual celebration, filling the centre for a weekend each May. Descended from a 1930s port festival and reshaped after the war, it is deliberately outward-looking, reflecting a port that has always been Japan’s most international city: the main parade down Flower Road mixes samba troupes in full carnival costume with marching bands, floats, dance teams and community groups from Kobe’s foreign communities. Smaller neighbourhood events run across the city’s wards, and the whole thing is free to watch.

item.title: Kobe's Covered Shopping Arcades: Local Life Under the Roof — Guide
item.description: Behind Kobe’s glossy department stores runs a very different city: long covered shotengai arcades where the shutters are old, the lighting is fluorescent and the shops have been in the same families for generations. Stretching for blocks between Motomachi and Sannomiya and on toward Shinkaichi, they mix greengrocers and fishmongers with secondhand record shops, tiny standing bars, cheap noodle counters and Showa-era cafes. It’s the antidote to the tourist waterfront — cheap, rainproof and full of everyday life, and among the most enjoyable ways to see how Kobe actually lives.

item.title: Kongobu-ji: Head Temple of Shingon Buddhism — Guide
item.description: Kongobu-ji is the head temple of the Koyasan Shingon sect and the administrative centre of the whole mountain, its wide cypress-roofed halls set behind a handsome gate in the middle of the temple town. Inside, a series of chambers is lined with beautiful gold-leaf fusuma sliding screens painted with cranes, willows and the life of Kobo Daishi, including the sombre Willow Room where the warlord Toyotomi Hidetsugu was ordered to commit ritual suicide in 1595.

item.title: Koyasan (Mount Koya): The Sacred Mountain of Shingon Buddhism — Guide
item.description: Koyasan, high in the forested mountains of northern Wakayama, is the spiritual heart of Shingon Buddhism and one of Japan’s most extraordinary places to visit. Founded in 816 by the monk Kukai — posthumously Kobo Daishi — as a remote monastic retreat, the mountaintop basin now holds a whole town of around 100 temples, a World Heritage Site where daily monastic life continues much as it has for twelve centuries. Visitors come to walk the vast cedar-shaded cemetery of Okunoin, see the great halls of the Danjo Garan and Kongobu-ji, and above all to stay overnight in a temple lodging, joining the monks for vegetarian cuisine and dawn prayers.

item.title: Koyasan Candle Festival: 100,000 Lights Along Okunoin — Guide
item.description: The Koyasan Candle Festival (Rosoku Matsuri), held on the evening of August 13th at the start of Obon, is one of Japan’s most moving summer sights. Along the entire two-kilometre approach to Okunoin, from Ichinohashi bridge to Kobo Daishi’s mausoleum, some 100,000 candles are set out and lit by visitors and pilgrims, so that the path through the ancient cedars becomes a shimmering river of small flames winding between 200,000 tombs.

item.title: Koyasan Shukubo: Staying Overnight in a Temple — Guide
item.description: A shukubo stay is the heart of a Koyasan visit: around 50 of the mountain’s temples open their guest wings to travellers, giving visitors a night inside a working monastery. Rooms are simple tatami spaces with futon bedding and sliding screens, often looking onto a beautiful garden; dinner and breakfast are shojin ryori, the refined Buddhist vegetarian cuisine of tofu, mountain vegetables and Koya-dofu served on lacquer trays. Guests are welcome to join the monks for morning prayers at dawn and sometimes a fire ritual, and simply to experience the deep quiet of the mountain once the day visitors have gone.

item.title: Kumano Beef: Wakayama's Mountain-Raised Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Kumano beef (Kumano-gyu) is Wakayama’s premium wagyu brand, raised in small numbers in the mountains of the Kii Peninsula where clean air, pure water and careful feeding produce beef with fine marbling and a notably sweet fat. Because production is small compared with the famous national brands, it is mostly eaten within the region, making it something of a local secret — served as grilled steak, yakiniku, shabu-shabu or in donburi at restaurants around Tanabe, Shingu and the Kumano area.

item.title: Kumano Hayatama Taisha: The Vermilion Shrine of Shingu — Guide
item.description: Kumano Hayatama Taisha stands in the river town of Shingu near the mouth of the Kumano River, the third of the three grand shrines of Kumano and the most vividly coloured: its halls glow in brilliant vermilion, a striking contrast to the unpainted austerity of Hongu. In its grounds grows a sacred nagi tree said to be around 1,000 years old, Japan’s largest, whose leaves pilgrims once carried as talismans for safe travel.

item.title: Kumano Hongu Taisha: Head Shrine of the Kumano Faith — Guide
item.description: Kumano Hongu Taisha is the head shrine of the some 3,000 Kumano shrines across Japan and the spiritual heart of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage, the destination toward which most pilgrims walked. Reached by a stone stairway lined with banners, its cypress-bark-roofed halls stand in dignified, unpainted simplicity beneath tall cedars. A short walk away lies Oyunohara, the shrine’s original site on a river sandbank until a flood destroyed it in 1889, now an empty sacred field approached through the largest torii gate in the world — a colossal steel arch 34 metres high, standing starkly against the sky.

item.title: Kumano's Hot Springs: Yunomine, Kawayu and Watarase — Guide
item.description: The mountains around Kumano Hongu hold some of Japan’s most remarkable hot springs, long used by pilgrims to purify themselves before visiting the grand shrine. Yunomine Onsen, said to be the oldest hot spring in Japan at some 1,800 years, is a tiny village of steaming waters where Tsuboyu — a two-person rock bath in a hut over the stream — is the only bath in the world inscribed as a World Heritage Site.

item.title: Maiko Park: Under the Bridge, Over the Strait — Guide
item.description: Maiko Park occupies the narrow strip of Kobe shoreline directly beneath the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge, and it exists to let you get close to the thing. Its centrepiece is the Maiko Marine Promenade, a walkway built into the bridge structure that carries you 150 metres out over the water on a deck 47 metres up, with glass floor panels looking straight down at the churning tidal currents. In the same grounds stands the Ijokaku, a striking octagonal green villa built in 1915 for a Chinese merchant, along with pines, sea views and picnic lawns.

item.title: Nachi Falls and Kumano Nachi Taisha: Japan's Iconic Waterfall View — Guide
item.description: Nachi Falls, plunging 133 metres in a single unbroken drop, is the tallest waterfall of its kind in Japan and has been worshipped as a deity since before recorded history — the origin of the Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine that stands on the slope above. The classic view, one of Japan’s most reproduced images, sets the vermilion three-storied pagoda of the neighbouring Seiganto-ji temple against the white column of falling water.

item.title: Nachi Fire Festival: Flaming Torches Before the Waterfall — Guide
item.description: The Nachi Fire Festival (Nachi no Ogi Matsuri), held every year on July 14th, is one of Japan’s three great fire festivals and the most dramatic event of the Kumano year. Twelve towering fan-shaped mikoshi — representing the twelve deities of Kumano Nachi Taisha and decorated with red silk fans and mirrors — are carried down to the foot of Nachi Falls, where they are met by priests in white swinging twelve enormous burning torches weighing some 50 kilos each.

item.title: Nada Sake Blending Workshop: Make Your Own Bottle — Guide
item.description: Blending — deciding how different tanks are combined into the final product — is one of the quiet arts of sake brewing, and a few Nada breweries now let visitors try it. You are given a set of base sakes that differ in rice variety, yeast, polishing ratio and age, a measuring cylinder and a tasting glass, and talked through how each component behaves: one contributing aroma, another body, another acidity or a dry finish.

item.title: Nada Sake District: Japan's Greatest Brewing Quarter — Guide
item.description: Nada, a narrow coastal strip running east from Kobe, is the greatest sake-brewing district in Japan, producing roughly a quarter of the country’s entire output. Its dominance comes from a rare combination: Miyamizu, a hard mineral-rich spring water that drives vigorous fermentation, the celebrated Yamada Nishiki rice grown in the Hyogo hills behind, and cold winter winds off Mount Rokko. The five brewing villages known collectively as Nadagogo hold a dozen brewery museums within walking or cycling distance of one another, most of them free, each with a tasting counter and a shop.

item.title: Nankinmachi: Kobe's Chinatown — Guide
item.description: Nankinmachi, Kobe’s Chinatown, is one of only three in Japan and grew from the Chinese merchant community that settled here after the port opened to foreign trade in 1868. Compact and lively, it centres on a small square with an ornate pavilion, entered through vivid red-and-gold gates and lined with lanterns overhead. The real draw is the street food: stalls and shopfronts sell steaming buta-man pork buns, dumplings, fried noodles, sweet sesame balls and roast duck, and the pleasure is simply to graze your way through the lanes with something hot in each hand.

item.title: Nunobiki Falls: Four Waterfalls Minutes from Central Kobe — Guide
item.description: Nunobiki Falls is one of the most remarkable things about Kobe: a chain of four waterfalls, celebrated in classical Japanese poetry for over a thousand years and counted among the country’s finest, sitting barely fifteen minutes' walk from a Shinkansen station. A shaded stone path climbs from behind Shin-Kobe Station past the Mendaki, Ondaki, Tsuzumigadaki and Meotodaki falls, the largest dropping some 43 metres into a green pool. Keep climbing and the trail reaches a viewing plaza over the city, the Nunobiki Herb Garden and a ropeway back down.

item.title: Oji Zoo: Kobe's Family Zoo Under the Cherry Trees — Guide
item.description: Oji Zoo is Kobe’s much-loved city zoo, a compact and refreshingly inexpensive place set in parkland between Nada and Sannomiya. Its collection covers the usual favourites — elephants, big cats, giraffes and a well-known group of koalas — alongside a small old-fashioned amusement corner with rides for younger children and a preserved Meiji-era Western residence in the grounds. In spring the zoo’s cherry trees make it one of the best hanami spots in central Kobe, when families picnic under the blossoms between animal enclosures.

item.title: Okunoin: Japan's Largest Cemetery Beneath the Cedars — Guide
item.description: Okunoin is the spiritual climax of Koyasan and the largest cemetery in Japan: a two-kilometre path winding beneath towering, centuries-old cedars past some 200,000 tombstones, memorials and mossy stupas, from feudal lords and famous samurai to company memorials and modern graves. At its far end stands the Gobyo, the mausoleum of Kobo Daishi, who is believed by the faithful not to have died but to rest in eternal meditation, awaiting the future Buddha — monks still carry him meals twice daily.

item.title: River Rafting in Wakayama: Rapids Through the Kii Gorges — Guide
item.description: The steep, forested gorges of the Kii Peninsula channel a series of fast, remarkably clear rivers that make Wakayama one of the best river-sports destinations in western Japan. Guided rafting trips run through rapids framed by cliffs and cedar forest, with operators offering everything from gentle family-friendly floats to genuinely exciting whitewater, while canyoning and the traditional log-raft rides of the Kitayama River add further variety. The water is famously clear, the scenery is superb, and the mountain setting keeps things cool through the summer months when trips are at their peak.

item.title: Sakoshi: A Preserved Harbour Village on the Inland Sea — Guide
item.description: Sakoshi, a small harbour village on a sheltered bay near Ako in western Hyogo, is one of the quietest and most atmospheric old townscapes on the Seto Inland Sea. It prospered in the Edo period as a port of call for the kitamaebune coastal trading ships, and that wealth built the white-plastered merchant houses, storehouses and lanes that survive along its main street today. Its landmarks are a working sake brewery that has operated here for centuries and now welcomes visitors, and the hillside Osake Shrine overlooking the bay — a rewarding, uncrowded stop for anyone drawn to old Japan.

item.title: Shirahama: White Sand Beach and Ancient Hot Springs — Guide
item.description: Shirahama, on Wakayama’s southwestern coast, is one of Japan’s oldest and most popular hot-spring resorts, its name literally meaning ‘white beach’. Shirarahama Beach curves for 600 metres in dazzling white sand — famously replenished with sand from Australia — while the town’s onsen are among the three oldest in Japan, recorded in 7th-century chronicles as a retreat for emperors. Beyond the beach lie dramatic coastal sights: the sheer cliffs of Sandanbeki, the sunset-framed sea arch of Engetsuto island, and Saki-no-yu, a rustic open-air bath set on the rocks where waves break metres away.

item.title: Sorakuen Garden: Kobe's Finest Traditional Garden — Guide
item.description: Sorakuen is the finest traditional Japanese garden in Kobe, laid out in the Meiji era as the private grounds of a former city mayor and opened to the public after the war. Its winding paths circle a pond fed by a waterfall, passing through groves of pine, camphor and maple in the middle of the modern city. Two unusual buildings share the grounds: the Hassam House, a Western-style villa built for a British trader in Kobe’s foreign settlement, and a rare surviving feudal-lord’s stable relocated here — and each May the garden’s several thousand azaleas turn it brilliant.

item.title: Taiji: Whale Watching and Whaling Heritage — Guide
