item.description: Taiji, a small harbour town on Wakayama’s southeast coast, has one of the most complicated relationships with whales of anywhere in Japan: organised whaling began here in the early 1600s and shaped the town’s entire identity, while today it also runs whale- and dolphin-watching boats into the rich Kumano-nada waters offshore. The Taiji Whale Museum documents this long history with skeletons, historic whaling equipment and displays on the town’s traditions, and also keeps live cetaceans.

item.title: Taisanji Temple: A National Treasure in Kobe's Western Hills — Guide
item.description: Taisanji sits in a forested valley in Kobe’s Nishi Ward, far enough from the city that most visitors never hear of it — which is a pity, because its main hall, rebuilt in 1293 after a fire, is a designated National Treasure and one of the finest medieval buildings in the Kansai region. The wooded grounds hold a vermilion three-storey pagoda, an Important Cultural Property gate, sub-temples and a strolling garden, and the surrounding valley turns brilliant with maples in late autumn.

item.title: Takarazuka Grand Theater: Japan's All-Female Revue — Guide
item.description: The Takarazuka Revue is one of the most singular institutions in Japanese theatre: founded in 1914 to draw passengers to a new railway line, it stages lavish musicals — European romances, historical epics, manga adaptations and glittering revue finales — performed entirely by women. Its five troupes are led by otokoyaku, actresses who specialise in male roles and command extraordinary devotion from a largely female audience. The 2,500-seat Grand Theater in Takarazuka is its home, and the whole town around it, with its rose-lined avenue and theatre shops, revolves around the company.

item.title: Takeda Castle Ruins: The Castle in the Sea of Clouds — Guide
item.description: Takeda Castle is one of Japan’s most photographed ruins, and deservedly so. Built in the 15th century on a narrow ridge 353 metres above the Asago valley and abandoned around 1600, all that survives is its remarkable stonework — tiers of ramparts, bailey walls and gate foundations tracing the whole plan of the castle along the mountaintop. On calm, cold mornings in autumn, mist pools in the valley below and the ruins stand clear above a white sea of cloud, an image that has earned it the nicknames ‘Japan’s Machu Picchu’ and ‘the castle in the sky’.

item.title: Tamba-yaki: 800 Years of Unglazed Stoneware — Guide
item.description: Tamba-yaki is one of the Six Ancient Kilns of Japan, the handful of pottery centres that have fired continuously since the medieval period, and its kilns have been working in the hills of Tamba-Sasayama for roughly 800 years. The style is defined by what it refuses to add: no applied glaze, the surfaces instead coloured by wood ash falling on the clay in long climbing-kiln firings, producing greens, browns and glassy runs no two of which are alike.

item.title: Tanabe: Castle Ruins and the Gateway to the Kumano Kodo — Guide
item.description: Tanabe, a port town on Wakayama’s western coast, is best known today as the main gateway to the Kumano Kodo, where most pilgrims begin their journey and where the excellent Kumano Tourism Bureau helps foreign walkers arrange routes and lodging. The town itself rewards a wander: the stone walls and water gate of Tanabe Castle survive near the harbour, Morihei Ueshiba, the founder of aikido, was born here and is remembered at a memorial hall, and after dark the narrow lanes of the Aji-koji district fill with small izakaya serving the day’s catch.

item.title: The Kako River Wetlands: Birds and Riverside Paths — Guide
item.description: The Kako River is the longest river in Hyogo, and where it widens toward the Seto Inland Sea at Kakogawa it becomes something quietly rewarding: a broad, shallow, braided channel of reed beds, gravel bars and shifting sandbanks. Herons and egrets stalk the shallows all year, and autumn and winter bring ducks, waders and other migrants down onto the open water. Level, well-surfaced paths run for kilometres along both banks, making this one of the easiest places in the prefecture for an unhurried walk or a flat cycle ride with a hire bike.

item.title: The Kasumi Coast: Sea Cliffs and Caves of the San'in Geopark — Guide
item.description: The Kasumi coast, on the Sea of Japan shore of northern Hyogo, is the finest coastal scenery in the prefecture and part of the San’in Kaigan UNESCO Global Geopark. Millions of years of volcanic rock and relentless northern swell have carved the shoreline into columned cliffs, arches, sea caves and pine-topped islets standing in strikingly clear green water. Small sightseeing boats thread among them from the fishing harbour, clifftop paths link viewpoints along the shore, and the same port that draws visitors in summer lands the snow crab that fills the town’s inns in winter.

item.title: The Kumano Kodo: Japan's Ancient Pilgrimage Trails — Guide
item.description: The Kumano Kodo is a network of ancient pilgrimage routes threading the mountains of the Kii Peninsula, walked for over a thousand years by emperors, monks and commoners alike on their way to the three grand shrines of Kumano. Registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site — one of only two pilgrimage routes in the world so listed, alongside Spain’s Camino de Santiago — its stone-paved paths climb through deep cedar forest, past moss-covered oji shrines and mountain hamlets.

item.title: Wakayama Castle: Stronghold of a Tokugawa Branch — Guide
item.description: Wakayama Castle stands on Torafusu Hill in the middle of the prefectural capital, founded in 1585 by Toyotomi Hidenaga, brother of Hideyoshi, and later the seat of the Kishu Tokugawa — one of the three branch families of the shogunal house, from which the eighth shogun Yoshimune came. Its keep was destroyed in the war and rebuilt in concrete in 1958, but the extensive stone walls, gates and the winding hilltop layout remain impressive, and the Nishinomaru garden below, with its pond, teahouse and vermilion Ohashi covered bridge, is one of the finest in the region.

item.title: Wakayama Mikan: Japan's Mandarin Orange Capital — Guide
item.description: Wakayama is Japan’s leading producer of mikan (satsuma mandarin), and the fruit is woven into the prefecture’s identity: the warm, sunny hillsides above the Kii coast are terraced with orange groves that turn the slopes brilliant orange from late autumn, and the region’s Arida district is one of the most famous mikan names in the country. From October through winter, orchards around Arida, Yuasa and the coast open for all-you-can-pick sessions, and roadside stands sell fruit picked that morning — sweeter and juicier than anything found in a supermarket.

item.title: Wakayama Ramen: The Pork-and-Soy Bowl of Kishu — Guide
item.description: Wakayama ramen, known to locals simply as chuka soba, is one of Japan’s classic regional bowls: a broth blending pork bones and soy sauce into something rich, dark brown and deeply savoury, served with thin straight noodles, chashu pork, menma and spring onion. Its most charming tradition is the counter service: bowls of hayazushi (pressed mackerel sushi) and boiled eggs sit ready on the table, and diners help themselves while waiting, paying by the honour system at the end.

item.title: Wakayama's Marine Museums and Aquariums: Life of the Kuroshio — Guide
item.description: The Kii Peninsula’s coast is washed by the warm Kuroshio current, which carries subtropical marine life far north and makes Wakayama’s waters some of the richest in Japan — home to coral, sea turtles and an enormous variety of fish. The prefecture’s marine museums and aquariums showcase this abundance, with displays on the Kuroshio ecosystem, coral communities and the loggerhead sea turtles that nest on local beaches, alongside touch pools and conservation exhibits.

item.title: Akahada Ware: Nara's Tea-Ceremony Pottery — Guide
item.description: Akahada ware (Akahada-yaki) is the traditional pottery of Nara, made for centuries at kilns on the slopes of Mount Akahada near Yamatokoriyama. Counted among the celebrated ‘Enshu Seven Kilns’ favoured by tea masters, it is a warm, understated stoneware with a soft cream or reddish glaze, prized for tea-ceremony bowls and vessels. A distinctive local style decorates the pieces with ‘Nara-e’ — charming hand-painted pictures of Nara’s deer, Buddhist figures and landscapes — giving the ware a gentle, storytelling character.

item.title: Asuka-nabe: The Ancient Milk Hot Pot of Asuka — Guide
item.description: Asuka-nabe is one of Japan’s most unusual regional hot pots: a chicken-and-vegetable nabe simmered in a broth enriched with milk, giving it a mellow, creamy character unlike any other Japanese pot. Its origins are traced to the Asuka period over 1,300 years ago, when dairy foods and cattle-keeping were introduced to Japan from the Asian mainland via the imperial court based in Asuka — making this humble dish a living echo of Japan’s very first encounter with milk.

item.title: Asuka: Cradle of the Japanese State and Its Ancient Tombs — Guide
item.description: Asuka, a quiet farming village south of Kashihara, was the political heart of Japan in the 6th and 7th centuries, before the capital moved to Nara — the era when Buddhism and continental culture first took root and the imperial state was forged. Its gentle countryside is scattered with the enigmatic remains of that dawn age: ancient temple sites, mysterious carved granite stones whose purpose is still debated, decorated tomb mounds, and above all the Ishibutai Kofun, a monumental 7th-century burial chamber whose earth mound has eroded away to reveal enormous megaliths, the largest weighing some 77 tons.

item.title: Firefly Viewing in Nara: Summer Evenings by the Water — Guide
item.description: For a few weeks in early summer, usually late May into June, Nara offers one of Japan’s most magical fleeting sights: the soft glow of fireflies (hotaru) drifting over its ponds and waterways after dark. The gentle streams and clean water around the old capital — from the reflective Sarusawa Pond with its Ukimido pavilion to Isuien’s garden channels and the quiet moats and rivers on the city’s fringes — provide the still, unpolluted habitat these luminous insects need.

item.title: Gangoji: The Ancient Temple Within Naramachi — Guide
item.description: Gangoji is one of Nara’s quietest World Heritage treasures, tucked into the lanes of Naramachi — the merchant quarter that in fact grew up within this once-vast temple’s former grounds. Gangoji traces its origins to Asuka-dera, Japan’s very first full-scale Buddhist temple founded in 588, and when the capital moved to Nara the temple moved with it. Though far smaller today, its main hall (Gokurakubo) is a National Treasure, and remarkably some of its roof still bears original tiles from the Asuka period, over 1,400 years old — among the oldest roofing in the world — making a modest visit a brush with the very dawn of Japanese Buddhism.

item.title: Hasedera: The Flower Temple and Its Grand Stairway — Guide
item.description: Hasedera, in the mountains of eastern Nara near Sakurai, is one of Japan’s great flower temples and the head of the Buzan Shingon school. Its signature is the Noboriro, a magnificent roofed corridor of 399 stone steps that climbs the hillside beneath hanging lanterns to the main hall, which stands on a stilted veranda overlooking the valley in the manner of Kiyomizu-dera. Inside towers a magnificent 10-metre-plus gilded statue of Kannon, the goddess of mercy — one of the largest wooden statues in Japan.

item.title: Heijo Palace: The Heart of Japan's Ancient Capital — Guide
item.description: Heijo Palace was the political and ceremonial heart of Heijo-kyo, Japan’s capital through most of the 8th-century Nara period, and its vast excavated site — a green plain on the northern edge of the city — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Long left as archaeological fields, it has been brought vividly to life by full-scale reconstructions: the towering vermilion Suzakumon main gate, the majestic Daigokuden (Former Imperial Audience Hall) where the emperor once held state ceremonies, and a garden and excellent museums explaining daily life in the ancient capital.

item.title: Horyuji: The World's Oldest Wooden Buildings — Guide
item.description: Horyuji, in the quiet town of Ikaruga southwest of Nara, is one of the most important temples in Japan and among the most significant in the Buddhist world: founded by Prince Shotoku, the great early patron of Japanese Buddhism, in 607, its central Kondo (Golden Hall) and five-story pagoda are the oldest surviving wooden buildings anywhere on Earth, standing for over 1,300 years. Registered in 1993 as one of Japan’s first UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the temple preserves an unrivalled trove of early Buddhist art and architecture across its Western and Eastern precincts, a serene pilgrimage into the very origins of Japanese civilisation.

item.title: Isuien and Yoshikien: Nara Park's Strolling Gardens — Guide
item.description: Tucked beside the bustle of Nara Park near Todaiji lie two of the city’s loveliest Japanese gardens. Isuien is a classic strolling garden built around ponds and teahouses, celebrated for its masterful use of shakkei, ‘borrowed scenery’, framing the distant Todaiji Nandaimon gate and the green hills of Mount Wakakusa within its own composition — different in every season and paired with the fine Neiraku Museum of ancient art. Next door, Yoshikien offers three distinct gardens — a pond garden, a moss garden and a tea-ceremony garden — in a compact, tranquil space that most visitors miss.

item.title: Kakinoha-zushi: Nara's Persimmon-Leaf Sushi — Guide
item.description: Kakinoha-zushi is the signature sushi of landlocked Nara, especially the Yoshino mountains, and a clever solution to an old problem: with the sea far away, salted mackerel (and now salmon) was pressed with vinegared rice and wrapped in a persimmon leaf, whose natural antibacterial qualities preserved the fish and lent it a subtle aroma. The result is a neat, leaf-wrapped parcel of pressed sushi, unwrapped like a small gift, with a firm bite and clean, slightly tart flavour that keeps well — traditionally made for festivals and now a beloved everyday specialty sold in shops and stations across the prefecture.

item.title: Kashihara Jingu: Shrine of Japan's First Emperor — Guide
item.description: Kashihara Jingu, at the foot of Mount Unebi in southern Nara, is one of Japan’s most important modern shrines, built in 1890 on the legendary spot where, according to myth, Emperor Jimmu — the first emperor of Japan — acceded to the throne and founded the nation in 660 BC. Its grand halls of unpainted hinoki cypress, some relocated from the Kyoto Imperial Palace, stand within vast, serene wooded grounds designed as a national sanctuary.

item.title: Kasuga Mantoro: The Lantern-Lighting of Kasuga Taisha — Guide
item.description: The Mantoro (literally ‘ten thousand lanterns’) is one of Nara’s most magical events, held at Kasuga Taisha twice a year — at Setsubun in early February and during Obon in mid-August. On these evenings, all of the shrine’s roughly 3,000 lanterns are lit at once: the some 2,000 moss-covered stone lanterns lining the forest approach and the around 1,000 bronze lanterns hanging from the vermilion halls, each flame an offering from worshippers over the centuries.

item.title: Kasuga Taisha: The Lantern Shrine in the Sacred Forest — Guide
item.description: Kasuga Taisha, founded in 768 as the tutelary shrine of the powerful Fujiwara clan, is one of Nara’s most atmospheric sites: a vivid vermilion shrine set deep within the Kasugayama primeval forest, reached along a wooded approach lined with some 2,000 moss-covered stone lanterns. Inside, around a thousand bronze lanterns hang from the eaves, and twice a year — at Setsubun in February and Obon in August — all 3,000 are lit at once for the Mantoro festival, filling the shrine with flickering gold.

item.title: Kasugayama Primeval Forest: Nara's Sacred Ancient Woodland — Guide
item.description: Rising behind Kasuga Taisha, the Kasugayama Primeval Forest is one of the most remarkable green spaces in Japan: a genuine virgin forest protected since 841, when hunting and logging were banned to honour the shrine’s gods, and left untouched for nearly 1,200 years. The result is a rare surviving lowland primeval woodland of towering evergreens, ancient cedars and dense undergrowth, alive with birds and deer, forming part of Nara’s World Heritage listing.

item.title: Kofukuji: The Five-Story Pagoda of Nara — Guide
item.description: Kofukuji, founded by the Fujiwara clan and moved to Nara in 710, was once among the most powerful temples in Japan, and its five-story pagoda — at 50 metres the second-tallest wooden pagoda in the country — is an icon of the city, rising beside Sarusawa Pond at the very entrance to Nara Park. Beyond the pagoda and the rebuilt Central Golden Hall, the temple’s greatest treasure is its National Treasure Museum, home to a celebrated collection of ancient Buddhist sculpture including the beloved three-faced, six-armed Ashura statue, one of Japan’s most admired religious artworks.

item.title: Mitarai Gorge: Emerald Pools and Suspension Bridges — Guide
item.description: Mitarai Gorge, in the mountain village of Tenkawa deep in southern Nara, is one of the prefecture’s most beautiful natural landscapes: a river ravine of astonishingly clear, emerald-green water tumbling over falls and gathering in jewel-like pools between forested cliffs. A well-built riverside trail follows the gorge, crossing swaying suspension bridges and passing viewpoints over the vivid water, cool and shaded even in high summer. Rated among Japan’s most beautiful walking spots and part of the Yoshino-Kumano National Park, it rewards hikers with fresh green in early summer and spectacular maple colour in autumn.

item.title: Miwa Somen: The Birthplace of Japan's Thin Noodles — Guide
item.description: The Miwa region around Sakurai, at the foot of sacred Mount Miwa, is considered the birthplace of somen, the ultra-thin white wheat noodles now eaten across Japan. Local tradition holds that noodle-making began here some 1,200 years ago near Omiwa Shrine, and the area’s makers still hand-stretch the dough into fine threads dried in the winter air, a craft prized for its delicate, firm texture. Miwa somen is enjoyed two ways: chilled and dipped in cold tsuyu on hot summer days (sometimes as flowing nagashi-somen caught from bamboo flumes), or warm in a soothing nyumen broth in the colder months.

item.title: Mount Ikoma: Retro Cable Cars and City Night Views — Guide
item.description: Mount Ikoma, rising on the border between Nara and Osaka, is a fun and nostalgic mountain escape easily reached from either city. It’s climbed by the Ikoma Cable Car, the oldest cable railway in Japan (opened 1918), whose famously quirky cars are shaped like a cat (Mike) and a dog (Bull) — a hit with children. At the top sit the charmingly retro Ikoma Sanjo Amusement Park, one of Japan’s oldest, and the atmospheric Hozanji temple on the slope below.

item.title: Mount Odaigahara: Nara's Wild Rooftop Wilderness — Guide
item.description: Mount Odaigahara, straddling the Nara–Mie border deep in the Yoshino-Kumano National Park, is one of the wildest and most beautiful high places in western Japan — and one of the rainiest spots in the whole country, which cloaks it in lush, moss-draped primeval forest. A road climbs to a trailhead at around 1,570 metres, from which well-made loop trails (including boardwalks over fragile terrain) lead through ancient woodland, past the dramatic Daijagura cliff viewpoint with its vast panorama, and to the summit of Hidegatake.

item.title: Mount Wakakusa: The Grassy Hill Above Nara — Guide
item.description: Mount Wakakusa (Wakakusayama) is the smooth, grassy hill that rises directly behind Nara Park’s temples, its bare turf standing out against the wooded slopes around it. A gentle climb up its open grassland — where deer graze freely — leads in about 30–40 minutes to a summit with one of the finest panoramas in the region, taking in Todaiji, Kofukuji’s pagoda, the whole city of Nara and the mountains beyond, especially magical at sunset.

item.title: Mount Yoshino: Japan's Greatest Cherry-Blossom Mountain — Guide
item.description: Mount Yoshino (Yoshinoyama), in southern Nara, is celebrated as the greatest cherry-blossom destination in all of Japan: some 30,000 cherry trees, planted over more than a thousand years as sacred offerings, cover its slopes and bloom each spring in staggered waves that climb the mountain from the Shimo (lower) grove to the Oku (upper) grove over about two weeks. The effect — whole ridgelines washed in shifting pink, dotted with temples and shrines — is breathtaking, and the mountain is also a sacred centre of Shugendo mountain asceticism and part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

item.title: Muroji: The Mountain Temple of Women — Guide
item.description: Muroji, hidden in the wooded mountains of eastern Nara near Uda, is one of the prefecture’s most atmospheric temples, an ancient Shingon complex set beside a mountain stream and climbing the forested slope on moss-covered stone stairways. It became known as the ‘Women’s Koya’ (Nyonin Koya) because, unlike the great monastery of Mount Koya, it welcomed women pilgrims. Its jewel is a small, exquisitely proportioned five-story pagoda, among the oldest and smallest in Japan, and the temple is celebrated for its natural setting — a blaze of rhododendrons in spring, fresh green in summer and brilliant maple colour in autumn.

item.title: Nakatanidou: Nara's High-Speed Mochi Pounding — Guide
item.description: Nakatanidou, a small mochi shop near Sarusawa Pond in central Nara, has become one of the city’s most popular attractions thanks to its jaw-dropping high-speed mochi pounding (kosokumochitsuki). Several times a day, its artisans perform the traditional mochitsuki with breathtaking rhythm and speed — one wielding the heavy wooden mallet in a blur of strikes, the other flipping the sticky rice by hand between blows, the crowd counting along in astonishment.

item.title: Nara Fude: The Calligraphy Brushes of the Ancient Capital — Guide
item.description: Nara fude (calligraphy brushes) are among Japan’s most esteemed, a craft that arrived with Buddhism and brush-writing in the 8th century and has been refined in the old capital ever since. Making a fine brush is exacting handwork: hairs from goats, horses, weasels and other animals are sorted, cleaned, blended in precise proportions and bundled by hand into a tip that holds ink perfectly and springs back with just the right resilience — qualities calligraphers prize above all.

item.title: Nara National Museum: Masterpieces of Buddhist Art — Guide
item.description: The Nara National Museum, set within Nara Park, is Japan’s premier museum of Buddhist art, its elegant Meiji-era Main Building and modern galleries housing a superb permanent collection of Buddhist statues, paintings, sutras and ritual objects spanning centuries. Its most famous event is the annual Shosoin Exhibition each autumn, when a rotating selection of the fabled 8th-century treasures of the Shosoin — the imperial repository at Todaiji, holding artifacts from along the Silk Road — goes on rare public display, drawing visitors from across the country.

item.title: Nara Park and Its Sacred Deer: Meeting the Bowing Deer — Guide
item.description: Nara Park is a vast green expanse at the heart of the old capital, home to Todaiji, Kasuga Taisha and Kofukuji — and to over a thousand wild sika deer that wander freely among the temples and lawns. Revered for centuries as sacred messengers of the gods of Kasuga Shrine and now designated a natural treasure, the deer are Nara’s most beloved sight: gentle, bold and famous for bowing their heads to request the shika-senbei crackers sold at stalls throughout the park.

item.title: Nara Persimmons: Kaki, Dried Fruit and Leaf-Wrapped Sushi — Guide
item.description: Nara is one of Japan’s foremost producers of kaki (persimmon), its warm valleys — especially around Gojo and the Yoshino foothills — filled with orchards that turn brilliant orange each autumn. The fruit runs deep in local culture: eaten fresh and crisp in autumn, slowly air-dried into intensely sweet, chewy hoshigaki (dried persimmon) hung in curtains under the eaves, worked into wagashi and jams, and even its leaves are used to wrap the region’s famous kakinoha-zushi.

item.title: Nara Sake: The Birthplace of Refined Sake — Guide
item.description: Nara has a strong claim to be the birthplace of modern refined sake: it was in the temples of Nara, above all Shoryaku-ji, that the techniques for brewing clear, filtered sake (as opposed to cloudy doburoku) were perfected in the 15th century, in the style known as sobo-shu that shaped all Japanese sake that followed. The prefecture remains a distinguished brewing region, its historic kura clustered in Naramachi and towns across the Yamato plain, several producing celebrated labels.

item.title: Nara Sumi Ink and Calligraphy: The Craft of Black Ink — Guide
item.description: Nara is the historic heart of Japanese sumi ink-making, producing the great majority of the country’s traditional ink sticks (nara-zumi) for around 600 years. The craft is beautifully simple and painstaking: fine soot collected from burning oils or pine is kneaded with animal glue and fragrance, pressed in wooden moulds, and slowly dried over weeks into the solid ink sticks that are ground with water on a stone inkstone to make ink for calligraphy and painting.

item.title: Naramachi: The Old Merchant Quarter — Guide
item.description: Naramachi, spreading south from Sarusawa Pond and Kofukuji, is the former merchant district of Nara, a well-preserved warren of narrow lanes lined with traditional machiya townhouses — deep, wooden merchant homes with latticed facades that grew up in the grounds of the vanished Gangoji temple. Today the quarter is one of Nara’s most enjoyable strolls, its historic buildings converted into stylish cafes, craft boutiques, sake shops, galleries and small museums, including a restored machiya open to visitors and a shop of the red ‘migawari-zaru’ good-luck monkey charms that hang from the eaves throughout the district.

item.title: Narazuke: Nara's Amber Sake-Lees Pickles — Guide
item.description: Narazuke are Nara’s celebrated sake-lees pickles, one of the city’s oldest food traditions, dating back over a thousand years to when temple brewers preserved vegetables in the fragrant lees (kasu) left over from making sake. Melon, cucumber, ginger, gourd and other vegetables are repeatedly re-pickled in fresh sake lees over months or even years, slowly turning a deep translucent amber and taking on a complex, richly aromatic flavour — sweet, savoury, and distinctly boozy.

item.title: Omiwa Shrine: Japan's Oldest Shrine and Its Sacred Mountain — Guide
item.description: Omiwa Shrine (Oomiwa) near Sakurai is often called the oldest shrine in Japan, and it preserves the most ancient form of Shinto worship: it has no honden, no main sanctuary building, because the object of worship is Mount Miwa itself, the sacred conical mountain rising behind it, revered as the dwelling of the deity since before recorded history. Worshippers pray at a hall facing the mountain, passing beneath one of Japan’s largest torii gates.

item.title: Omizutori: The Fire and Water Rites of Todaiji — Guide
item.description: Omizutori is the popular name for Shuni-e, a series of sacred Buddhist rites held at Todaiji’s Nigatsudo hall over the first two weeks of March, and one of Japan’s oldest ceremonies — performed every year without interruption since 752, over 1,270 years. Its most spectacular moment is the Otaimatsu each evening, when monks race along the hall’s wooden veranda swinging enormous flaming pine torches, showering embers over the crowd gathered below (sparks are said to bring good luck and blessing).

item.title: Shika no Tsunokiri: Nara's Deer Antler-Cutting Ceremony — Guide
item.description: Shika no Tsunokiri (deer antler-cutting) is a traditional autumn ceremony held near Kasuga Taisha since the 17th century, when the sacred stags of Nara Park have their antlers safely removed before the rutting season. During autumn the bucks grow aggressive and their sharp antlers can injure people and other deer, so in this ritual — part animal management, part spectacle — Shinto-costumed handlers (seko) chase and catch a stag with ropes in a wooden arena, calm it, and a priest ceremonially saws off the antlers as an offering.

item.title: Soni Highland: Silver Seas of Autumn Pampas Grass — Guide
item.description: Soni Kogen (Soni Highland), on a mountain plateau in far-eastern Nara near Uda, is one of Japan’s most beautiful grassland landscapes, especially in autumn. Across some 38 hectares of gently sloping upland, vast fields of susuki (Japanese pampas grass) grow head-high and, from late September through November, ripen to a silvery gold that shimmers and ripples in waves under the wind and low autumn sun. Well-made trails climb through the grass to viewpoints over the plateau and surrounding peaks, and at dusk the backlit silver plumes are unforgettable — a favourite of photographers and one of Nara’s great natural spectacles.

item.title: Tanzan Shrine: The Wooden Pagoda in the Autumn Hills — Guide
item.description: Tanzan Shrine, tucked into the wooded mountains south of Sakurai, is one of Nara’s most beautiful hidden gems, dedicated to Fujiwara no Kamatari, founder of the mighty Fujiwara clan, whose plot to reform the state was supposedly hatched on this mountain. Its treasure is unique: a graceful vermilion thirteen-story wooden pagoda, the only one of its kind surviving anywhere in the world, rising in tiers among the trees. The shrine is above all an autumn destination, when some 3,000 maple trees set the mountainside ablaze in reds and golds around the pagoda, one of the finest foliage sights in the Kansai region.

item.title: Tea Ceremony in Nara: Matcha in the Ancient Capital — Guide
item.description: Nara, the cradle of much of Japan’s early culture, is a wonderfully calm and uncrowded place to experience the Japanese tea ceremony (sado). Away from Kyoto’s bustle, tea houses, temple sub-temples, garden pavilions and restored machiya in and around Naramachi welcome beginners into serene tatami rooms to learn the etiquette, watch a host prepare thick or thin matcha, and whisk a bowl of their own. Sessions are often paired with seasonal wagashi — sometimes the local kuzumochi or persimmon sweets — and with Nara’s own Yamato tea, making the experience a gentle, deeply rooted encounter with Japanese hospitality and aesthetics.

item.title: Todaiji and the Great Buddha: Nara's Colossal Temple — Guide
item.description: Todaiji is the grandest of Nara’s temples and one of Japan’s most awe-inspiring sights: founded in 752 as the head of all provincial Buddhist temples, it houses the Daibutsu, a 15-metre seated bronze Great Buddha, one of the largest bronze statues in the world, enshrined within the Daibutsuden — for centuries the largest wooden building on earth. The approach passes through the towering Nandaimon gate, guarded by a pair of ferocious 8-metre Nio guardian statues carved in the 13th century, while sacred deer roam the grounds.

item.title: Toshodaiji: The Temple of the Blind Master Ganjin — Guide
item.description: Toshodaiji, in Nishinokyo near Yakushiji, was founded in 759 by Ganjin (Jianzhen), the revered Chinese monk who, after five failed attempts and the loss of his eyesight, finally reached Japan to establish proper Buddhist ordination — a story of extraordinary devotion. His temple is one of Nara’s most serene: its Kondo (Golden Hall), built in the classical Tenpyo style with a colonnade of eight great pillars, is considered one of the most beautiful ancient buildings in Japan, and the temple grounds, quieter and more wooded than most, hold a lacquered seated statue of Ganjin himself, a National Treasure shown to the public just a few days each year.

item.title: Wakakusa Yamayaki: Nara's Mountain-Burning Fire Festival — Guide
item.description: The Wakakusa Yamayaki, held on the fourth Saturday of January, is one of Nara’s oldest and most spectacular festivals: after nightfall, the entire dry grassy dome of Mount Wakakusa behind Nara Park is deliberately set on fire, its whole slope glowing red and orange against the winter dark. The blaze is preceded by a large fireworks display over the hill, making a rare and dramatic combination of fireworks and mountain fire.

item.title: Yakushiji: The Twin-Pagoda Temple of Nishinokyo — Guide
item.description: Yakushiji, in the Nishinokyo district west of central Nara, was founded in the late 7th century by an emperor praying for his consort’s recovery, and remains one of Japan’s most beautiful temple complexes. Its signature is symmetry: a pair of elegant three-story pagodas (that appear to have six roofs each) flank the Kondo hall, the East Pagoda an original 8th-century survivor and the West Pagoda a vivid modern reconstruction. Within the Kondo sits the Yakushi Triad, a magnificent bronze Medicine Buddha flanked by two bodhisattvas, counted among the supreme masterpieces of early Japanese Buddhist art.

item.title: Yamato Tea: Nara's Highland Green Tea — Guide
item.description: Yamato-cha is the green tea of Nara, grown for centuries on the cool, mist-wrapped highlands of the prefecture’s east around Tsukigase, Yamazoe and the Yamato plateau. The region’s elevation, temperature swings and morning fogs create ideal conditions for tea of fine aroma and mellow depth, and though less famous than Uji or Shizuoka, Yamato-cha is a quietly excellent tea prized by connoisseurs, produced as sencha, kabusecha and hojicha. Neatly terraced plantations climb the highland slopes, some farms welcome visitors for tastings, and the tea makes a natural pairing with Nara’s wagashi and a refined local souvenir.

item.title: Yamatokoriyama: Japan's Goldfish Town — Guide
item.description: Yamatokoriyama, a castle town just southwest of Nara, is famous across Japan as a capital of ornamental goldfish, bred here for some 300 years since samurai took up the hobby in the Edo period. Today goldfish are woven right into the town’s identity: rows of breeding ponds shimmer on its outskirts, goldfish motifs decorate the streets, and playful touches — goldfish in an old telephone booth, goldfish vending machines and shop displays — turn a stroll into a treasure hunt.

item.title: Yoshino Kuzu: The Translucent Sweet of the Mountains — Guide
item.description: Yoshino kuzu is one of Japan’s most refined traditional ingredients: a pure white starch painstakingly extracted from the roots of wild kudzu vines and refined by hand in cold mountain water, a labour-intensive craft centred on the Yoshino region. Prized for its smooth, glossy texture, real Yoshino hon-kuzu transforms into some of the most elegant wagashi in Japan — silken, jelly-like kuzumochi dusted with kinako and syrup, translucent kuzukiri noodles dipped in kuromitsu, and, in winter, kuzuyu, a warm, soothing thickened drink.

item.title: Yoshino Woodworking and Kumiko: Craft of the Cedar Forests — Guide
item.description: The mountains of Yoshino are famed not only for cherry blossoms but for their forests: Yoshino cedar (sugi) and cypress (hinoki), grown for centuries in one of Japan’s oldest managed plantations, are prized as some of the finest timber in the country, used for everything from temple beams to sake barrels. From this woodworking heritage comes kumiko, the delicate craft of assembling tiny wooden pieces into intricate geometric latticework without nails, traditionally used in shoji screens and transoms.

item.title: Ago Bay: Pearl Rafts and Island-Dotted Waters — Guide
item.description: Ago Bay is the scenic heart of the Ise-Shima region, a deeply indented ria coastline where the sea reaches inland among dozens of forested islets and countless rafts of cultivated pearl oysters, forming one of Japan’s most beautiful and productive stretches of water. This is the cradle of the pearl industry Mikimoto founded, and the classic way to appreciate it is from the water — sightseeing boats, some styled as Spanish galleons, and glass-bottom cruises glide among the islands and pearl rafts, revealing the oyster culture below.

item.title: Akafuku Mochi: Ise's 300-Year-Old Sweet — Guide
item.description: Akafuku is the definitive sweet of Ise, made and served on the pilgrim road to Ise Jingu since 1707. Each piece is a pillow of soft mochi topped with a generous wave of smooth sweet red-bean paste, its three ridges said to represent the flow of the clear Isuzu River that runs beside the shrine. The historic main shop stands on Oharaimachi at the Naiku gate, its tatami tearoom opening onto the river, where a plate of two freshly made akafuku with a cup of roasted green tea is one of the simple, perfect pleasures of an Ise visit.

item.title: Akame 48 Waterfalls: A Valley of Cascades and Ninja Legend — Guide
item.description: The Akame 48 Waterfalls are a beautiful forested ravine in western Mie where a well-built riverside trail threads past a long succession of cascades — not literally 48, but dozens, including several named grand falls — over a round-trip of roughly 4 kilometres. The valley is lushly green and cool, home to the protected Japanese giant salamander (which can be seen at a small centre at the entrance), and steeped in legend as a training ground of the Iga ninja, a heritage that lives on in ninja-experience programs offered on site.

item.title: Ama Divers and Their Seafood Huts: Ise-Shima's Living Tradition — Guide
item.description: The ama are the traditional women free-divers of Ise-Shima, who for perhaps 3,000 years have plunged into the coastal waters without tanks or air, holding their breath to gather abalone, turban shells, sea urchin and seaweed — a physically astonishing craft passed down through generations of women, some still diving into their eighties. Today many ama welcome visitors into their amagoya, the huts where they once warmed themselves between dives, to grill the day’s catch — abalone, scallops, spiny lobster and turban shells — over a charcoal hearth while sharing stories of a fast-vanishing way of life.

item.title: Iga Ninja Experience: Train Like a Shinobi — Guide
item.description: For anyone who has ever wanted to be a ninja, Iga is the place to actually try it. In the shinobi homeland, experience centres and the grounds around the Ninja Museum let visitors rent the black shozoku costume and learn the real skills under instruction: throwing shuriken stars at targets, handling a ninja sword, firing a blowgun (fukiya), and even scaling walls or crossing beams. Aimed squarely at families and the curious, the sessions are playful but rooted in the genuine techniques of the Iga-ryu tradition, turning a museum visit into an active, memorable half-day.

item.title: Iga Ueno: Castle and Home of the Ninja — Guide
item.description: The mountain-ringed basin of Iga was one of the two great cradles of ninja tradition, home to the Iga-ryu school whose spies and saboteurs shaped Japan’s shadow history — and the town of Iga Ueno celebrates that legacy fully. Its centrepiece is the Iga-ryu Ninja Museum, a real thatched farmhouse riddled with hidden doors, reversible walls, secret passages and weapon caches demonstrated by costumed guides, paired with live shows of shuriken-throwing and ninja weaponry.

item.title: Ise Jingu Geku: The Outer Shrine of Ise — Guide
item.description: The Geku (Outer Shrine) of Ise Jingu is where a proper pilgrimage to Ise begins, as tradition dictates it be visited before the Naiku. It enshrines Toyouke-Omikami, the goddess of agriculture, food and industry, who was summoned some 1,500 years ago to provide sacred meals to the sun goddess Amaterasu at the Inner Shrine — a duty still performed twice daily. Its unpainted hinoki halls, in the same austere ancient style as the Naiku and likewise rebuilt every 20 years, sit within a hushed forest just a short walk from Ise-shi Station, making it the natural first stop.

item.title: Ise Jingu Kagura: Sacred Music and Dance at Ise — Guide
item.description: Beyond the quiet act of prayer, Ise Jingu preserves kagura — formal ceremonies of sacred music and dance offered to the deities on a worshipper’s behalf. Performed in the kaguraden halls of both the Naiku and Geku by shrine musicians in courtly costume and miko shrine maidens, these rituals set ancient gagaku court music and slow, stylised dance to convey prayers for health, gratitude or family blessing. Anyone can request a kagura offering for a fee, making it a rare opportunity to witness — and personally commission — living ceremonial tradition at the heart of Japan’s most sacred shrine.

item.title: Ise Jingu Naiku: Japan's Holiest Shrine — Guide
item.description: Ise Jingu’s Naiku (Inner Shrine) is the most sacred site in all of Shinto, enshrining Amaterasu-Omikami, the sun goddess and mythical ancestor of the imperial line, whose sacred mirror — one of the three imperial regalia — is said to be kept here. Reached across the arched Uji Bridge and up a broad gravel path through towering thousand-year cedars, the shrine is famous for the Shikinen Sengu, the ritual by which its main halls are rebuilt from fresh hinoki cypress on an adjacent site every 20 years — a 1,300-year-old cycle of renewal, most recently in 2013, that keeps this ancient architecture eternally new.

item.title: Ise-ebi: The Spiny Lobster of Ise-Shima — Guide
item.description: Ise-ebi, the Japanese spiny lobster, is the most celebrated seafood of the Ise-Shima coast and a symbol of good fortune, its armoured red form long used as an auspicious New Year decoration. Caught in the rocky waters off Mie from autumn through spring, it is prized for firm, sweet, springy flesh that outshines clawed lobsters, and the region serves it every luxurious way: as translucent sashimi (ise-ebi no o-tsukuri), grilled or steamed in the shell, deep-fried, and simmered into a rich miso soup made from the heads.

item.title: Kumano Kodo Iseji: The Pilgrimage Route Through Mie — Guide
item.description: The Kumano Kodo is a network of ancient pilgrimage routes across the Kii Peninsula, registered as a UNESCO World Heritage site, and its Iseji route is the one that runs through Mie — linking the great shrine of Ise with the sacred Kumano region down the prefecture’s rugged southern coast. Walked by pilgrims for over a thousand years, the Iseji climbs a series of atmospheric mountain passes paved with moss-covered cobblestones, threading through towering cedar forest between glimpses of the Pacific.

item.title: Matsusaka Beef Festival: Prize Wagyu and Affordable Feasts — Guide
item.description: The Matsusaka Beef Festival (Matsusaka Ushi Matsuri), held each November in the wagyu’s home town, is the year’s great celebration of Japan’s most luxurious beef. Its centrepiece is a prestigious cattle-judging competition in which the finest Matsusaka cows are paraded and ranked, the champion fetching astonishing prices — but for visitors the real draw is the chance to eat: festival stalls and special sales offer premium Matsusaka beef, from grilled skewers to bento and cuts to take home, at prices far below the usual, in a rare democratic feast of one of the world’s most exclusive foods.

item.title: Matsusaka Beef: Japan's Most Luxurious Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Matsusaka beef is among the most prestigious and expensive wagyu in Japan, ranked with Kobe and Omi at the very top of the country’s beef. It comes from virgin female cattle raised with legendary care in and around the castle town of Matsusaka — famously massaged and, in old lore, given beer to stimulate appetite — over an unusually long fattening period that produces an extraordinarily fine, low-melting marble that dissolves on the tongue.

item.title: Meoto Iwa: The Wedded Rocks of Futami — Guide
item.description: Meoto Iwa, the ‘Wedded Rocks’, are two sea stones off the coast of Futami near Ise, joined by a great shimenawa rope of rice straw and revered as a symbol of the sacred union of the creator deities Izanagi and Izanami — and of marriage and harmony ever since. The larger ‘husband’ rock wears a small torii on its crown, and the pair belong to nearby Futami Okitama Shrine, a traditional place of purification before visiting Ise Jingu.

item.title: Mikimoto Pearl Island: Birthplace of the Cultured Pearl — Guide
item.description: Mikimoto Pearl Island, a small islet linked by bridge to central Toba, is where the modern pearl was born: here in 1893 Kokichi Mikimoto succeeded in culturing the world’s first spherical pearl, founding an industry and a global brand. The island’s museum traces how cultured pearls are made and graded, displays dazzling pearl artworks — including a pagoda and crown set with thousands of pearls — and, most memorably, stages live demonstrations by white-clad ama, the traditional women free-divers who once harvested the pearl oysters.

item.title: Okage Yokocho: Ise's Edo-Era Pilgrim Street — Guide
item.description: Stretching along the Isuzu River before the Naiku’s gate, Oharaimachi is the historic approach street to Ise Jingu, its stone-paved kilometre lined with traditional wooden merchant houses that have served pilgrims for centuries. At its heart is Okage Yokocho, a lovingly recreated quarter of Edo- and Meiji-era townscape packed with some 50 shops and eateries — a place to try soft Ise udon, grilled skewers, seafood and craft, and above all the famous Akafuku mochi, red-bean sweets served here since 1707.

item.title: Onigajo: The Demon's Castle Sea Cliffs of Kumano — Guide
item.description: Onigajo, the ‘Demon’s Castle’, is a spectacular stretch of coastline near Kumano in southern Mie, where centuries of wind, waves and tectonic uplift have carved the cliffs into a surreal landscape of honeycombed hollows, jutting terraces and cave-like recesses stacked in tiers above the crashing Pacific. A walking path threads along and through the formations, and the site — part of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage World Heritage area — comes wrapped in legend as the lair of a demon slain by a hero of old.

item.title: Tekone Sushi: Ise-Shima's Fisherman's Bowl — Guide
item.description: Tekone-zushi is the beloved fisherman’s dish of the Ise-Shima coast, born of practicality on the katsuo (bonito) boats: fishermen would slice their fresh catch, marinate it quickly in soy sauce, and mix it by hand into vinegared rice to eat between hauls — ‘tekone’ meaning ‘hand-mixed’. Today it is a regional specialty served in restaurants around Ise, Toba and Shima: glossy slices of soy-marinated bonito (or tuna) fanned over sushi rice, scattered with shiso, ginger and sesame, its rich, savoury simplicity a delicious counterpoint to the refined seafood kaiseki of the coast.

item.title: Toba Aquarium: Home of Japan's Only Dugong — Guide
item.description: Toba Aquarium, on the pearl-fishing coast of Toba, is one of Japan’s largest and most beloved aquariums, home to around 1,200 species — one of the highest counts in the country — displayed across twelve themed zones with no fixed route, so visitors wander freely. Its greatest celebrity is Serena, the only dugong on public display anywhere in Japan, joined by playful sea otters, capybaras, rare finless porpoises and a giant spider-crab tank.

item.title: Toba Sea Fireworks Festival: Summer Nights Over the Bay — Guide
item.description: The Toba Minato Fireworks Festival lights up the island-studded waters of Toba Bay on a summer evening, one of the Ise-Shima region’s highlights of the warm season. Thousands of shells burst over the sea directly off the port, their colours doubled in the dark water and set against the silhouettes of the bay’s forested islets and pearl rafts, with the grand water-fireworks (suichu hanabi) fired low across the surface a signature moment.

item.title: A Nagoya Meshi Food Tour: Eating Through Japan's Boldest Food City — Guide
item.description: No Japanese city guards a food identity as fiercely as Nagoya, whose ‘Nagoya meshi’ canon — eel hitsumabushi, miso-sauced katsu, peppery tebasaki wings, clay-pot miso nikomi udon, morning ogura toast and more — grew from the region’s dark hatcho miso and tamari brewing traditions into a cuisine found nowhere else. Eating through it is the city’s best itinerary: a self-guided day can run from kissaten breakfast through a noodle lunch to an izakaya wing crawl, while guided evening food tours thread the lantern-lit alleys and counter bars with a local who knows which queue is worth it.

item.title: Atsuta Jingu: Shrine of the Sacred Sword — Guide
item.description: Atsuta Jingu is one of the most venerable shrines in all of Shinto, said to have guarded the Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi — the sacred sword of the imperial regalia — for some 1,900 years, and ranking second only to Ise among the nation’s shrines. Its halls stand hushed within a deep evergreen forest of ancient camphor trees that shuts out the surrounding city, and every June the Atsuta Festival (Shobukan) fills the grounds with martial-arts dedications, hundreds of glowing makiwara lantern stands and evening fireworks, the shrine’s most spirited day of the year.

item.title: Azuchi Castle Ruins: Nobunaga's Vanished Golden Tower — Guide
item.description: Azuchi Castle was the wonder of its age: the revolutionary fortress-palace Oda Nobunaga raised above Lake Biwa in 1579, its seven-storey tower gilded and painted inside by the era’s finest artists — and it stood barely three years before burning down in the chaos after Nobunaga’s assassination in 1582. What remains is one of Japan’s most evocative ruins: grand stone stairways climbing through cedar woods past the foundation stones of vanished gates and residences to the tower base, where the view over the lake explains at a glance why Nobunaga chose this hill to rule Japan from.

item.title: Biwaichi: Cycling Around Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Biwaichi, literally ‘once around Biwa’, is one of Japan’s great cycling pilgrimages: a full lap of Lake Biwa’s shoreline, roughly 200 kilometres on the classic route, designated a National Cycle Route and marked throughout with the blue arrows and distance countdowns that make it navigable without a map. The mostly flat course rolls past lakeside torii, pine beaches, reed marshes and mountain backdrops, with the quieter, more scenic northern half often ridden alone as a 150 km ‘short lap’.

item.title: Biwako Valley: Ropeway, Sky Views and Winter Slopes — Guide
item.description: Biwako Valley, on the Hira mountains above Otsu, is Shiga’s easiest mountain thrill: a ropeway climbs some 1,100 metres in about five minutes to a summit plateau with one of the finest panoramas in the Kansai region — the whole silver expanse of Lake Biwa spread out below. In the green season the draw is the cliff-edge ‘Biwako Terrace’, a café-lounge with infinity-style decks that seem to float over the lake, plus ziplines and treetop adventure courses; in winter the same slopes become a ski and snowboard resort within an hour of Kyoto, making it a rare day-trip peak for city-based visitors.

item.title: Chikubushima: The Sacred Island of Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Chikubushima is the sacred island of Lake Biwa, a steep green islet off the lake’s northern shore that has drawn pilgrims for more than a thousand years as one of Japan’s foremost sanctuaries of Benzaiten, goddess of music, water and fortune. Its stone stairways climb from the ferry dock through Hogonji temple — a stop on the Saigoku Kannon pilgrimage — to Tsukubusuma Shrine, whose National Treasure worship hall and the ornate Karamon gate preserve carvings and structures transferred from Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s vanished Fushimi Castle, and visitors cast kawarake clay discs from the cliff-edge toward a torii below, a wish granted if the disc sails through.

item.title: Funazushi: Japan's Oldest Sushi, Fermented on Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Funazushi is the ancestor of all sushi: nigorobuna carp from Lake Biwa, salted and then buried in cooked rice to ferment for one to three years, a preservation method over a millennium old from which modern sushi eventually evolved. The result is nothing like the sushi the world knows — the flesh turns dense, tangy and creamy, with an aroma often compared to strong cheese — and it remains a proud, polarising delicacy cured by family houses around the lake, served sliced with the golden fermented rice, floated in hot broth as ochazuke, or nibbled alongside local sake, which flatters it best.

item.title: Hikone Castle Cherry Blossoms: 1,000 Trees Around a National Treasure — Guide
item.description: Hikone Castle in cherry-blossom season is one of Shiga’s most beautiful sights: around 1,000 cherry trees bloom across the castle hill, ramparts and the surrounding moats each early April, framing the National Treasure keep in clouds of pale pink. The classic view is from the inner and outer moats, where boat rides and moat-side paths set the blossoms against the castle’s stone walls and the petals drift down to carpet the water, and the whole scene is lit after dark for yozakura evening viewing, making Hikone a fixture on lists of Japan’s finest hanami spots.

item.title: Hikone Castle: A National Treasure Above Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Hikone Castle, completed in 1622 by the Ii clan — hereditary retainers of the Tokugawa — is one of just twelve castles in Japan to keep its original keep and one of only five designated National Treasures. The elegant three-storey tower, built partly from materials salvaged from defeated rivals' castles, crowns a hill of spiralling ramparts, plunging stone walls and trick gates above the eastern shore of Lake Biwa, and its foot holds the strolling garden of Genkyuen, whose ponds and teahouse borrow the keep itself as scenery.

item.title: Hitsumabushi: Nagoya's Three-Way Eel Feast — Guide
item.description: Hitsumabushi is the flagship of ‘Nagoya meshi’, the city’s proudly idiosyncratic food culture, and it turns grilled eel into a ritual of three acts: finely sliced, crisp-grilled unagi arrives on rice in a lacquered wooden tub, and you eat the first quarter plain, the second with wasabi, spring onion and shredded nori, and the third drowned in hot dashi as a fragrant ochazuke — before finishing with a fourth portion in whichever style won.

item.title: Inuyama Castle: Japan's Oldest Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Inuyama Castle, completed in 1537 on a bluff above the broad Kiso River, holds what is generally considered Japan’s oldest surviving original castle keep, one of only a dozen that escaped demolition, fire and war — and one of just five designated National Treasures. Climbing its steep, creaking wooden stairs is a walk through unrestored history that ends on a top-floor balcony with sweeping views over the river to the mountains of Gifu, and each spring several hundred cherry trees ring the castle hill and the old town below, making the season’s festival the prettiest time to visit.

item.title: Inuyama Cormorant Fishing: Firelit Nights on the Kiso River — Guide
item.description: Ukai, the ancient art of fishing with trained cormorants, has been practised on the Kiso River for some 1,300 years, and Inuyama’s summer performances unfold in one of its finest settings — the dark river beneath the floodlit silhouette of Japan’s oldest castle keep. From June to mid-October, spectators board wooden yakata boats hung with lanterns and drift alongside the fishing craft as usho masters in traditional grass skirts and ceremonial dress work a dozen leashed birds by the light of blazing pine-fire baskets, the flames, splashing and handlers' calls conjuring a scene unchanged for centuries.

item.title: Irago Cape and the Atsumi Peninsula: Lighthouse at Land's End — Guide
item.description: Irago Cape marks the tip of the Atsumi Peninsula, the long green arm that encloses Mikawa Bay, and its white lighthouse — one of Japan’s fifty famous lighthouses — stands on the rocks where the bay’s calm waters meet the open Pacific swell. Beside it curves Koijigahama, the ‘Beach of the Road of Love’, a kilometre of pale sand celebrated in poetry and popular with couples, while the peninsula behind is one of Japan’s most productive flower and vegetable coasts, blanketed in yellow rapeseed blossom each early spring and serving some of Aichi’s best seafood in the port shacks around the ferry terminal.

item.title: Kishimen and Nagoya's Noodle Traditions — Guide
item.description: Kishimen are Nagoya’s signature noodles: broad, flat and silky ribbons that slip through a delicate broth tinted with the region’s tamari soy sauce, topped simply with fried tofu, spinach, bonito flakes and a swirl of green onion. The dish’s most beloved settings are its least formal — the standing noodle counters on Nagoya Station’s platforms, where travellers slurp a bowl between trains, and the venerable shop inside Atsuta Jingu’s forest — while the city’s other noodle monument, miso nikomi udon, simmers firm udon directly in a scalding hatcho-miso broth in individual clay pots, the two dishes bracketing Nagoya’s noodle culture from delicate to mighty.

item.title: Korankei Gorge: Central Japan's Greatest Autumn Foliage — Guide
item.description: Korankei is the most celebrated autumn foliage spot in central Japan, a river gorge near Toyota city where some 4,000 maple trees — descendants of those planted by a temple priest in the 1630s — blaze crimson and gold across the slopes of Mount Iimori each November. The scarlet Taigetsukyo bridge and the reflections doubling every colour in the slow Tomoe River provide the signature views, and throughout the month-long Korankei Momiji Festival the entire gorge is illuminated nightly until 21:00, when the tunnels of glowing maples take on an almost theatrical beauty.

item.title: Lake Biwa Cruises: Paddlewheelers and Island Boats — Guide
item.description: Cruising is the classic way to feel the sheer scale of Lake Biwa, and the lake runs a whole fleet for it. From Otsu near Kyoto sails the Michigan, an American-style paddlewheeler offering sightseeing, lunch and dinner cruises with live music along the southern lake; from the northern ports of Nagahama and Imazu, pilgrimage ferries cross to the sacred island of Chikubushima; and seasonal boats run to beaches and viewpoints around the shore.

item.title: Lake Biwa Fireworks: Summer Nights Over Otsu — Guide
item.description: The Lake Biwa Great Fireworks Festival, held on an evening in early August off Otsu, is one of the Kansai region’s biggest summer displays: some 10,000 shells burst over the open lake, their colours mirrored in the broad dark water and reflected off the lakeside towers of Otsu, drawing hundreds of thousands of spectators to the shore. Because the launches are over water with no obstructions, the shells hang huge and clear above the lake, and the setting — Japan’s largest lake, an easy ten minutes from Kyoto — makes it one of the most accessible major hanabi for visitors based in the old capital.

item.title: Lake Biwa Watersports: SUP, Kayak, Sailing and Windsurfing — Guide
item.description: Lake Biwa is Kansai’s great freshwater playground, big enough to offer serious watersports without the salt, chop and tides of the sea. Its calm mornings are made for stand-up paddleboarding and kayaking, gliding over water so clear along the western and northern shores that you can watch fish beneath the board, while the reliable afternoon winds funnelling down the lake turn beaches like Omi-Maiko and Omi-Shirahama into busy sailing and windsurfing centres.

item.title: Lake Biwa's Freshwater Cuisine: Ayu, Biwa Trout and Lake Delicacies — Guide
item.description: Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest and oldest lake, supports a food culture found nowhere else in the country: more than a thousand species live in its waters, dozens of them endemic, and lakeside kitchens have turned them into a distinctive freshwater cuisine over the centuries. The stars are ayu sweetfish — grilled whole over charcoal with salt, at their best in early summer — and the endemic Biwa trout (biwamasu), whose cool-water flesh makes sashimi as silky as fine salmon, joined by simmered tiny gobies and moroko, shijimi-clam miso soup and tempura of lake shrimp, served everywhere from venerable ryotei to market stalls.

item.title: Lake Biwa's Reed Marshes: Golden Wetlands of the Lakeshore — Guide
item.description: The reed marshes of Lake Biwa are one of the lake’s quietest treasures: broad beds of yoshi reed fringe the shoreline, most beautifully around the Nishinoko lagoon near Omihachiman, where a maze of willow-lined waterways winds between the reeds. These wetlands are a designated cultural landscape, harvested each winter for traditional reed screens and thatch, and alive with herons, grebes and migrating waterfowl. The classic way to experience them is a slow flat-bottomed boat, poled or motored through the corridors of reed that filter the lake’s water and glow gold in the low light of autumn.

item.title: Lake Biwa: Japan's Largest and Oldest Lake — Guide
item.description: Lake Biwa is the vast heart of Shiga — Japan’s largest freshwater lake, covering roughly a sixth of the entire prefecture, and one of the oldest lakes on Earth at some four million years, old enough to have evolved dozens of species found nowhere else. It supplies drinking water to the whole Kansai region and shapes life around its 235-kilometre shoreline, where beaches, marinas, cruise piers, cycling paths and lakeside shrines ring waters that turn from morning mirror-calm to windsurfing chop.

item.title: Legoland Japan and the Minato Area: Nagoya's Family Playground — Guide
item.description: Legoland Japan opened in Nagoya’s redeveloped Kinjofuto port district as the country’s only Legoland resort, its seven themed zones built from some 10 million bricks and pitched squarely at families with children aged roughly two to twelve. The park’s showpiece is Miniland, where Japanese landmarks from Tokyo Tower to Nagoya Castle are rebuilt in astonishing brick detail, and the surrounding Minato area rounds out a family day with the Sea Life aquarium, the Maker’s Pier shopping village and the neighbouring SCMaglev railway museum.

item.title: Meiji Mura: A Village of Japan's Modernising Age — Guide
item.description: Meiji Mura is one of Japan’s great open-air museums, preserving more than 60 authentic buildings of the Meiji era (1868–1912) — the tumultuous age when Japan flung open its doors and hybridised Western brick, clapboard and stained glass with its own carpentry. Rescued from demolition across the country and rebuilt on a wooded hillside above Lake Iruka near Inuyama, the collection ranges from churches, post offices and a kabuki theatre to its crown jewel, the reconstructed main entrance hall of Frank Lloyd Wright’s Imperial Hotel, while a working steam locomotive and vintage Kyoto trams carry visitors between the districts.

item.title: Metasequoia Avenue: Makino's Dawn-Redwood Tunnel — Guide
item.description: The Metasequoia Avenue in Makino, on Lake Biwa’s northwestern edge, is one of Japan’s most photographed tree-lined roads: some 500 metasequoia (dawn redwood) trees march dead-straight for 2.4 kilometres across open farmland toward the mountains, their tall conical crowns meeting overhead in a soaring green tunnel. Planted as a windbreak in the 1980s and now grown magnificent, the avenue transforms with the seasons — fresh green in spring, deep shade in summer, a blaze of coppery russet in late November, and a monochrome corridor after winter snow — and is regularly named among Japan’s most beautiful streets.

item.title: Miho Museum: I.M. Pei's Shangri-La in the Shiga Mountains — Guide
item.description: The Miho Museum, designed by I.M. Pei — architect of the Louvre pyramid — is one of the world’s most theatrical museum arrivals: visitors walk or ride through a curving stainless-steel tunnel that opens onto a suspended bridge, the glass roofline of the museum appearing across the gorge like the hidden valley of Shangri-La that inspired it. To preserve the Shigaraki mountains, some 80% of the building is buried underground, its limestone-and-glass halls lit like a temple of light, and the collection matches the setting: superb antiquities from Egypt, Gandhara, Persia, China and Japan assembled by the Koyama family, joined by ambitious special exhibitions.

item.title: Mikawa Bay and Laguna Ten Bosch: Aichi's Seaside Playground — Guide
item.description: Mikawa Bay is Aichi’s sheltered inland sea, its calm waters and mild shores long developed as the prefecture’s seaside playground around the resort town of Gamagori. The bay’s landmark is Takeshima, a tiny sacred islet crowned with a shrine and linked to the shore by a 387-metre footbridge, while the modern draw is Laguna Ten Bosch, a waterfront leisure complex whose theme-park zone mixes summer pools, rides, some of central Japan’s most lavish winter illuminations and a festival marketplace of shops and restaurants, making the area an easy family day out of Nagoya.

item.title: Miso Katsu: Nagoya's Dark-Sauced Tonkatsu — Guide
item.description: Miso katsu is Nagoya’s answer to tonkatsu: a crisp, golden pork cutlet draped in a glossy deep-brown sauce built on hatcho miso, the intensely savoury soybean miso that has been aged for years in giant cedar barrels near Okazaki since the age of the shoguns. The sauce — sweet, earthy and almost chocolatey in its depth — soaks gently into the panko crust and transforms the dish into the region’s definitive comfort food, served everywhere from the famous Yabaton chain with its pig mascot to old kissaten and department-store restaurants.

item.title: Mt. Ibuki: Wildflower Peak on the Shiga Border — Guide
item.description: Mount Ibuki, at 1,377 metres the highest mountain in Shiga, stands as a bold isolated massif on the Gifu border northeast of Lake Biwa, its limestone bulk catching the heaviest snows in western Japan — it holds a world record for snow depth. In the warm months its upper slopes become one of the country’s celebrated wildflower gardens, some 280 species carpeting the summit meadows through summer, while the panorama takes in Lake Biwa, the Suzuka range and the peaks of the Northern Alps.

item.title: Nagahama Hikiyama Festival: Child Kabuki on Golden Floats — Guide
item.description: The Nagahama Hikiyama Festival, held each year in mid-April, is one of Japan’s three great float festivals and a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: its treasures are the hikiyama, towering gilded and lacquered ‘moving stages’ built in the 16th century, said to have begun when Toyotomi Hideyoshi celebrated the birth of an heir. What sets Nagahama apart is the performance — each float is a portable kabuki theatre on which local boys aged roughly five to twelve act out full classical kabuki dramas, mastering the stylised poses, voices and quick changes with a poise that draws gasps, cheered on by whole neighbourhoods.

item.title: Nagahama: Glass Studios in a Castle Town — Guide
item.description: Nagahama, the castle town Toyotomi Hideyoshi built as his first domain on Lake Biwa’s northeastern shore, has reinvented its historic core as one of Japan’s most successful heritage-revival districts. Its centrepiece is Kurokabe Square, named for the handsome ‘black wall’ Meiji-era bank building that now anchors a quarter of glass studios, galleries and workshops where artisans blow, cut and lamp-work glass before your eyes, threaded through streets of latticed townhouses, sake shops and the venerable Daitsuji temple, with Hideyoshi’s rebuilt lakeside castle keep watching from its park.

item.title: Nagoya Castle: Golden Shachihoko and the Honmaru Palace — Guide
item.description: Nagoya Castle was built on the orders of Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1612 as the seat of the Owari branch of his family, and its keep — crowned with a pair of golden shachihoko, the mythical tiger-headed dolphins that became the symbol of the city — presides over broad moats and massive stone ramparts. The great prize of a visit today is the Honmaru Palace, destroyed in the war and painstakingly rebuilt using original techniques, its chambers lined with dazzling gold-leaf screens of tigers and pines and its fresh hinoki cypress halls among the finest examples of shoin-zukuri palace architecture anywhere in Japan.

item.title: Nagoya Festival: The Three Heroes Parade Through the City — Guide
item.description: The Nagoya Festival, held over a weekend in mid-October, is the city’s biggest annual celebration, and its heart is the Three Heroes procession: costumed riders portraying Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu — the three unifiers of Japan, all born in what is now Aichi — lead some 600 participants in samurai armour through the streets between Nagoya Station and Sakae. Around the parade swirl historic karakuri mechanical-puppet floats, flower cars, marching bands and neighbourhood dance troupes, and many of the city’s museums and gardens open free for the weekend.

item.title: Nagoya Morning Culture and Ogura Toast: Breakfast, the Nagoya Way — Guide
item.description: Nagoya’s kissaten coffee-house culture runs deeper than anywhere in Japan, and its beloved institution is the ‘morning service’: order a coffee before around 11am and toast, boiled egg and often more arrive at little or no extra charge, a custom born in the city’s frugal merchant culture that turned cafes into the region’s living rooms. The essential order is ogura toast — thick-cut bread, butter and a generous pile of sweet ogura red-bean paste — a combination invented in Nagoya a century ago, served everywhere from creaking Showa-era kissaten to the hometown Komeda’s Coffee chain.

item.title: Nagoya Port Fireworks: Summer Lights Over the Harbour — Guide
item.description: The Nagoya Port Festival (Minato Matsuri), held around Marine Day in late July, is the city’s signature summer night: some 3,000 fireworks burst directly over the harbour basin, their colours mirrored in the black water and framed by the silhouettes of cranes and ships in one of Japan’s busiest working ports. Through the afternoon the Garden Pier area fills with festival dance parades, taiko drumming and rank upon rank of food stalls, so the evening builds from street-festival bustle to the concentrated spectacle of the finale barrages.

item.title: Nagoya Women's Marathon: The World's Largest Women's Race — Guide
item.description: The Nagoya Women’s Marathon, run each year on a Sunday in early March, is recognised as the world’s largest women-only marathon, bringing some 20,000 runners from around the globe onto a flat, fast course that loops from Nagoya Dome past Nagoya Castle, the Sakae skyline and the city’s broad avenues. The race is famous for its finisher’s reward — an exclusive Tiffany & Co. pendant handed over by tuxedoed presenters — and for the city-wide festival mood, with cheering squads, taiko teams and a running expo that make marathon weekend one of Nagoya’s liveliest.

item.title: Noritake Garden: Porcelain Craft in a Red-Brick Park — Guide
item.description: Noritake Garden occupies the site of the original 1904 works of Noritake, the porcelain maker whose fine tableware graced dinner tables worldwide, and turns the old factory grounds into a leafy urban park framed by red-brick workshops and the chimney stubs of former kilns. The craft centre is the heart of the visit: you watch artisans shape, fire and hand-paint porcelain at every stage, browse a museum of the company’s dazzling early ‘Old Noritake’ art pieces, and can even paint your own design onto a plate before browsing the outlet shop’s tableware bargains.

item.title: Omi Beef: Japan's Oldest Wagyu Brand — Guide
item.description: Omi beef is Japan’s oldest wagyu brand, raised in Shiga’s mild lake basin for over 400 years and famously supplied to the Tokugawa shoguns as ‘medicinal’ miso-cured beef in an age when eating meat was officially taboo. Counted with Kobe and Matsusaka among Japan’s top three wagyu, it is prized for silken, fine-grained marbling with a low melting point that dissolves on the tongue, and Shiga serves it every way: bubbling sukiyaki in century-old restaurants, charcoal-grilled steak, shabu-shabu, and affordable lunchtime beef bowls in the castle towns of Hikone and Omihachiman.

item.title: Omi Chanpon: Hikone's Gentle Noodle Soul Food — Guide
item.description: Omi chanpon is Shiga’s homegrown noodle dish, born at a Hikone noodle shop in the 1960s and now the prefecture’s definitive everyday comfort food. Unlike its rich, pork-boned Nagasaki namesake, the Omi version rests on a delicate golden broth of kombu and bonito — closer to refined udon dashi — over which a mountain of stir-steamed cabbage, bean sprouts, onions and pork is piled onto springy medium noodles, and the local ritual is to douse the last third with a swirl of vinegar, which brightens the whole bowl.

item.title: Osu: Nagoya's Liveliest Shopping District — Guide
item.description: Osu is Nagoya’s liveliest and most eclectic quarter, its covered shopping arcades spreading east from the vermilion halls of Osu Kannon, a venerable Buddhist temple whose library holds one of the oldest manuscript copies of the Kojiki. Some 1,200 shops pack the streets in a gleeful jumble — vintage clothing and streetwear, secondhand electronics and maid cafes, anime figures and old kimono — threaded with street food from taiwanese fried chicken to fresh croissant taiyaki, giving the district a youthful, slightly chaotic energy often compared to a compact Akihabara-meets-Harajuku.

item.title: SCMaglev and Railway Park: Japan's Fastest Trains Up Close — Guide
item.description: The SCMaglev and Railway Park is JR Central’s superb railway museum on Nagoya’s port side, lining up 39 full-size vehicles that trace the evolution of Japanese rail speed — steam locomotives, early electric trains, generations of Shinkansen, and the superconducting maglev test car that set a world record of 581 km/h. Visitors can walk through cab and cabin interiors, drive train simulators including a Shinkansen cockpit, and linger over one of Japan’s largest railway dioramas, a miniature day-in-the-life of the Tokaido corridor that cycles from sunrise to night.

item.title: Seto: The Pottery Town That Named Japan's Ceramics — Guide
item.description: Seto, in the hills east of Nagoya, has fired ceramics for some 1,300 years — so long and so centrally that ‘setomono’, literally ‘things from Seto’, became the everyday Japanese word for pottery itself. The town wears its trade openly: alley walls are built from stacked kiln bricks and discarded tools, shrine guardians and even bridge railings are ceramic, and along the Kamagaki-no-Komichi kiln-wall path the workshops of working potters open for browsing.

item.title: Shiga's Sake Breweries: Lake Water, Mountain Rice — Guide
item.description: Shiga is one of Japan’s quietly excellent sake regions: more than 30 breweries work the prefecture, drawing soft water filtered through the mountains of the Lake Biwa watershed and rice from the fertile Omi plain, producing sake known for gentle umami depth that pairs naturally with the lake’s cuisine. Historic kura cluster around Otsu — where the brewery quarter near the old Tokaido road keeps its earthen storehouses — and in merchant towns like Hino and Harie, whose springs run so pure that households channel them through their kitchens, and many breweries open their doors for tastings, tours and seasonal fresh-pressed namazake.

item.title: Shirahige Shrine: The Floating Torii of Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Shirahige Shrine, said to be nearly 1,900 years old and the head shrine of some 300 Shirahige shrines nationwide, is famous for its vermilion torii rising directly from the shallows of Lake Biwa — an image so reminiscent of Miyajima that the spot is called the ‘Itsukushima of Omi’. The shrine venerates a white-bearded god of longevity, and its lakeside halls climb the wooded slope behind, but the great moment is dawn, when the sun lifts over the lake’s far shore and the gate floats in a path of gold, mist and morning birdsong.

item.title: Tagata Jinja and the Honen Matsuri: Japan's Famous Fertility Festival — Guide
item.description: Tagata Jinja, an ancient shrine near Komaki north of Nagoya, is home to the Honen Matsuri, Japan’s most famous fertility festival, held every year on March 15th. The rite is exactly what its reputation promises and older than embarrassment: a team of men carries a newly carved hinoki-cypress owasegata — some 2.5 metres long and several hundred kilos — in procession between shrines, accompanied by sake barrels, banner bearers and shrine maidens, as a prayer for bountiful harvests, prosperity and children.

item.title: Tea Ceremony in Nagoya: The Oribe Tradition — Guide
item.description: Nagoya sits at the heart of the tea culture shaped by Furuta Oribe, the samurai tea master who succeeded Sen no Rikyu and stamped the ceremony with a bolder, more playful spirit — deliberately warped bowls, dramatic green-glazed Oribe ware from the region’s kilns, and an embrace of imperfection livelier than his teacher’s austerity. Tea-ceremony experiences in and around the city welcome beginners into tatami tea rooms to learn the gestures, whisk their own bowl of matcha and taste seasonal wagashi sweets, with some sessions held in historic gardens and machiya townhouses that deepen the sense of stepping into another century.

item.title: Tebasaki: Nagoya's Peppery Glazed Chicken Wings — Guide
item.description: Tebasaki are Nagoya’s iconic chicken wings: fried crisp without batter, brushed while hot with a sweet-savoury tare glaze, then hit hard with white pepper, salt and sesame, producing a lacquered, peppery crunch that has made them the city’s definitive beer food. The style was born at the restaurant Furaibo in the 1960s, and its friendly rivalry with the cheekier chain Yamachan — whose wings bite back with even more pepper — divides the city into loyal camps that visitors are honour-bound to adjudicate over a cold beer.

item.title: The Kiso River: Japan's Rhine Below Castle and Mountains — Guide
item.description: The Kiso River flows down from the Kiso Valley of the Central Alps to sweep past Inuyama in a broad, green corridor that a Meiji-era geographer famously nicknamed the ‘Japanese Rhine’ — like the German river, it pairs castle-crowned bluffs with vine-green gorges and long gravel shoals. The Inuyama reach is the scenic heart: National Treasure Inuyama Castle rises directly above the water, sightseeing boats and seasonal cormorant-fishing cruises work the current, and riverside paths make for easy cycling and strolling, while upstream the river threads toward the old Nakasendo post towns of Tsumago and Magome on the Gifu-Nagano border.

item.title: Toyota Commemorative Museum: From Looms to Cars — Guide
item.description: The Toyota Commemorative Museum of Industry and Technology occupies the handsome red-brick spinning mill that Sakichi Toyoda founded in Nagoya in 1911, and it tells one of Japan’s great industrial stories: how a maker of automatic textile looms transformed itself into the world’s largest carmaker.
