The textile pavilion sets dozens of historic looms clattering in live demonstrations, from hand spinning to the revolutionary Type G automatic loom, while the automobile pavilion walks through car development and production with cutaway engines, robots and demonstrations that make manufacturing genuinely fascinating even for visitors who never thought they cared.

item.title: Tsuruma Park: Nagoya's Great Hanami Gathering — Guide
item.description: Tsuruma Park, opened in 1909 as Nagoya’s first public park, is the city’s great hanami stage: some 700 cherry trees, mostly clouds of Somei-Yoshino, bloom in late March and early April over a gracious landscape of fountains, a Western-style rose garden and a Japanese garden. This is where Nagoya comes to celebrate spring in earnest — blue tarpaulins and office parties pack the lawns by mid-morning, food stalls line the paths, and after dark lanterns and lights turn the central avenues into glowing tunnels of blossom for yozakura night viewing.

item.title: Atami Onsen: The Classic Seaside Hot Spring Resort — Guide
item.description: Atami, meaning ‘hot sea’, is one of Japan’s most famous hot spring resorts, its salty, mineral-rich waters used for over a thousand years and beloved by shoguns, writers and honeymooners across the centuries. The town tumbles down a steep hillside to a palm-lined bay, mixing grand historic ryokan and seaside baths with the retro charm of its Showa-era heyday, and after years of decline it is enjoying a stylish revival, with renovated inns, cafes and a young crowd drawn by the 40-minute Shinkansen hop from Tokyo.

item.title: Atami Sea Fireworks: Year-Round Displays in a Natural Amphitheatre — Guide
item.description: The Atami Sea Fireworks Festival is unusual among Japan’s fireworks events in being held not once but on many dates throughout the year, including winter, when the crisp air makes the bursts especially sharp. The display explodes directly over Atami Bay, whose mountain-wrapped shape acts as a natural amphitheatre that amplifies each boom, and every show ends with the famous ‘silver waterfall’ finale, a curtain of light poured low across the water; ryokan rooms and the beachfront both make fine vantage points.

item.title: Climbing Mount Fuji from Shizuoka: The Fujinomiya Trail — Guide
item.description: The Fujinomiya Trail is the main climbing route up Mount Fuji from the Shizuoka side, starting from the highest of the mountain’s four fifth-station trailheads at around 2,400 metres and offering the shortest, most direct path to the 3,776-metre summit, though its steeper, rockier terrain makes it more demanding step for step than the popular Yoshida route. Climbing is only permitted during the official summer season, roughly early July to early September, marked by the traditional trail-opening ceremonies, with mountain huts along the route and the summit crater and highest point, Kengamine, closest to this trail’s top.

item.title: Dogashima Sea Caves: West Izu's Skylight Grotto and Boat Tours — Guide
item.description: Dogashima, on the Izu Peninsula’s wild west coast, is famous for its white volcanic tuff cliffs and wave-carved sea caves, the striking result of layered volcanic ash sculpted by the sea. The highlight is Tensodo, a skylight cave whose roof has collapsed to leave a natural round opening, sending a shaft of light onto the blue-green water below; small sightseeing boats cruise into the cave itself, while a clifftop path above lets you peer down through the skylight, and at low tide a tombolo land bridge appears to a nearby island.

item.title: Hamamatsu Kite Festival: Giant Kite Battles Over the Dunes — Guide
item.description: The Hamamatsu Festival, held every year over Golden Week (3–5 May), is famous for its giant kite battles, in which more than a hundred neighbourhood teams fly enormous kites — some several metres across, each painted with their district’s emblem — above the Nakatajima sand dunes, deliberately crossing lines to cut rivals from the sky amid trumpet fanfares and chanting. The tradition began as a celebration of firstborn children and continues today, with evenings bringing a second spectacle as ornately carved palace-like floats parade through the city streets.

item.title: Hamamatsu Unagi: Japan's Eel Capital on Lake Hamana — Guide
item.description: Hamamatsu is Japan’s unagi (freshwater eel) capital, the brackish waters of neighbouring Lake Hamana having hosted the country’s first commercial eel farming over a century ago, and the city’s restaurants have refined the craft of grilling eel ever since. The classic dish is unagi glazed in a sweet-savoury tare sauce, grilled over charcoal and served on rice, and Hamamatsu sits on the historic boundary between styles, so both the Kanto method (steamed then grilled, meltingly soft) and the Kansai method (grilled straight through, crisp-edged) are served here side by side.

item.title: Hamamatsu: Japan's City of Musical Instruments — Guide
item.description: Hamamatsu is Japan’s city of music, the birthplace and home of Yamaha, Kawai and Roland, whose factories grew from the city’s craft traditions into the instruments played on stages worldwide. The centrepiece for visitors is the Hamamatsu Museum of Musical Instruments, the only public museum of its kind in Japan, displaying some 1,500 instruments from every corner of the world with headphone stations to hear them and a hands-on room where many can actually be played, while piano fans can also tour associated factory and brand facilities.

item.title: Izu Cycling: The Nishi Izu Skyline Ridge Road — Guide
item.description: The Izu Peninsula has become one of Japan’s notable cycling destinations, its roads having hosted Olympic cycling events, and the Nishi Izu Skyline is among its most rewarding rides: a ridge-top road winding along the mountains of western Izu with sweeping views over Suruga Bay toward Mount Fuji on clear days. The climbs are genuine and the descents long, making it a route best suited to reasonably fit road cyclists, while drivers and motorcyclists enjoy the same panoramas from the frequent lookouts.

item.title: Izu Peninsula Scuba Diving: Japan's Favourite Dive Coast — Guide
item.description: The Izu Peninsula is mainland Japan’s most popular scuba diving region, its volcanic underwater terrain washed by the warm Kuroshio Current, which carries subtropical fish and nurtures soft coral gardens surprisingly close to Tokyo. Famous sites include Osezaki on the west coast, whose sheltered bay suits beginners and training while its outer wall drops steeply into Suruga Bay’s depths, and the east coast’s rocky points, with dive shops in the seaside towns running guided boat and shore dives year-round.

item.title: Izu Peninsula: Hot Springs, Wild Coasts and a UNESCO Geopark — Guide
item.description: The Izu Peninsula juts into the Pacific south of Mount Fuji, formed over millions of years by volcanic islands colliding with Honshu, a geological origin so distinctive that the entire peninsula is designated a UNESCO Global Geopark. Its dramatic coastlines range from the rugged cliffs and sea caves of the west to white-sand beaches in the south, while inland valleys grow Japan’s finest wasabi, and celebrated onsen towns like Atami and Shuzenji have drawn bathers for centuries, all within a couple of hours of Tokyo.

item.title: Izu Wasabi Farms: Japan's Finest Wasabi in Spring-Fed Terraces — Guide
item.description: The mountain valleys of the Izu Peninsula are one of Japan’s premier wasabi-growing regions, the plant cultivated in terraced stone beds through which cold, pure spring water flows constantly, a traditional method recognised as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System. Real fresh wasabi, grated to order from the root, is aromatic and gently sweet, a world away from the fiery horseradish paste most people know, and valley farms and roadside shops offer tastings, freshly grated wasabi over rice, and the region’s beloved novelty: wasabi ice cream.

item.title: Kakegawa Castle: Japan's First Authentically Wooden-Rebuilt Keep — Guide
item.description: Kakegawa Castle, a compact hilltop castle on the old Tokaido highway between Edo and Kyoto, was rebuilt in 1994 as Japan’s first castle keep reconstructed authentically in wood using traditional methods, rather than the concrete used at most modern reconstructions. The site also preserves its original goten palace building, one of only a handful of surviving castle palaces in Japan, giving visitors a rare combination of a faithful wooden keep and genuine Edo-period administrative halls in one visit.

item.title: Kunozan Toshogu: The Original Resting Place of Tokugawa Ieyasu — Guide
item.description: Kunozan Toshogu is the original shrine of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, built on Mount Kuno overlooking Suruga Bay immediately after his death in 1616 as his first burial place, before his remains were later enshrined at the more famous Nikko. Its brilliantly ornate halls, decorated with lacquer, gold leaf and intricate carvings, are designated National Treasures and predate Nikko’s, and the shrine is reached either by a scenic ropeway from the Nihondaira plateau or by climbing more than 1,100 stone steps up from the coast below.

item.title: Miho no Matsubara: The Legendary Pine Grove With Mount Fuji Views — Guide
item.description: Miho no Matsubara is a seven-kilometre stretch of coastline planted with some 30,000 pine trees, framing one of Japan’s most celebrated views: Mount Fuji rising across the waters of Suruga Bay beyond the black-sand beach and twisted pines. The grove is a component site of Mount Fuji’s UNESCO World Heritage listing and the setting of the famous Hagoromo legend, in which a celestial maiden left her feathered robe hanging on a pine here, a story still honoured at the ‘Hagoromo pine’ and in Noh theatre.

item.title: Nishi Izu Wild Coast: Sunset Cliffs and Roadside Onsen — Guide
item.description: Nishi Izu, the western shore of the Izu Peninsula, is the peninsula’s wildest and least developed coast, a winding stretch of volcanic cliffs, fishing villages and coves largely untouched by big resort development because no railway reaches it. The reward for making the drive is some of Japan’s finest coastal scenery: sunsets over the sea considered among the country’s best, and unpretentious roadside and cliff-top onsen where you can soak in the open air with views across Suruga Bay to Mount Fuji.

item.title: Okuno-in Cedar Forest Walk: A Quiet Sacred Grove — Guide
item.description: The Okuno-in cedar forest walk is a peaceful trail through a grove of towering old cedar trees leading to a secluded okuno-in, the ‘inner sanctuary’ traditionally set deep behind a temple’s main halls, where the atmosphere of filtered light, moss and massive trunks makes the walk itself the point. Well off Shizuoka’s main tourist routes, it offers a quiet forest-bathing escape, the kind of unhurried, contemplative woodland stroll that rewards travellers looking beyond the famous sights.

item.title: Ryugenbuchi: An Emerald River Pool Beneath Mount Fuji — Guide
item.description: Ryugenbuchi is a quiet, lightly visited beauty spot on the Shiba River near Fujinomiya, where the river gathers into deep pools of a striking emerald-green colour, fed by the clear waters flowing down from Mount Fuji. On clear days the mountain itself rises in the background, and in spring cherry blossoms line the banks, making it a rewarding stop for photographers seeking a Fuji view without crowds, though it remains a modest local spot rather than a developed attraction.

item.title: Sakura Shrimp: Suruga Bay's Pink Treasure — Guide
item.description: Sakura shrimp (sakura-ebi) are tiny, translucent deep-water shrimp with a delicate pink colour like cherry blossom, caught commercially nowhere in Japan but the deep waters of Suruga Bay, making them one of the country’s most localised delicacies. The fishing seasons run in spring and autumn from the port of Yui, whose restaurants serve the catch raw over rice, fried into crisp golden kakiage fritters, or dried, and in season the drying yards spread the shrimp in pink carpets against a backdrop of Mount Fuji.

item.title: Shiraito Falls: A Curtain of Fuji Spring Water — Guide
item.description: Shiraito Falls, near Fujinomiya at the southwestern foot of Mount Fuji, is one of Japan’s most graceful waterfalls, its name meaning ‘white threads’ after the hundreds of silky streams of water that pour over a curved, 20-metre-high and 150-metre-wide cliff face. Almost all of the water is Mount Fuji’s rain and snowmelt, filtered through the volcanic rock for decades before emerging from the cliff itself, and the falls are a component site of Fuji’s World Heritage listing, long revered as a place of worship and purification.

item.title: Shizuoka Green Tea: Japan's Tea Capital — Guide
item.description: Shizuoka is Japan’s tea capital, producing around 40% of the nation’s green tea, its rolling hillsides striped with the neat emerald rows of tea fields that have shaped the prefecture’s landscape and identity since the 13th century. The year peaks with the spring shincha season, when the prized first flush of new leaves is picked from late April through May, celebrated with hands-on tea-picking experiences, fresh-leaf tastings and the grassy, sweet flavour of new tea served everywhere from farm stands to fine tea salons.

item.title: Shizuoka Oden: Black-Broth Skewers With Dashi Powder — Guide
item.description: Shizuoka oden is the city’s beloved take on Japan’s winter stew, its skewered ingredients — dark beef-sinew, boiled eggs, daikon and the local black hanpen fish cake — simmered in a jet-black broth built on beef stock and dark soy that shops keep alive and topped up, sometimes for decades. Everything is eaten off the skewer with a sprinkle of dashi powder and dried green seaweed, and the classic settings are as memorable as the food: the lantern-lit alley bars of the Aoba Oden Yokocho district and, uniquely, old-fashioned candy shops where children have snacked on oden for generations.

item.title: Shizuoka Tea Plantation Tours: Walks, Tastings and Tea Ceremony — Guide
item.description: The tea country around Shimada and the vast Makinohara plateau is the deepest heartland of Japanese tea, and a number of working farms and tea-garden temples here open their gates to visitors, offering guided walks between the emerald rows, comparative tastings of different grades and cultivars, and seated tea ceremonies overlooking the fields. These plantation experiences turn tea from a drink into a place: you see the leaf on the bush, learn how steaming and rolling shape its flavour, and finish with a properly prepared bowl in sight of the rows it came from.

item.title: Shuzenji Onsen: Izu's Most Atmospheric Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Shuzenji Onsen, set in a wooded valley in the centre of the Izu Peninsula, is widely considered Izu’s most atmospheric hot spring town, its history beginning with the temple said to have been founded by the monk Kukai some 1,200 years ago. The town wraps around the Katsura River, where vermilion bridges, a riverside footbath at the Tokko-no-yu spring, and a lantern-lit bamboo grove path create a compact, strollable scene of classic Japan, backed by ryokan whose baths draw on the valley’s long-flowing waters.

item.title: Suruga Bay: Japan's Deepest Bay Beneath Mount Fuji — Guide
item.description: Suruga Bay is Japan’s deepest bay, plunging to around 2,500 metres, an extraordinary depth so close to shore that it creates a unique marine environment home to deep-sea creatures and Japan’s only commercial sakura shrimp fishery. For visitors, the bay pairs dramatic views of Mount Fuji rising directly across the water with scenic coastal drives, ports serving remarkably fresh seafood, and a deep-sea aquarium in Numazu dedicated to the strange creatures hauled from its depths.

item.title: Ayu Sweetfish from the Nagara River — Guide
item.description: Ayu (sweetfish) from the Nagara River are a prized summer delicacy in Gifu, the clear, undammed river’s purity giving the fish a delicate, subtly sweet flavour and clean aroma that make Nagara ayu especially esteemed among Japanese food lovers. The most classic preparation is shioyaki, the whole fish skewered and salt-grilled over charcoal until the skin is crisp, eaten head to tail, and the ayu season, roughly summer, coincides with the river’s famous ukai cormorant fishing that traditionally caught them.

item.title: Bessho Onsen: A Historic Hot Spring Town Called 'Little Kamakura' — Guide
item.description: Bessho Onsen is one of Japan’s oldest hot spring towns, its waters used since ancient times, and today combines traditional public bathhouses and ryokan with an unusual concentration of important historic temples, pagodas and Buddhist statues dating from the Kamakura period, earning it the nickname the ‘Kamakura of Shinshu’. This blend of restorative hot springs and cultural heritage, set in a quiet valley in eastern Nagano, makes it a rewarding destination for travellers wanting to combine a relaxing soak with genuine historical sightseeing.

item.title: Gero Onsen: One of Japan's Three Great Hot Springs — Guide
item.description: Gero Onsen has been ranked among Japan’s three greatest hot springs since the Edo period, prized for its smooth, skin-softening alkaline waters, and sits in a scenic river valley conveniently located on the rail line between Nagoya and Takayama. The town is built around the Hida River, lined with ryokan and public bathhouses, and offers several free foot baths scattered along the streets and riverbank, plus a riverside open-air bath, making it easy to sample the famous waters whether staying overnight or passing through.

item.title: Gifu Castle: A Mountaintop Castle With Sweeping Valley Views — Guide
item.description: Gifu Castle sits dramatically atop 329-metre Mount Kinka, reached by a ropeway followed by a short walk, and was once the stronghold of the warlord Oda Nobunaga, who launched his campaign to unify Japan from here in the 16th century. Though the current keep is a modern reconstruction, its commanding hilltop position offers sweeping panoramic views over Gifu City, the Nagara River winding below and the surrounding plains, making the journey up as much about the vista as the castle itself.

item.title: Gujo Hachiman: A Historic Water Town of Clear Streams — Guide
item.description: Gujo Hachiman is a historic castle town in central Gifu famous for its exceptionally clear water, with canals, springs and streams threaded through the old streets, small waterways running beside houses, and a culture built around treasuring and using the pure water in daily life. Above the town sits a small reconstructed mountain castle with valley views, while the streets below are lined with traditional houses, sweet shops and workshops, and the town is especially renowned for the Gujo Odori, a lively folk dance held over many summer nights.

item.title: Gujo Odori: Japan's Longest Summer Dance Festival — Guide
item.description: Gujo Odori is one of Japan’s three great folk dances and one of its longest-running summer festivals, held over roughly 30 nights across the summer in the water town of Gujo Hachiman. Unlike festivals watched from the sidelines, Gujo Odori is a participatory dance in which anyone, locals and visitors alike, joins the circle around a central stage to dance to live music and singing, and during the famous Obon period in mid-August the celebration continues in all-night dances that run until dawn.

item.title: Hakuba: Nagano's Premier Ski and Mountain Resort — Guide
item.description: Hakuba is one of Japan’s premier ski and mountain resort areas, a cluster of interconnected ski resorts beneath the towering Northern Japan Alps that hosted several events during the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics. Renowned for its abundant, reliable powder snow, extensive and varied terrain and a lively international resort scene, Hakuba draws skiers and snowboarders from around the world in winter, while the green season offers hiking, alpine scenery and outdoor activities amid the same dramatic mountain backdrop.

item.title: Hida Beef: Gifu's Premium Marbled Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Hida beef is one of Japan’s top premium wagyu brands, produced from black-haired cattle raised in the Hida region of Gifu and prized for its fine, delicate marbling, melt-in-the-mouth tenderness and rich, sweet flavour. It is served across Takayama and the wider region in many forms, from steak and hoba-miso (grilled over a magnolia leaf with miso) to Hida beef sushi, croquettes and grilled skewers sold as street food in the old town, giving visitors plenty of ways to sample it at every price point.

item.title: Hida Folk Village: An Open-Air Museum of Traditional Mountain Houses — Guide
item.description: Hida Folk Village (Hida no Sato) is an open-air museum set on a hillside above Takayama, gathering more than 30 traditional houses relocated from across the mountainous Hida region, including steep gassho-zukuri farmhouses, and arranged around a central pond with mountain views. Visitors can enter many of the buildings to see the tools, hearths and layouts of old rural life, and craft demonstrations bring the traditional mountain culture to life, making it an accessible way to understand the region’s heritage in one place, especially useful alongside or instead of a trip to Shirakawa-go.

item.title: Hida Mountains: Northern Alps Views from the Gifu Side — Guide
item.description: The Hida Mountains form the Gifu side of the Northern Japan Alps, rising to over 3,000 metres in dramatic peaks including Okuhotaka, Japan’s third-highest mountain, and offer some of the country’s most spectacular high-mountain scenery. The most accessible way to experience it is the Shinhotaka Ropeway, a double-decker cable car that climbs to a viewing platform at over 2,150 metres, delivering sweeping panoramas of the surrounding peaks without any hiking, while the Okuhida onsen villages below offer hot springs with mountain views.

item.title: Hida Tofu & Dengaku: The Firm Mountain Tofu of the Hida Region — Guide
item.description: Hida tofu is a notably firm, dense style of tofu made in the mountainous Hida region using the area’s cold, clean water, traditionally pressed harder and made sturdier than typical tofu so it could withstand the region’s cold winters and be handled and cooked more robustly. A classic way to enjoy it is dengaku, in which the tofu is skewered, coated with a sweet-savoury miso glaze and grilled over charcoal, and it also features in the region’s simmered and hotpot dishes, offering a hearty, warming taste of Hida mountain cuisine.

item.title: Jigokudani Snow Monkey Park: Wild Macaques Bathing in Hot Springs — Guide
item.description: Jigokudani Snow Monkey Park is famous worldwide as the only place where wild Japanese macaques (snow monkeys) regularly bathe in natural hot springs, soaking in a steaming pool to keep warm, most iconically surrounded by deep snow in winter. Reached by a roughly 30-minute walk along a forest trail from the car park, the park lets visitors observe the wild troop up close as they relax, groom and play around the pool, an experience possible year-round but at its most magical and photogenic when snow blankets the valley.

item.title: Kamikochi: The Northern Alps' Pristine Alpine Valley — Guide
item.description: Kamikochi is a protected high-altitude valley in the Northern Japan Alps, roughly 1,500 metres above sea level, renowned for its pristine scenery: the clear Azusa River winding beneath towering peaks, the iconic Kappa Bridge, marshes and ponds, and forests carpeted with alpine wildflowers in summer. Private cars are banned to protect the fragile environment, so access is by bus or taxi only, and the valley offers everything from easy flat riverside walks and flower-viewing trails to serious mountaineering routes into the surrounding Alps, all within a genuinely spectacular natural setting.

item.title: Karuizawa: Nagano's Fashionable Highland Resort Town — Guide
item.description: Karuizawa is a fashionable highland resort town in eastern Nagano, long favoured since the late 19th century as a cool summer retreat from the heat of Tokyo, and now easily reached by Shinkansen in around an hour. The town combines refreshing forested scenery and cycling paths with an upmarket resort atmosphere of cafes, restaurants, historic churches and a large outlet shopping mall by the station, making it a relaxed and accessible destination that blends nature, leisure and shopping across the seasons.

item.title: Keichan: Gifu's Miso-Marinated Grilled Chicken — Guide
item.description: Keichan is a hearty local dish from the Gujo and Hida areas of Gifu, consisting of chicken marinated in a savoury sauce, usually miso-based but sometimes soy or salt, then grilled together with cabbage and other vegetables on a hot plate, frequently cooked at the table. Originally a home-style farmhouse dish, its bold, garlicky-miso flavour and satisfying, communal cooking style have made it a beloved regional comfort food, served at restaurants and sold as marinated packs to cook at home.

item.title: Matsumoto Castle: Japan's Oldest Five-Tiered Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Matsumoto Castle, nicknamed ‘Crow Castle’ for its striking black exterior, is one of Japan’s most important original castles and a designated National Treasure, its five-tiered keep dating to the late 16th century and standing as one of the oldest surviving original keeps in the country. Unlike hilltop castles, it sits on flat land surrounded by a wide moat that mirrors the black-and-white keep, and the scene is especially memorable when framed by cherry blossoms in late April or lit up during seasonal night illuminations reflecting on the still water.

item.title: Mino Washi: UNESCO-Recognised Japanese Paper & Papermaking — Guide
item.description: Mino washi is among Japan’s finest traditional handmade papers, produced in the town of Mino in central Gifu for over 1,300 years and prized for its exceptional thinness, strength and even texture, with the traditional ‘hon-minoshi’ technique recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. The historic town of Mino preserves a beautiful old merchant street of udatsu-walled houses built by prosperous paper traders, and visitors can explore a dedicated washi museum and try hands-on papermaking workshops, forming their own sheet of Mino paper to take home.

item.title: Mitarashi Dango: Takayama's Savoury Grilled Rice Dumplings — Guide
item.description: Mitarashi dango are skewered rice dumplings grilled over charcoal and glazed with soy sauce, and Takayama’s version is distinctive for being savoury rather than the sweet, syrupy style found in much of the rest of Japan, brushed simply with a soy-based sauce and grilled until fragrant. Sold hot from street stalls along the old town’s lanes, they are a popular, inexpensive snack to eat while walking, the smell of the grilling dango a familiar part of the Sanmachi Suji atmosphere.

item.title: Mount Ontake: A Sacred Volcanic Mountain of Pilgrimage — Guide
item.description: Mount Ontake is Japan’s second-highest volcano at 3,067 metres, straddling the border of Gifu and Nagano, and has been revered as a sacred mountain for centuries, serving as a major centre of the shugendo and Ontake-kyo mountain-worship traditions with shrines, stone monuments and pilgrim trails on its slopes. The mountain offers dramatic high-altitude volcanic scenery and hiking, though it is an active volcano; following an eruption in 2014, access to certain areas near the summit has at times been restricted, so current conditions and any restrictions should always be checked before planning to climb.

item.title: Nagano Apple Picking & Cider Tasting: The Orchard Prefecture — Guide
item.description: Nagano is one of Japan’s leading apple-growing regions, its cool climate, sunny days and well-drained highland soil producing crisp, flavourful apples in varieties from Fuji to Shinano Gold, and each autumn its orchards open to visitors for apple picking. In a picking session, visitors harvest ripe apples straight from the tree, often with all-you-can-eat options, and many orchards and nearby producers also offer fresh apple juice and cider tasting, turning a simple harvest activity into a fuller taste of the region’s orchard culture.

item.title: Nagara River Ukai: 1,300 Years of Cormorant Fishing — Guide
item.description: Ukai, or cormorant fishing, on the Nagara River near Gifu City is one of Japan’s most spectacular living traditions, practised for roughly 1,300 years, in which master fishermen (usho) in traditional grass skirts guide trained cormorants to dive for ayu sweetfish by the light of blazing baskets of fire hung from their boats. Held on summer nights, the fishing is watched from passenger viewing boats that drift alongside, and the usho of the Nagara River even hold a special imperial appointment, underlining the cultural importance of this atmospheric nighttime spectacle.

item.title: Nagara River Valley: One of Japan's Clearest Rivers — Guide
item.description: The Nagara River is counted among Japan’s three clearest rivers, flowing from the mountains of central Gifu through scenic gorges and green valleys on a largely undammed course that has kept its water exceptionally pure. This clarity supports the river’s famous ayu sweetfish and the centuries-old tradition of ukai cormorant fishing near Gifu City, while upstream the valley offers scenic drives, riverside walks and rafting, and the water itself is central to the culture and cuisine of the towns along its banks.

item.title: Narai-juku: A Beautifully Preserved Edo-Era Post Town — Guide
item.description: Narai-juku is one of the best-preserved post towns (shukuba) on the old Nakasendo, the Edo-period highway that connected Tokyo and Kyoto through the mountains, and was historically one of the most prosperous stops thanks to its position before a difficult mountain pass. Today its roughly one-kilometre street of dark wooden merchant houses, traditional inns, craft shops and cafes is preserved largely intact, letting visitors walk through an atmospheric slice of Edo-era travel history far quieter than Japan’s more famous historic streets.

item.title: Norikura Highland: An Alpine Plateau of Meadows and Waterfalls — Guide
item.description: Norikura Highland (Norikura Kogen) is a scenic alpine plateau at the foot of 3,026-metre Mount Norikura, offering cool highland scenery of marshland boardwalk trails, waterfalls, ponds and alpine meadows that bloom with wildflowers in summer and colour in autumn. Private cars are banned on the mountain road to protect the environment, but a bus climbs to Tatamidaira at over 2,700 metres, near the summit, giving relatively easy access to some of Japan’s highest road-reachable alpine scenery, with short walks to viewpoints and, for the prepared, a hike to the peak.

item.title: Northern Japan Alps: Hotaka, Yari and Japan's High Peaks — Guide
item.description: The Northern Japan Alps (Hida Mountains) rise to over 3,000 metres along Nagano’s western edge, forming some of the most dramatic high-mountain terrain in the country and home to iconic peaks including the spear-like Yarigatake and the Hotaka range, Japan’s third-highest mountain. These are serious mountaineering destinations, drawing experienced climbers to multi-day routes with mountain huts, rocky ridgelines and demanding ascents, while accessible base points like Kamikochi let less experienced visitors admire the peaks from the valley below without attempting the summits themselves.

item.title: Nozawa Onsen Dosojin Fire Festival: One of Japan's Great Fire Festivals — Guide
item.description: The Nozawa Onsen Dosojin Fire Festival, held every 15 January, is considered one of Japan’s three great fire festivals, a dramatic and intense nighttime spectacle centred on a huge wooden shrine (shaden) built by the villagers. In the festival’s climax, men aged 25 and 42 (considered unlucky ages) defend the structure from villagers attacking with flaming torches in a fierce battle of fire, before the shrine is finally set alight, all as a prayer for a good harvest, family wellbeing and the blessing of children, set against the deep snow of the mountain village.

item.title: Nozawa Onsen: A Traditional Ski Village With Free Public Baths — Guide
item.description: Nozawa Onsen is a rare and appealing combination of a major ski resort and an atmospheric, centuries-old hot spring village, where visitors can ski or snowboard on the powder slopes above and then descend into a village of narrow lanes, ryokan and no fewer than thirteen free public bathhouses (soto-yu) maintained by the local community. This blend of world-class winter sports and authentic onsen village character, complete with steaming public foot baths and a communal hot-spring cooking area, gives Nozawa a distinctive atmosphere unlike purpose-built modern resorts.

item.title: Nozawana Pickles: Nagano's Signature Pickled Greens — Guide
item.description: Nozawana are the long leafy greens of a local turnip variety originally from the Nozawa Onsen area, traditionally salt-pickled in large batches after the autumn harvest to preserve them through the long mountain winter, resulting in one of Nagano’s most characteristic tsukemono (pickles). The pickled greens have a savoury, gently tangy flavour and are eaten on their own, chopped over rice, wrapped around rice, or used as a filling for oyaki dumplings, appearing on tables and in shops throughout the prefecture as an everyday local staple.

item.title: Obuse: Hokusai Museum & Chestnut Town — Guide
item.description: Obuse is a charming small town northeast of Nagano City, best known as the place where the great ukiyo-e artist Katsushika Hokusai spent his final years, producing works now displayed at the town’s dedicated Hokusai Museum, including painted ceiling panels for local festival floats. Beyond its artistic heritage, Obuse is famous for chestnuts, with shops selling chestnut sweets and rice, alongside sake breweries and beautifully kept lanes and gardens, making it an ideal spot for a relaxed half-day of walking, art and food.

item.title: Oyaki: Nagano's Savoury Stuffed Dumplings — Guide
item.description: Oyaki are one of Nagano’s most beloved home-style foods, round dumplings of wheat or buckwheat dough wrapped around a savoury (or sometimes sweet) filling, then grilled, steamed or baked, historically a practical staple in a mountainous region where rice was harder to grow. Common fillings include nozawana pickled greens, eggplant, sweet red bean and seasonal vegetables, and the dumplings are sold at specialty shops, markets and roadside stands throughout the prefecture as a warm, satisfying and affordable local snack.

item.title: Sanzoku-yaki: Matsumoto's Giant Garlic Fried Chicken — Guide
item.description: Sanzoku-yaki, literally ‘bandit grill’, is a hearty specialty of the Matsumoto area, consisting of a large piece of chicken thigh marinated in a bold garlic-and-soy sauce, then coated and deep-fried until crisp and golden, typically served as a single generous, satisfying portion. The dish’s punchy garlic flavour and substantial size have made it a beloved local comfort food, found at restaurants around Matsumoto and the wider central Nagano region, often accompanied by cabbage and rice.

item.title: Shiga Kogen: Japan's Largest Ski Resort and Highland Plateau — Guide
item.description: Shiga Kogen is Japan’s largest interconnected ski resort, a vast highland area of linked ski slopes served by a single combined lift pass that hosted events during the 1998 Nagano Olympics, renowned for its high elevation and long, reliable snow season. Beyond winter, the same plateau is a designated UNESCO biosphere reserve, and in the green season its ponds, marshes, forests and hiking trails at over 1,500 metres offer cool highland nature, alpine plants and autumn foliage, making it a genuine year-round mountain destination.

item.title: Shinshu Miso: Japan's Most Widely Produced Miso — Guide
item.description: Shinshu miso, the rice-based miso produced in Nagano, is Japan’s most widely made variety, accounting for around half of all the country’s miso production, thanks to the region’s cool climate being ideal for the slow fermentation that gives it its characteristic golden colour and balanced, medium-salty flavour. Beyond seasoning countless dishes, the miso can be explored at breweries around the prefecture, some historic and centuries old, which offer tours, tastings and shops explaining the fermentation process behind this staple of Japanese cooking.

item.title: Shinshu Soba: Nagano's Celebrated Buckwheat Noodles — Guide
item.description: Shinshu soba (buckwheat noodles) is one of Nagano’s signature foods, the region’s cool climate, clean mountain water and buckwheat-friendly highland terrain making it one of Japan’s most celebrated soba-producing areas. The noodles are prized for their firm texture and rich, nutty buckwheat flavour, served cold with dipping sauce or hot in broth at countless restaurants across the prefecture, and many places also offer hands-on soba-making classes where visitors mix, roll, and cut their own noodles under a master’s guidance before eating them fresh.

item.title: Shirakawa-go Winter Illumination: The Snow Village Lit Up at Night — Guide
item.description: On a small number of select evenings each winter, usually in January and February, the snow-covered gassho-zukuri farmhouses of Shirakawa-go are illuminated after dark, their thatched roofs glowing warmly against the deep snow in one of Japan’s most magical and photographed seasonal sights. The event has become so popular that access is now strictly managed by advance reservation, with limited spots for both viewing and parking, so visiting requires planning ahead rather than simply turning up on the night.

item.title: Shirakawa-go: Japan's Famous UNESCO Gassho-Zukuri Village — Guide
item.description: Shirakawa-go is Japan’s most famous gassho-zukuri village and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its steep, thatched-roof farmhouses, some more than 250 years old, designed to shed the region’s heavy winter snowfall and built without nails using a distinctive prayer-hands roof structure. Set amid rice paddies against a mountain backdrop in a remote valley, the village of Ogimachi is beautiful across every season, and a number of the historic farmhouses operate as guesthouses offering overnight farmhouse stays, letting visitors experience the interior and hospitality of these remarkable buildings first-hand.

item.title: Skiing at Dynaland & Hirugano: Gifu's Accessible Ski Resorts — Guide
item.description: The Gujo highlands in central Gifu are home to several accessible ski resorts, most notably Dynaland and the adjacent Takasu Snow Park, which connect to form one of the region’s largest ski areas with extensive, varied terrain and popular night skiing. Nearby Hirugano Kogen offers gentler, family-friendly slopes, and the whole area’s convenient location within easy reach of Nagoya and central Gifu makes it a popular winter destination for day trips and weekend visits from the surrounding region.

item.title: Suwa Grand Shrine (Suwa-taisha): One of Japan's Oldest Shrines — Guide
item.description: Suwa Grand Shrine, or Suwa-taisha, is among Japan’s oldest and most important Shinto shrines, with a history stretching back beyond reliable records, and unusually comprises four separate shrine sites spread around Lake Suwa rather than a single location. Each site features four towering sacred wooden pillars (onbashira) at its corners, which are ceremonially replaced every six years during the Onbashira Festival, one of Japan’s most dramatic and dangerous festivals, in which huge tree trunks are dragged down mountainsides and ridden by participants.

item.title: Suwa Lake Fireworks: One of Japan's Grandest Fireworks Displays — Guide
item.description: The Lake Suwa Fireworks Festival, held each August, is one of Japan’s largest and most spectacular fireworks displays, launching tens of thousands of shells over the lake in a show that lasts around two hours. The surrounding mountains form a natural amphitheatre that amplifies and echoes the booms, while the lake reflects the bursts across the water, creating an overwhelming sensory experience; a separate autumn ‘new fireworks championship’ also showcases innovative competitive pyrotechnics, making Suwa one of Japan’s premier fireworks destinations.

item.title: Takayama Festival Float Museum: See the Ornate Festival Yatai Year-Round — Guide
item.description: The Takayama Festival’s elaborate wooden yatai floats, considered masterworks of Hida carpentry decorated with gilding, intricate carvings, lacquer and mechanical marionettes, only appear on the streets during the twice-yearly festival, but the Takayama Festival Float Museum (Yatai Kaikan) lets visitors see several of them up close throughout the year. Displayed in a hall beside the Sakurayama Hachimangu shrine, the rotating selection of towering floats offers a rare chance to appreciate the extraordinary craftsmanship in detail, whatever season you visit.

item.title: Takayama Sanmachi Suji: A Beautifully Preserved Merchant Old Town — Guide
item.description: Sanmachi Suji is the beautifully preserved heart of Takayama’s old town, a cluster of narrow lanes lined with dark wooden merchant houses dating from the Edo period, when the town prospered as a centre of skilled carpenters and merchants in the mountainous Hida region. Today the lanes are home to sake breweries marked by cedar-ball signs, cafes, craft shops, and stalls selling Hida beef and local sweets, making it one of Japan’s most atmospheric and enjoyable historic districts to explore on foot.

item.title: Takayama Spring & Autumn Festivals: Among Japan's Most Beautiful — Guide
item.description: The Takayama Festivals are held twice a year, the Sanno Matsuri in April (spring) and the Hachiman Matsuri in October (autumn), and are counted among Japan’s three most beautiful festivals. Both feature parades of the town’s spectacular yatai floats, masterpieces of Hida carpentry decorated with gilding and carvings, alongside mechanical marionette (karakuri) performances that draw gasps from the crowds. The evening processions, when the illuminated floats are pulled through the old town by lantern light, are a particular highlight of these centuries-old celebrations.

item.title: Togakushi Shrine: A Sacred Mountain Shrine and Towering Cedar Avenue — Guide
item.description: Togakushi Shrine is a sacred mountain shrine complex set deep in the forested mountains north of Nagano City, comprising three main shrines (the lower, middle and upper) connected by walking trails and steeped in centuries of mountain-worship and shugendo ascetic tradition. Its most famous feature is the approach to the Okusha inner shrine, a roughly two-kilometre forest path lined for its final stretch with towering ancient cedar trees, some over 400 years old, creating one of the most atmospheric shrine approaches in Japan; the area is also historically linked to the Togakure school of ninja.

item.title: Zenkoji Gokaicho: The Once-in-Seven-Years Grand Pilgrimage — Guide
item.description: The Zenkoji Gokaicho is a grand religious event held at Zenkoji Temple roughly once every seven years, during which a special ‘substitute’ image of the temple’s normally hidden Buddha is revealed, and a tall wooden pillar (kaicho-bashira) is erected in front of the main hall, connected by a sacred cord to the image inside. Millions of pilgrims travel to Nagano over the roughly two-month event to touch the pillar, believed to forge a direct connection with the Buddha and its blessings, making it one of Japan’s largest and most significant recurring religious gatherings.

item.title: Zenkoji Temple: Nagano's Great Non-Sectarian Pilgrimage Temple — Guide
item.description: Zenkoji is one of Japan’s most important and popular pilgrimage temples, founded in the 7th century and unusual in welcoming worshippers of all Buddhist sects, which helped make it a destination for pilgrims from across the country for centuries. The temple’s grand main hall houses a famous ‘hidden Buddha’, an image never shown to the public, and visitors can walk the o-kaidan, a pitch-black underground passage beneath the main hall where they feel for a metaphorical ‘key to paradise’ in total darkness, one of the temple’s most memorable experiences.

item.title: Aokigahara Forest: The 'Sea of Trees' on Fuji's Lava Plateau — Guide
item.description: Aokigahara Forest, known as the Jukai or ‘Sea of Trees’, is a dense woodland grown atop a hardened lava plateau formed by an ancient eruption of Mount Fuji over a thousand years ago, its trees rooted in the rocky volcanic ground rather than deep soil. The forest offers well-marked nature trails and access to lava caves, including atmospheric ice caves that stay cold year-round, and while it has a reputation in popular culture, for visitors it is simply a striking and unusual volcanic woodland best explored along its established, signposted paths.

item.title: Chureito Pagoda: The Iconic Five-Storey Pagoda With Mount Fuji — Guide
item.description: Chureito Pagoda is a five-storey red pagoda set on a hillside above Fujiyoshida, reached by a climb of just under 400 steps, and frames one of Japan’s most iconic views: the vermilion pagoda in the foreground with Mount Fuji rising behind it across the town below. The scene is especially striking in spring when cherry blossoms surround the pagoda, and in autumn with coloured foliage, drawing photographers from around the world to what has become one of the most recognisable images of Japan.

item.title: Climbing Mount Fuji: The Yoshida Trail and Climbing Season — Guide
item.description: The Yoshida Trail is the most popular route to the 3,776-metre summit of Mount Fuji, starting from the Fuji Subaru Line 5th Station on Yamanashi’s northern side and offering the most mountain huts, first-aid stations and facilities of any Fuji route. Climbing is only permitted during a short official season each summer, roughly early July to early September, marked by the traditional Yamabiraki (mountain-opening) ceremony, with most climbers timing their ascent to reach the summit for the famous goraiko sunrise before descending the same day or after an overnight hut stay.

item.title: Fuji Shibazakura Festival: A Carpet of Pink Moss Phlox Beneath Fuji — Guide
item.description: The Fuji Shibazakura Festival is held each spring near Lake Motosuko at the foot of Mount Fuji, when hundreds of thousands of shibazakura (moss phlox) plants bloom in sweeping carpets of pink, white and purple across the ground, set directly beneath the snow-capped mountain. Running roughly from mid-April to late May, it is one of Japan’s most spectacular flower festivals, with the low-growing blooms creating a vivid foreground to Fuji, alongside food stalls, viewpoints and photo spots that draw large crowds during its short season.

item.title: Fuji-Q Highland: Record-Breaking Roller Coasters Beneath Mount Fuji — Guide
item.description: Fuji-Q Highland is a major amusement park at the foot of Mount Fuji, famous for its collection of record-breaking roller coasters, several of which have held world records for height, speed or number of inversions, all set against the dramatic backdrop of the mountain itself. Beyond the thrill rides, the park offers themed attractions, character-based areas popular with families, and a notoriously long and elaborate haunted-house attraction, making it a popular day out combining adrenaline with unbeatable Fuji views.

item.title: Hoto: Yamanashi's Hearty Miso Noodle Hotpot — Guide
item.description: Hoto is Yamanashi’s signature soul food, a hearty hotpot dish of thick, flat, chewy wheat noodles simmered directly in a rich miso-based broth alongside pumpkin, root vegetables and other seasonal produce, traditionally served bubbling in a cast-iron pot. Unlike udon, the noodles are cooked straight in the broth without pre-boiling, thickening it as the starch releases, and the dish’s warming, filling character made it a staple of the mountainous region’s diet, historically associated with the samurai warlord Takeda Shingen’s provisions.

item.title: Kawaguchiko & the Fuji Five Lakes: Mount Fuji Across the Water — Guide
item.description: The Fuji Five Lakes (Fujigoko) are a string of five lakes at the northern foot of Mount Fuji, formed by ancient lava flows, offering some of the mountain’s most celebrated reflections across the water and panoramic viewpoints in every season. Kawaguchiko is the most accessible and developed of the five, ringed with lakeside resorts, ropeways, museums and hot springs, and famous for the ‘upside-down Fuji’ reflection on calm days, autumn foliage framing the peak, and clear winter panoramas when the snow-capped mountain is at its sharpest.

item.title: Kawaguchiko Lakeside Cycling: Circle the Lake Beneath Mount Fuji — Guide
item.description: Cycling around Lake Kawaguchiko is one of the most enjoyable ways to experience the Fuji Five Lakes, following a mostly flat route that circles the lake with ever-changing views of Mount Fuji reflected across the water. Rental shops near Kawaguchiko Station offer bicycles, including e-bikes for the gentle hills, and the roughly 18-kilometre loop passes quiet lakeside stretches, viewpoints, cafes, museums and hot springs, letting riders set their own pace and stop wherever the Fuji views are best.

item.title: Kofu Castle Ruins (Maizuru Castle Park): The City's Central Historic Park — Guide
item.description: Kofu Castle, also known as Maizuru Castle, was built in the late 16th century, and while the main keep no longer stands, its impressive surviving stone walls, gates and reconstructed turrets remain at the heart of Kofu City as Maizuru Castle Park. The park is a pleasant central green space just a short walk from Kofu Station, with climbable stonework offering views over the city toward the surrounding mountains, making it an easy, free stop for visitors exploring central Kofu on foot.

item.title: Lake Yamanakako SUP: Paddleboarding Beneath Mount Fuji — Guide
item.description: Lake Yamanakako is the largest and highest of the Fuji Five Lakes, and its relatively calm, shallow waters make it a popular spot for stand-up paddleboarding (SUP) with an unbeatable backdrop: Mount Fuji rising directly across the lake. Rental operators and guided sessions cater to beginners and experienced paddlers alike, and gliding across the water with the mountain reflected below is one of the region’s most memorable and photogenic water experiences, especially in the calm conditions of early morning.

item.title: Mount Fuji UNESCO World Heritage Sites: The Sacred Mountain's Cultural Legacy — Guide
item.description: Mount Fuji was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013 not as a natural wonder but as a cultural site, recognised as a ‘sacred place and source of artistic inspiration’ that has shaped Japanese religion, art and identity for centuries. The designation includes numerous component sites across the mountain’s northern foot in Yamanashi, from the Fujisan Hongu Sengen shrines that served as bases for pilgrim ascents, to the Fuji Five Lakes, Oshino Hakkai springs and other sacred natural features tied to Fuji worship, offering visitors a way to understand the mountain’s deep cultural significance beyond the view alone.

item.title: Nishizawa Valley: A Waterfall Hiking Trail Through Pristine Nature — Guide
item.description: Nishizawa Valley offers one of Yamanashi’s most rewarding half-day hikes, a loop trail that follows a clear mountain river through pristine forest past a series of waterfalls, culminating in the Nanatsugama Godan-no-taki, a beautiful tiered cascade of pools and falls counted among Japan’s 100 most celebrated waterfalls. The valley is especially popular in autumn when the foliage peaks, and the well-maintained trail combines genuine natural beauty with a manageable half-day of walking suited to reasonably fit visitors.

item.title: Oshino Hakkai: Eight Crystal-Clear Ponds Fed by Fuji Snowmelt — Guide
item.description: Oshino Hakkai is a set of eight spring-fed ponds of extraordinary clarity, filled by snowmelt from Mount Fuji that has filtered slowly through underground lava layers over many decades before emerging here, giving the water its famous transparency and vivid blue-green depths. Set within a traditional village of thatched-roof houses with Mount Fuji rising behind on clear days, the ponds are a designated Natural Monument and part of the mountain’s World Heritage listing, making a popular and highly photogenic stop between the Fuji Five Lakes.

item.title: Shingen Mochi: Yamanashi's Beloved Kinako-and-Syrup Sweet — Guide
item.description: Shingen mochi is one of Yamanashi’s most beloved local sweets, consisting of soft, chewy rice cake (mochi) generously dusted with kinako (roasted soybean flour) and served with a small pot of kuromitsu (black sugar syrup) to drizzle over the top. Named after the region’s revered samurai warlord Takeda Shingen, the sweet is sold in distinctive small boxes wrapped in a furoshiki cloth, and its combination of nutty soybean flour, chewy mochi and rich dark syrup makes it a popular souvenir and teatime treat.

item.title: Shosenkyo Gorge: One of Japan's Most Beautiful Ravines — Guide
item.description: Shosenkyo Gorge, near Kofu, is often ranked among Japan’s most beautiful gorges, offering a scenic walking trail that follows a clear river past towering granite rock formations, sculpted cliffs and the striking Sengataki Waterfall at its upper end. The gorge is especially renowned for its autumn foliage, when the mix of coloured maples against the pale granite draws large crowds, and a ropeway near the top offers panoramic views extending to Mount Fuji and the Southern Alps on clear days.

item.title: Yamanashi Peaches & Grapes: Fruit Picking in Japan's Orchard — Guide
item.description: Yamanashi is Japan’s top producer of both peaches and grapes, its sun-drenched, well-drained valleys around Kofu and Katsunuma filled with orchards that open to visitors for seasonal fruit picking. Peaches ripen from around June to August, followed by grapes through late summer and autumn, including the native Koshu variety also used for wine, and many orchards offer time-limited all-you-can-eat picking sessions where visitors harvest and eat fruit straight from the vine or tree, a popular family activity that pairs naturally with the region’s wine culture.

item.title: Yamanashi Prefectural Museum: The Region's History, Nature and Culture — Guide
item.description: The Yamanashi Prefectural Museum presents the region’s history, natural environment and culture through engaging, hands-on exhibits, themed around the long relationship between the people of Yamanashi and the land they live on, from the mountains and rivers to the wine and craft traditions. Set within a spacious park with outdoor areas to explore, the museum is designed to be accessible and interactive, making it a good indoor option for families and for visitors wanting deeper context on the region beyond its famous Mount Fuji views.

item.title: Yamanashi Wine & Katsunuma: Japan's Birthplace of Wine — Guide
item.description: Yamanashi is the birthplace and heart of the Japanese wine industry, centred on the Katsunuma area near Kofu, where the mild climate and the native Koshu grape, a pale pink variety used to make crisp, delicate white wines, have supported winemaking since the 1870s. Today the region is home to dozens of wineries ranging from historic family operations to modern estates, many offering tastings, cellar tours and even hands-on blending experiences, set among vineyards that turn golden in autumn and often within walking or cycling distance of one another.

item.title: Yamanashi Wine Festival: Tasting the Harvest in Japan's Wine Country — Guide
item.description: Yamanashi’s wine festivals are held in autumn around the grape harvest, gathering local wineries together for open-air tasting events that let visitors sample dozens of regional wines in a single place, often for a set entry fee that includes a tasting glass. Centred on the Katsunuma and Kofu wine districts, these festivals celebrate the region’s identity as the birthplace of Japanese wine, combining tastings with food stalls, local produce and a festive harvest-season atmosphere among the golden vineyards.

item.title: Yoshida Fire Festival: Giant Torches Marking Fuji's Climbing Season Close — Guide
item.description: The Yoshida Fire Festival, held each late August in Fujiyoshida, is one of Japan’s three most unusual festivals, traditionally marking the close of Mount Fuji’s climbing season with a dramatic display of fire. On the main evening, dozens of giant torches, some three metres tall, are lit along the town’s main street alongside smaller fires outside homes and shops, filling the streets with flame and smoke as portable shrines are paraded through, in a centuries-old ritual tied to the Sengen shrine and Fuji worship, praying for safety on the mountain.

item.title: Yoshida Udon: Fujiyoshida's Famously Firm, Chewy Noodles — Guide
item.description: Yoshida udon, a specialty of Fujiyoshida at the foot of Mount Fuji, is renowned for having some of the firmest, chewiest udon noodles in all of Japan, a texture so distinctively robust that it has become the dish’s defining characteristic. Typically served in a broth blending miso and soy sauce, topped with boiled cabbage, sometimes horse meat, and a spicy condiment called suridane, the dish is often found at simple, family-run shops, some operating out of private homes with limited lunchtime hours, giving it a genuinely local, unpretentious character.

item.title: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art: A Circular Museum With No Front or Back — Guide
item.description: The 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art is housed in a distinctive circular glass building designed with no defined front or back, intended to be equally approachable from every direction, and has become one of Kanazawa’s most visited cultural landmarks since opening in 2004. The museum’s best-known work is Leandro Erlich’s ‘Swimming Pool’ installation, which creates the illusion of a submerged pool viewable from both above and below, and several public exhibition spaces around the building can be enjoyed free of charge without a ticket to the paid galleries.

item.title: Anko Nabe: Ibaraki's Signature Monkfish Hot Pot — Guide
item.description: Anko nabe, monkfish hot pot, is Ibaraki’s signature winter dish, drawing on the abundant monkfish catch landed along the prefecture’s Pacific coast, particularly around Oarai. The dish traditionally uses nearly every part of the fish — liver, skin, and meat simmered together with vegetables and miso in a technique historically performed by hanging the fish and carving it directly, as monkfish’s slippery texture makes it difficult to prepare on a standard cutting board.

item.title: Ashikaga Flower Park: A 150-Year-Old Giant Wisteria Tree — Guide
item.description: Ashikaga Flower Park is home to a single great wisteria tree over 150 years old, its sprawling branches trained across a vast trellis covering roughly 1,000 square metres, blooming each late April into May into a cascading canopy of purple, pink and white blossoms that CNN once ranked among the world’s ‘dream destinations.’ Beyond the wisteria season, the park hosts seasonal displays year-round, including a large-scale winter illumination that transforms the flower beds into a light show after dark.

item.title: Awara Onsen: Fukui's Premier Hot Spring Resort Town — Guide
item.description: Awara Onsen is Fukui’s most prominent hot spring resort town, having welcomed guests for over 130 years since its waters were first developed in the late 19th century, and today offers numerous ryokan, public bathhouses and a relaxed resort atmosphere. Its convenient location near the coast makes it a natural base for winter Echizen crab trips and sightseeing at nearby Tojinbo Cliffs, and a foot bath in the town centre offers a free, casual way to sample the waters even for day visitors not staying overnight.

item.title: Chirihama Nagisa Driveway: Drive Directly on the Beach — Guide
item.description: Chirihama Nagisa Driveway is one of very few beaches in the world where cars can drive directly on the sand, a roughly 8-kilometre stretch of unusually firm, fine-grained beach on the Noto Peninsula’s coast that supports vehicle weight well enough for regular driving. The unusual experience of driving along the open beach with the sea just metres away, waves sometimes lapping close to the tyres, has made it a popular stop for road-trippers exploring the Noto Peninsula, offering photo opportunities and a memorable coastal drive found nowhere else in Japan.

item.title: Echigo Mountains & Sea of Japan Coastline: A Landscape of Contrasts — Guide
item.description: Niigata’s geography is defined by a striking contrast between the snow-capped Echigo mountain ranges inland, among Japan’s snowiest regions, and the rugged Sea of Japan coastline stretching along the prefecture’s western edge. Scenic coastal roads wind past dramatic cliffs, fishing villages and sunset viewpoints over the Sea of Japan, while inland routes climb into the mountains through forests and terraced rice paddies, together showcasing the full range of Niigata’s varied natural landscape within a single road trip.

item.title: Echigo-Tsumari Art Field: Contemporary Art Across Rice Terraces — Guide
item.description: Echigo-Tsumari Art Field is the site of one of the world’s largest international art festivals (Triennale), held every three years since 2000, though a substantial number of installations remain permanently on display across a sprawling rural area covering roughly 760 square kilometres. Works by artists from dozens of countries are integrated into the landscape of terraced rice paddies, forests, abandoned schools and traditional farmhouses, creating an unusual art-viewing experience that doubles as an exploration of depopulating rural Japan and its efforts at revitalisation through contemporary art.

item.title: Echizen Crab: Fukui's Prized Winter Snow Crab — Guide
item.description: Echizen crab, a variety of male snow crab (zuwaigani) landed along Fukui’s coast, is one of Japan’s most prized winter delicacies, distinguished by an official yellow tag attached to each certified crab to guarantee its origin and quality. The crab is in season from around November through March, and coastal towns like Echizen fill with markets and restaurants serving it during these months, prepared as sashimi, boiled, grilled or in hot pot, with prices reflecting its premium status, especially for the largest, highest-graded specimens.

item.title: Echizen Misaki Lighthouse: A Dramatic Cliffside Coastal Lighthouse — Guide
item.description: Echizen Misaki Lighthouse sits perched on rugged cliffs at the tip of the Echizen Peninsula, offering magnificent views of the open Sea of Japan and access to atmospheric coastal walking trails winding along the promontory. The austere beauty of this remote headland, considerably less visited than Fukui’s more famous Tojinbo Cliffs, makes it a good choice for travellers seeking solitude and dramatic seascape photography away from larger crowds. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Echizen, Fukui Hours Always accessible (exterior); lighthouse grounds daylight hours Admission Free Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Echizen Pottery: One of Japan's Six Ancient Kilns — Guide
item.description: Echizen ware is one of Japan’s Six Ancient Kilns, the country’s most historically significant pottery-producing centres, with a ceramic tradition in the region spanning some 850 years, known for its unglazed, earthy, high-fired stoneware whose natural ash-glaze finishes develop during wood firing. Today the Echizen pottery area gathers kilns, galleries and a ceramic museum, and workshops let visitors try the potter’s wheel or hand-forming themselves under artisan guidance, shaping a piece to be fired and sent on later.

item.title: Echizen Regional Cuisine: Seasonal Local Dishes at a Fukui Restaurant — Guide
item.description: Echizen regional cuisine restaurants showcase Fukui’s seasonal ingredients, from the coast’s prized seafood to inland mountain vegetables and local rice, offering a curated introduction to the prefecture’s traditional cooking that goes beyond its individual famous dishes like oroshi soba or sauce katsu-don. A meal at a dedicated regional cuisine restaurant typically presents a range of local specialties together, giving visitors a fuller sense of Fukui’s culinary character across land and sea in a single sitting.

item.title: Echizen Washi Village: 1,500 Years of Japanese Papermaking — Guide
item.description: Echizen has produced washi (traditional Japanese paper) for around 1,500 years, making it one of Japan’s foremost and oldest papermaking regions, historically prized for high-quality paper used in everything from official documents to art and calligraphy. The Echizen Washi Village gathers the craft’s heritage in one area, with a paper museum, a preserved historic papermaking house and workshops where visitors can try hands-on paper-making themselves, dipping and forming a sheet of washi to take home as a souvenir.

item.title: Eiheiji Temple: A Working Zen Monastery Deep in the Cedar Forest — Guide
item.description: Eiheiji Temple was founded in 1244 by the monk Dogen, founder of the Soto school of Zen Buddhism, and remains one of the school’s two head temples and an active training monastery today, home to monks who follow a strict daily schedule of meditation, chores and study. The temple’s numerous wooden halls are connected by a network of covered wooden corridors deep within a towering cedar forest, and visitors can walk the same corridors used by resident monks, while a scenic valley nature trail nearby offers a quieter forest walk beyond the temple grounds themselves.

item.title: Fukiware Falls: The 'Niagara of the Orient' on the Tone River — Guide
item.description: Fukiware Falls, sometimes nicknamed the ‘Niagara of the Orient’ for its wide, low, sweeping profile rather than sheer height, is formed where the Tone River — Japan’s second-longest river — has carved through volcanic rock into a dramatic gorge roughly 7 m deep and up to 30 m wide at points. Wooden viewing platforms and walkways let visitors take in the scene from multiple angles, with the churning white water especially striking after rainfall and framed by vivid maple foliage each autumn.

item.title: Fukui Castle Ruins Park: The City's Central Historic Landmark — Guide
item.description: Fukui Castle was once home to a five-storey keep, destroyed by fire in the 17th century and never rebuilt, but the surviving stone walls and moat remain at the historic centre of Fukui City, now surrounded by prefectural government buildings and a pleasant public park open to visitors. Though the keep itself is gone, the site’s stonework and moat offer a glimpse of the castle’s former scale, and the surrounding park’s central location makes it an easy, low-commitment stop for visitors exploring Fukui City on foot.

item.title: Fukui Prefectural Art Museum: Japanese and Regional Art in the City — Guide
item.description: The Fukui Prefectural Art Museum is a centrally located cultural stop in Fukui City, showcasing a collection of Japanese paintings, works by artists connected to the prefecture and rotating special exhibitions that change throughout the year. Its convenient location near Fukui Castle Ruins and the city centre makes it easy to combine with other central sights, offering an indoor cultural option that pairs well with an itinerary of the surrounding historical and civic attractions.

item.title: Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum: One of the World's Top Three Dinosaur Museums — Guide
item.description: The Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum is considered one of the world’s top three dinosaur museums, housed in a striking dome-shaped building and showcasing full dinosaur skeletons, fossils and interactive exhibits, many excavated from Fukui itself, which has proven to be one of Japan’s richest dinosaur fossil sites. The museum displays around 50 full dinosaur skeletons alongside detailed exhibits on prehistoric life, and visitors can also join guided tours to an actual fossil excavation site nearby to see ongoing palaeontological work in progress.

item.title: Fukui Prefectural Natural History Museum: Local Ecology and Natural Science — Guide
item.description: The Fukui Prefectural Natural History Museum offers a broader look at the prefecture’s natural science beyond dinosaurs, covering local ecology, geology and wildlife through hands-on exhibits and displays that give visitors a fuller picture of Fukui’s natural environment across different eras. Considerably smaller and less visited than the famous Dinosaur Museum, it makes a good complementary stop for visitors with a genuine interest in natural history rather than dinosaurs alone, or a manageable outing for families with younger children.

item.title: Fukui Sake Brewery Museum: Tasting and the Craft of Local Sake — Guide
item.description: Fukui’s clean mountain water and quality locally-grown rice make it a respected sake-producing region, and a visit to a local brewery museum offers visitors an accessible look at the traditional brewing process, from rice polishing and fermentation through to bottling, often housed within a working or historic brewery building. Most brewery visits include tastings of the region’s sake, giving visitors the chance to sample different styles and grades and understand how Fukui’s natural conditions shape the character of its rice wine.

item.title: Fukui Tanabata Festival & Fireworks: A Summer Star Festival Celebration — Guide
item.description: The Fukui Tanabata Festival is part of the nationwide summer Tanabata (Star Festival) tradition, which celebrates the legend of two star-crossed lovers allowed to meet just once a year, and fills the city with colourful paper streamer decorations and bamboo branches hung with handwritten wishes. Fukui’s celebration typically combines these festive decorations with food stalls and, on the main evening, a fireworks display, making it a lively seasonal event drawing residents and visitors together for a summer night out.

item.title: Gokayama: UNESCO Gassho-Zukuri Village & Doburoku Sake Festival — Guide
item.description: Gokayama is a UNESCO World Heritage cluster of gassho-zukuri farmhouses, distinguished by their steep, thatched roofs designed to shed heavy mountain snowfall, sitting in a remote valley considerably quieter than its better-known counterpart Shirakawa-go across the prefectural border. Each autumn, the village of Kaminashi celebrates the harvest with the traditional Doburoku Festival, offering visitors a taste of unrefined doburoku sake alongside shrine rituals and folk performances rooted in the isolated valley’s centuries-old traditions.

item.title: Gunma Apple & Fruit Orchards: Mountain-Grown Autumn Harvest — Guide
item.description: Gunma’s mountainous terrain and cool climate, particularly around Numata and the northern reaches of the prefecture, create favourable conditions for growing apples and other tree fruit, earning the region recognition as one of the Kanto area’s notable fruit-growing districts. Dozens of orchards open to visitors each autumn for hands-on picking experiences, offering a range of apple varieties alongside seasonal pears, grapes and other fruit depending on the orchard and time of year, with many farms also selling fresh cider, jams and baked goods made from their harvest.

item.title: Gunma Konnyaku: Japan's Konjac Capital — Guide
item.description: Gunma produces roughly 90% of Japan’s konjac (konnyaku), a low-calorie, high-fibre food made from the corm of the konjac plant, which thrives in the prefecture’s well-drained volcanic soil and cool climate. The gelatinous, jelly-textured food appears across Japanese cuisine in countless forms — firm grey blocks used in oden and simmered dishes, thread-like shirataki noodles, and even novelty sweets — and Gunma’s dedicated konnyaku shops and the themed Konnyaku Park near Fujioka let visitors sample the full range for free.

item.title: Gunma Safari Park: A Drive-Through Wildlife Encounter — Guide
item.description: Gunma Safari Park lets visitors experience a drive-through safari within Japan, with lions, tigers, bears and other large animals roaming semi-freely across expansive enclosures that vehicles pass through at a slow, controlled pace. Visitors can drive their own car (following strict safety guidelines) or ride a park safari bus for a more guided experience, while a separate walking zoo section offers closer encounters with smaller animals, feeding experiences, and a petting zone suited to younger children.

item.title: Gunma Wagyu & Yakiniku: Premium Grilled Beef from the Mountains — Guide
item.description: Gunma produces several respected wagyu beef brands, including Jomo Wagyu, raised on the prefecture’s cool mountain pastures under careful breeding and feeding standards that produce fine, even marbling and a rich, tender flavour. The beef is served throughout Gunma in dedicated yakiniku (grilled meat) restaurants, where diners grill thin-cut slices themselves at the table, as well as in steakhouses and traditional sukiyaki and shabu-shabu preparations, offering visitors an accessible taste of high-grade Japanese beef outside the more famous Kobe and Matsusaka brands.

item.title: Hakkaisan Brewery & Sake Museum: Snow-Aged Sake at the Foot of a Sacred Mountain — Guide
item.description: Hakkaisan, named for the sacred Mount Hakkai it sits beneath, is one of Niigata’s most internationally recognised sake brands, its exceptional quality attributed to pure mountain water, meticulous brewing craftsmanship and a unique snow-aging facility where sake is stored in a naturally insulated chamber packed with compressed snow year-round. The brewery complex includes a museum explaining the sake-making process, a tasting area, and picturesque grounds set against the dramatic backdrop of Mount Hakkai.

item.title: Hakusan National Park: One of Japan's Three Sacred Mountains — Guide
item.description: Mount Hakusan has been venerated as one of Japan’s three sacred mountains, alongside Fuji and Tateyama, for over a thousand years, worshipped as a source of water and fertility by farming communities across the surrounding region, and remains an active pilgrimage site today. The national park surrounding the mountain offers alpine hiking trails ranging from accessible day walks to more demanding multi-day routes to the 2,702-metre summit, passing wildflower meadows, volcanic crater lakes and dramatic mountain scenery that draws hikers throughout the warmer months.

item.title: Hegi Soba: Seaweed-Bound Buckwheat Noodles, Elegantly Plated — Guide
item.description: Hegi soba is a distinctive Niigata noodle tradition, its buckwheat noodles bound with funori, a type of edible seaweed, rather than the egg typically used elsewhere in Japan, giving the noodles a notably smooth, glossy texture and slight chewiness. The dish takes its name from the wooden hegi tray it’s traditionally served on, with the noodles arranged in elegant, bite-sized folds (tsumami) rather than a simple pile, making it both a distinctive regional specialty and a visually memorable dining experience.

item.title: Higashi Chaya District: Kanazawa's Best-Preserved Geisha Quarter — Guide
item.description: Higashi Chaya District is Kanazawa’s largest and best-preserved geisha entertainment quarter, its streets lined with distinctive wooden latticed teahouses (chaya) dating back to the early 19th century, some of which still operate as working teahouses hosting geisha performances today. Beyond its historic architecture, the district is now also known for shops selling Kanazawa’s famous gold leaf crafts and traditional sweets, many housed within the same beautifully preserved wooden buildings that once hosted the entertainment district’s original clientele.

item.title: Hitachi Beef: Ibaraki's Premium Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Hitachi beef (Hitachi-gyu) is Ibaraki’s premium wagyu brand, raised on the prefecture’s rich pastureland under strict quality standards that govern feed, breeding and grading. Known for its fine, even marbling and tender texture, the beef is served across the prefecture in dedicated steakhouses, yakiniku grill restaurants and traditional sukiyaki and shabu-shabu establishments, offering a genuine taste of high-grade Japanese wagyu outside the more famous Kobe or Matsusaka brands. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Various towns across Ibaraki Hours Lunch & dinner, restaurant-dependent Admission Set meals typically ¥3,000–8,000+ Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Hitachi Seaside Park: Blue Nemophila Hills & Crimson Kochia — Guide
item.description: Hitachi Seaside Park is one of Japan’s most visually spectacular seasonal destinations, its rolling coastal hills transforming completely twice a year. Each April and May, roughly 5.3 million nemophila flowers blanket Miharashi Hill in a vivid blue that seems to merge with the sky, while each October the same hillside turns fiery red as thousands of kochia bushes change colour for autumn. Beyond the flower seasons, the park’s 350 hectares include cycling trails, a large Ferris wheel, cherry blossoms, and rose and tulip gardens across the changing seasons.

item.title: Hotaru-ika: Toyama Bay's Glowing Firefly Squid — Guide
item.description: Hotaru-ika, or firefly squid, are small bioluminescent squid that rise from the depths of Toyama Bay to the surface in vast numbers each spring, an event considered one of the bay’s signature natural phenomena and best experienced on a pre-dawn boat tour off the Namerikawa coast, where the glowing squid can sometimes be seen washing up along the shoreline itself. The season is also celebrated with a dedicated Hotaru-ika Squid Festival each spring, and the squid itself is served across Toyama as a seasonal delicacy, typically boiled and dressed with vinegar-miso sauce.

item.title: Hyakumangoku Matsuri: Kanazawa's Grand Samurai Procession Festival — Guide
item.description: Hyakumangoku Matsuri is Kanazawa’s largest annual festival, held each June to commemorate the 1583 entry of Maeda Toshiie into Kanazawa Castle, the event that established the powerful Maeda clan’s rule over the Kaga domain, whose rice yield of over a million koku gave the festival its name. The festival’s centrepiece is an elaborate procession of participants dressed in samurai-era costume re-enacting Toshiie’s triumphant entry, accompanied by traditional taiko drumming and dance performances, and the celebrations conclude with a lantern-lit boat parade along the Asano River.

item.title: Ibaraki Chestnuts: Japan's Top Chestnut-Producing Prefecture — Guide
item.description: Ibaraki produces more chestnuts (kuri) than any other prefecture in Japan, its mild climate and well-drained soil ideal for cultivating large, sweet varieties prized by chefs and confectioners nationwide.
