Each autumn harvest, roadside stalls and farm shops sell fresh chestnuts alongside roasted snacks, while patisseries and traditional wagashi confectioners across the prefecture transform the harvest into monts blancs, chestnut cakes, sweetened kuri kinton and other refined seasonal treats. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Various towns across Ibaraki Hours Peak season roughly September–November Admission Chestnuts and snacks from ~¥300–1,000 Time needed 30–45 min Best time Late September–October (peak harvest) What to Try Fresh roasted chestnuts, a classic autumn street snack.

item.title: Ibaraki Hanabi Taikai: Summer Fireworks Over the Water — Guide
item.description: Ibaraki hosts several large-scale fireworks festivals (hanabi taikai) each summer, with venues along Lake Kasumigaura and the Pacific coast offering particularly striking settings, as thousands of shells burst overhead and reflect on open water below. These events draw large local crowds who arrive early with picnic blankets and portable chairs, turning the festivals into full evenings of food stalls, yukata-clad visitors and community celebration rather than just a fireworks show.

item.title: Ibaraki Prefectural Museum of History: From Ancient Times to the Mito Domain — Guide
item.description: The Ibaraki Prefectural Museum of History offers a comprehensive overview of the prefecture’s past, from archaeological artefacts of ancient settlement through the feudal era of the powerful Mito Tokugawa domain, one of three branch families of the ruling shogunate. Exhibits cover local archaeology, folk traditions, and the intellectual and political legacy of Mito scholarship, which played an influential role in the ideas leading up to the Meiji Restoration. The museum grounds include a pleasant garden and a relocated historic building, set within walking distance of Mito Castle Remains.

item.title: Ichijodani Asakura Clan Ruins: A Reconstructed Sengoku-Era Castle Town — Guide
item.description: Ichijodani was the thriving castle town of the powerful Asakura clan during the Sengoku period, ruling much of the surrounding region for over a century before Oda Nobunaga’s forces destroyed the town in 1573, after which it was largely abandoned and buried, preserving the site remarkably intact beneath the soil for centuries. Extensive excavation since the 1960s has revealed samurai residences, gardens and merchant streets, and a partially reconstructed street of period buildings now lets visitors walk through a physical recreation of Sengoku-era daily life, one of the most complete such reconstructions in Japan.

item.title: Ikaho Onsen: A Historic Stone-Step Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Ikaho Onsen’s most distinctive feature is its main street — a flight of 365 stone steps, one for each day of the year, lined with ryokan, shops and shrines climbing up the hillside, said to represent life’s journey. The town’s hot spring water, tinged a striking rust-orange from its high iron content and known as ‘golden water’ (kogane no yu), contrasts with the clear ‘silver water’ (shirogane no yu) also found here, and each September the town celebrates its heritage with a lively Stone Steps Festival featuring traditional performances along the steps.

item.title: Itoigawa Geopark: UNESCO Site & Japan's Birthplace of Jade — Guide
item.description: Itoigawa Geopark, designated a UNESCO Global Geopark, sits at the dramatic meeting point of the Fossa Magna, a major geological fault line dividing Japan’s main island, creating a landscape of striking coastal cliffs, mountains and unique rock formations. The area holds particular significance as the site where jade (hisui) was first identified in Japan in the 1930s, later found to have been quarried and worked by ancient Jomon-period peoples thousands of years earlier, and visitors can search for jade fragments along designated beaches or visit dedicated museums exploring the region’s geology and jade heritage.

item.title: Jibu-ni: Kanazawa's Signature Simmered Duck Stew — Guide
item.description: Jibu-ni is considered one of Kanazawa’s defining traditional dishes, a refined stew of duck or chicken lightly dusted with flour before being gently simmered in a delicate dashi broth alongside seasonal vegetables and wheat gluten, the flour coating giving the broth a subtle thickness as it cooks. The dish is thought to date back several centuries, and its understated, savoury flavour profile is often cited as characteristic of Kaga cuisine’s refined, seasonally attentive cooking style.

item.title: Kaga Cuisine & Kaiseki Ryori: Kanazawa's Refined Multi-Course Dining — Guide
item.description: Kaga cuisine developed under the patronage of the wealthy Maeda clan, whose resources allowed Kanazawa’s culinary traditions to flourish alongside the region’s abundant seafood, Kaga vegetables and rice, resulting in a refined local cooking style closely associated with kaiseki ryori, Japan’s traditional multi-course haute cuisine. A full kaiseki meal typically progresses through a sequence of small, carefully composed courses, from appetisers and sashimi through grilled and simmered dishes to rice and dessert, each plated with attention to seasonal presentation.

item.title: Kaga Yuzen: A Hands-On Silk Dyeing Craft Experience — Guide
item.description: Kaga Yuzen is one of Japan’s most refined silk dyeing traditions, distinguished from Kyoto’s better-known Yuzen style by its more naturalistic, subtly shaded motifs of flowers, birds and autumn leaves rendered in five traditional colours (indigo, crimson, ochre, dark green and violet). The technique developed in Kanazawa under Maeda clan patronage, and visitors can try hands-on workshops today, working under artisan guidance to dye a small piece of silk or a simple item like a handkerchief, offering a genuine introduction to a craft that traditionally takes years to master.

item.title: Kairakuen Garden: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens — Guide
item.description: Kairakuen, meaning ‘garden to be enjoyed together,’ was created in 1842 by a Mito feudal lord who deliberately opened it to the public, a progressive gesture for its time that gave the garden its name. Ranked among Japan’s three great landscape gardens alongside Kanazawa’s Kenrokuen and Okayama’s Korakuen, Kairakuen is famed above all for its roughly 3,000 plum trees of some 100 varieties, which bloom in a fragrant wave of white, pink and red each February and March during the annual Plum Blossom Festival.

item.title: Kanazawa Castle & Gyokusen-inmaru Garden: Seat of the Powerful Maeda Clan — Guide
item.description: Kanazawa Castle was once the seat of the Maeda clan, rulers of the Kaga domain and the wealthiest feudal domain in Japan during the Edo period, though the original castle structure was lost to repeated fires over the centuries and much of what visitors see today is careful modern reconstruction using traditional techniques. Adjacent to the castle grounds, the Gyokusen-inmaru Garden was restored and reopened in 2015 after being rediscovered through historical research, offering a quieter garden counterpart to the crowds at nearby Kenrokuen.

item.title: Kanazawa Gold Leaf: 99% of Japan's Gold Leaf Production — Guide
item.description: Kanazawa produces roughly 99% of Japan’s gold leaf (kinpaku), a centuries-old craft tradition supported by the region’s naturally soft, mineral-rich water, ideal for the painstaking process of hammering gold into leaves thinner than a human hair. The craft’s influence is visible throughout the city, from gold leaf decoration on lacquerware and temple interiors to gold-flaked ice cream, sweets and cosmetics sold in shops across town, and hands-on workshops let visitors try applying gold leaf themselves to items like chopsticks, boxes or fans to take home.

item.title: Kanmangafuchi Abyss: A Row of Mossy Jizo Statues Beside a Gorge — Guide
item.description: Kanmangafuchi Abyss is a scenic volcanic gorge formed by an eruption of nearby Mount Nantai, carved by the Daiya River into striking columnar basalt formations. Along the riverside path stand a row of roughly 70 weathered stone Jizo statues (guardian deities of travellers and children), each wearing a red knitted cap, with a local legend claiming it’s impossible to count the same number twice. The quiet, moss-covered setting offers a peaceful contrast to Nikko’s more crowded shrine complex.

item.title: Kanuma Autumn Festival: Carved Floats & a Curious 'Butcher's' Nickname — Guide
item.description: The Kanuma Autumn Festival, designated a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage alongside 32 other Japanese float festivals, showcases roughly 27 elaborately carved wooden floats (yatai) built by craftsmen whose woodworking skills trace back to artisans who worked on nearby Nikko Toshogu shrine centuries ago. The festival’s English nickname, ‘Butcher’s Festival,’ is a quirky mistranslation of ‘Bukkake Matsuri’ (referring to the festival’s energetic float-pulling style), and today it draws large crowds each October to see the floats paraded through Kanuma’s streets accompanied by traditional music.

item.title: Kasama Pottery Workshop: 250 Years of Ceramic Tradition — Guide
item.description: Kasama-yaki, the pottery of Kasama, is one of Japan’s leading ceramic traditions, with a history stretching back roughly 250 years and prized for its simple, functional beauty rather than ornate decoration. The town is home to several hundred kilns and studios, many open to visitors for hands-on workshops where beginners can try wheel-throwing (rokuro) or freehand painting on pre-fired pieces, taking home a piece they made themselves after a firing and shipping period.

item.title: Kashima Jingu: An Ancient Shrine of Martial Arts & Deer — Guide
item.description: Kashima Jingu, with a history said to stretch back over 2,600 years, is one of Japan’s oldest and most revered shrines, historically associated with the deity of martial arts and long considered the spiritual birthplace of Japanese swordsmanship, with several historic dojos in the surrounding area still tracing their lineage to the shrine. Beyond the vermillion main gate, a dense sacred forest path leads past a small deer park (deer being messengers of the shrine’s deity) to an inner shrine and a mysterious ‘rock that binds earthquakes,’ with the shrine’s grand autumn festival drawing large crowds each September.

item.title: Kenrokuen Garden: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens — Guide
item.description: Kenrokuen Garden is ranked among Japan’s three most celebrated landscape gardens, its name meaning ‘garden of six attributes’, referring to the qualities of spaciousness, seclusion, artifice, antiquity, water and panoramic views that traditional garden theory considered essential to a perfect garden. Developed by the Maeda clan over roughly two centuries, the garden combines ponds, streams, teahouses and trees several hundred years old, and each winter its pine trees are fitted with distinctive rope supports called yukitsuri to protect their branches from heavy snowfall, creating a striking seasonal sight.

item.title: Kinugawa Onsen: A Riverside Hot Spring Resort Near Nikko — Guide
item.description: Kinugawa Onsen, developed as a hot spring resort in the early 20th century, sits along the dramatic Kinugawa River gorge, with tall ryokan hotels lining the cliffs above the rushing water. As one of the most accessible onsen towns near Tokyo, easily combined with a Nikko sightseeing trip, it has become a popular overnight base offering large-scale hotel facilities, river cruises through the gorge, and proximity to family attractions, alongside more traditional riverside bathing experiences.

item.title: Kuji Chicken (Okukuji Shamo): Free-Range Flavour from the Mountains — Guide
item.description: Kuji chicken, more formally known as Okukuji Shamo, is a heritage chicken breed raised free-range in the mountainous Okukuji region of northern Ibaraki, prized for a firmer texture and richer flavour than mass-produced broiler chicken. The breed’s slower growth and active outdoor rearing produce meat favoured by chefs for yakitori skewers, hot pot and other preparations where the chicken’s distinct character can shine, and it appears in regional bento boxes sold at local train stations.

item.title: Kurobe Dam: Japan's Tallest Dam and Its Dramatic Discharge — Guide
item.description: Kurobe Dam, Japan’s tallest dam at 186 metres, was built through one of the country’s most demanding postwar construction projects, driving a tunnel through unstable, high-pressure rock to reach the remote gorge site. Today the dam is best known for its dramatic summer water discharge, when huge volumes of water are released down the dam face, often accompanied by a visible rainbow in the spray, set against a backdrop of Northern Japan Alps peaks reached as part of the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route.

item.title: Kurobe Gorge Railway: An Open-Air Trolley Train Through a Dramatic Ravine — Guide
item.description: The Kurobe Gorge Railway is a narrow-gauge trolley train that winds slowly along a steep, densely forested ravine once used to transport workers and materials during construction of the Kurobe hydroelectric dams. Its open-air carriages, running between Unazuki Onsen and Keyakidaira, cross numerous bridges and tunnels above the rushing Kurobe River, and the gorge is considered one of Japan’s finest autumn foliage viewing spots, drawing large crowds each October and November.

item.title: Kusatsu International Ski Resort: Powder Snow Meets Hot Spring — Guide
item.description: Kusatsu International Ski Resort combines reliable, high-quality powder snow with the rare advantage of Japan’s top-ranked hot spring town at its base, letting skiers and snowboarders soak away the day’s exertion in Kusatsu’s mineral-rich waters. The resort offers slopes suited to a range of skill levels, from gentle beginner runs to more challenging terrain, with panoramic views over the surrounding mountains from the higher lift stations on clear winter days.

item.title: Kusatsu Onsen Manju: Steamed Buns Cooked with Hot Spring Vapour — Guide
item.description: Onsen manju, sweet steamed buns filled with red bean paste, are a beloved snack found across Japan’s hot spring towns, but Kusatsu’s version carries a particular local charm — traditionally, some shops cooked the buns using steam vented directly from the town’s natural hot springs rather than conventional kitchen equipment. Dozens of shops around the Yubatake sell warm, freshly steamed manju, each with slight variations in dough colour, sweetness, and bean paste texture, making a comparison tasting a popular activity for visitors strolling the town.

item.title: Kusatsu Onsen: Japan's Top-Ranked Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Kusatsu Onsen has topped national rankings of Japan’s best hot spring resorts for years running, its reputation built on an extraordinarily high natural water output and strongly acidic, mineral-rich springs believed to have therapeutic properties. At the centre of town, the Yubatake (‘hot water field’) channels steaming spring water through wooden troughs in a striking, photogenic display, surrounded by dozens of ryokan, public bathhouses and souvenir shops that have made Kusatsu a beloved retreat since the Edo period.

item.title: Kusatsu or Ikaho Ryokan Onsen Stay: An Overnight Hot Spring Retreat — Guide
item.description: An overnight ryokan stay in either Kusatsu or Ikaho, Gunma’s two most celebrated onsen towns, offers a complete traditional hot spring experience that a day trip can’t match — tatami-floored rooms, futon bedding, an elaborate multi-course kaiseki dinner, and typically unlimited access to the ryokan’s baths at any hour, allowing repeated soaks morning, evening and night. Kusatsu offers Japan’s top-ranked spring water and the dramatic Yubatake, while Ikaho’s distinctive rust-orange ‘golden’ waters and atmospheric stone-step main street offer a quieter, equally traditional alternative.

item.title: Kusatsu Winter Illumination & Fireworks: A Steaming Yubatake After Dark — Guide
item.description: Kusatsu Onsen takes on a magical atmosphere each winter as coloured lights illuminate the steaming Yubatake and surrounding streets, the rising vapour catching the light in an ethereal display against the cold night air. Some winter evenings feature fireworks displays over the town, adding to the festive atmosphere, while visitors wander between illuminated streets, warm public foot baths, and steaming restaurants serving hot regional dishes suited to the season. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kusatsu, Gunma Hours Evening illumination, roughly December–February Admission Free to view Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Weekday evenings for smaller crowds; check for specific fireworks dates What to See The steaming Yubatake illuminated with coloured lights.

item.title: Kusatsu Yumomi Performance: The Rhythmic Art of Cooling Hot Spring Water — Guide
item.description: Yumomi (‘hot water kneading’) is a traditional method developed in Kusatsu to cool the town’s naturally scalding, over 50°C spring water to a bathable temperature without diluting its mineral concentration, performed by stirring the water with large wooden paddles in a coordinated rhythm. At the historic Netsu-no-Yu bathhouse, performers in traditional dress demonstrate the technique on stage several times daily, accompanied by a folk song, turning a practical necessity into an entertaining cultural show that visitors can also try their hand at.

item.title: Kuzuryu River Gorge: A Scenic Ravine Along Fukui's Longest River — Guide
item.description: The Kuzuryu River, named after a mythical nine-headed dragon (kuzuryu) said to have once dwelled in the region, is Fukui’s longest river, and carves a scenic gorge through the inland mountains as it winds toward the coast. The gorge offers a dramatic scenic drive or walk along the water, with steep forested slopes rising on either side, and the autumn foliage season transforms the ravine into one of the region’s most striking seasonal landscapes.

item.title: Lake Chuzenji & Kegon Falls: A Volcanic Lake Beneath Mount Nantai — Guide
item.description: Lake Chuzenji was formed roughly 20,000 years ago when an eruption of nearby Mount Nantai dammed the Daiya River, creating a scenic highland lake sitting at over 1,200 m elevation. The lake’s outflow plunges dramatically 97 m as Kegon Falls, ranked among Japan’s three great waterfalls and viewable from both an upper platform and a lower observation deck reached by elevator, offering a close-up view of the thundering water. Both sites are especially striking during autumn foliage season.

item.title: Lake Haruna: A Crater Lake with Winter Ice Fishing — Guide
item.description: Lake Haruna sits within the caldera of Mount Haruna, its calm waters framed by the mountain’s distinctive jagged peaks, including the sharply pointed Sugenoyama, creating one of Gunma’s most photogenic natural landscapes. Warmer months bring pedal boats, lakeside walking paths and hiking trails up the surrounding peaks, while in the coldest winters, when the lake freezes solid, it transforms into a popular ice-fishing destination where visitors drill through the ice to catch smelt, a distinctive seasonal activity.

item.title: Lake Kasumigaura: Cycling Around Japan's Second Largest Lake — Guide
item.description: Lake Kasumigaura is Japan’s second-largest lake by surface area, its wide, flat horizons and traditional sailboats (once used for freshwater fishing) creating a distinctly open, peaceful landscape unlike the mountain-ringed lakes found elsewhere in Japan. A well-maintained cycling route, known as ‘Rin-Rin Road,’ circles roughly 180 km around the lake’s shoreline, passing lakeside towns, fishing harbours and rest stops, making it one of the most popular long-distance cycling routes in the Kanto region.

item.title: Lake Suigetsu: A Scientifically Significant Lake Among the Mikata Five — Guide
item.description: Lake Suigetsu is one of the Mikata Five Lakes in Fukui and holds particular scientific significance internationally, as its lakebed sediment has accumulated in unusually undisturbed annual layers over tens of thousands of years, making it a globally referenced dating standard used by scientists studying ancient climate and archaeology. For visitors, the lake offers a calm, scenic retreat away from any scientific context, with opportunities for boating, fishing and simply relaxing beside the water, surrounded by the gentle hills of the wider Mikata Five Lakes area.

item.title: Maebashi City & Akagi Shrine: Gunma's Understated Capital — Guide
item.description: Maebashi, Gunma’s prefectural capital, developed as a major silk-trading centre during the Meiji era, its wealth from the industry still visible in pockets of historic architecture around the city centre alongside modern commercial districts along the Tone River. On the slopes of nearby Mount Akagi, the picturesque Akagi Shrine sits beside Lake Onuma, its vermillion buildings and torii gate creating one of the region’s most photogenic combinations of nature and traditional architecture, particularly striking during autumn foliage season.

item.title: Maruoka Castle: One of Japan's Oldest Surviving Castle Keeps — Guide
item.description: Maruoka Castle was built in 1576 and its keep is considered one of the oldest surviving original castle structures in Japan, having survived centuries of conflict, fire and the widespread castle demolitions of the Meiji era that destroyed many of the country’s original fortifications. Unlike the larger, more elaborate reconstructed castles found elsewhere in Japan, Maruoka’s modest, sturdy keep with its distinctive stone-tiled roof offers visitors a rare, authentic look at genuine Sengoku-period castle architecture, and the surrounding park is a popular local cherry blossom spot each spring.

item.title: Mashiko Pottery Town: Rustic Ceramics & Twice-Yearly Fairs — Guide
item.description: Mashiko-yaki, the pottery of Mashiko, has been produced since the 1850s and gained international recognition through the mingei (folk craft) movement led by potter Shoji Hamada in the 20th century, prized for its rustic, earthy glazes and unpretentious functional beauty. The town is home to several hundred kilns and studios, many open for browsing and hands-on workshops, and twice each year — during the Mashiko Pottery Fair each May and November, alongside a related autumn Ceramic Art Week — hundreds of additional vendors set up stalls, transforming the town into one of Japan’s largest pottery markets.

item.title: Masuzushi: Toyama's Bamboo-Wrapped Pressed Trout Sushi — Guide
item.description: Masuzushi is Toyama’s signature local dish, a round, bamboo-wrapped pressed sushi topped with vinegar-cured trout that is pressed into a distinctive circular wooden mould lined with bamboo leaves, giving the finished sushi both its shape and a subtle bamboo fragrance. Long popular as one of Japan’s most famous ekiben (train-station boxed lunches), masuzushi is sold in specialty shops, department stores and at Toyama Station itself, with dozens of individual shops each offering slightly different recipes and levels of vinegar tartness.

item.title: Mihama Fireworks Festival: A Summer Fireworks Display Over Wakasa Bay — Guide
item.description: The Mihama Fireworks Festival is held each summer along the scenic Wakasa Bay coast in southern Fukui, lighting up the night sky over the water in one of the region’s most anticipated seasonal events. The setting over the bay allows the fireworks to reflect across the water’s surface, and the beachside location draws crowds who gather along the coast to watch the display, often combined with food stalls and a festive summer evening atmosphere in the surrounding area.

item.title: Minakami White-Water Rafting: Japan's Premier Rafting Destination — Guide
item.description: Minakami has established itself as one of Japan’s premier white-water rafting destinations, its stretch of the upper Tone River offering consistent, reliable rapids fed by mountain snowmelt through spring and summer. Numerous outfitters run guided rafting tours suited to a range of experience levels, from gentle introductions for first-time paddlers to more technical routes through faster water, with the surrounding gorge scenery — dramatic in spring’s fresh greenery and autumn’s colour — adding to the appeal beyond the adrenaline of the rapids themselves.

item.title: Mito Castle Remains: The Understated Seat of a Powerful Clan — Guide
item.description: Mito Castle was once the seat of the Mito Tokugawa, one of three branch families of the ruling Tokugawa shogunate, making it historically significant despite lacking the towering keep of more famous castles. Much of the original structure was lost over time, but the site preserves substantial earthworks and a dry moat (karabori), along with a reconstructed gate, offering visitors a quieter, more contemplative walk through the layered history of Mito’s feudal past, set within what is now a school and park complex.

item.title: Mito Natto: Japan's Fermented Soybean Capital — Guide
item.description: Mito is Japan’s most famous natto-producing region, so closely associated with the sticky, pungent fermented soybean dish that the city’s name has become a byword for it nationwide. The tradition is said to date back centuries, and today dozens of manufacturers across the city continue the craft, several offering factory tours that walk visitors through the fermentation process, from steaming soybeans to the addition of natto bacteria, followed by tastings of various grades and bean sizes.

item.title: Mizusawa Udon: One of Japan's Three Great Udon Styles — Guide
item.description: Mizusawa udon, ranked among Japan’s three great regional udon styles, is produced in the small area around Mizusawa Kannon temple near Ikaho, its silky, elastic hand-pulled noodles owing their exceptional texture to pure spring water sourced from the base of nearby Mount Haruna. Dozens of specialist restaurants cluster around the temple approach, most serving the noodles simply — cold, with a light dipping sauce — allowing the noodles' clean flavour and springy bite to take centre stage.

item.title: Mount Akagi & Lake Onuma: A Volcanic Crater Lake Above Maebashi — Guide
item.description: Mount Akagi, ranked among Japan’s 100 famous mountains, is a dormant volcanic complex rising above the Kanto plain, its multiple peaks encircling Lake Onuma, a crater lake formed within the volcano’s caldera. Hiking trails of varying difficulty wind across the peaks and around the lake, and each October the mountainside erupts in vivid crimson and gold as maple and other deciduous trees change colour, drawing large numbers of visitors to combine foliage viewing with a visit to the picturesque lakeside Akagi Shrine.

item.title: Mount Tsukuba: Twin Peaks & Cable Car Views Over the Kanto Plain — Guide
item.description: Mount Tsukuba, despite standing just 877 m tall, is ranked among Japan’s 100 famous mountains, its distinctive twin peaks (male and female summits) rising dramatically from the flat Kanto plain, visible from a striking distance. A cable car and separate ropeway make the summit accessible without a demanding hike, leading to observation points with panoramic views that, on exceptionally clear days, stretch as far as Tokyo Skytree and Mount Fuji. Hiking trails also wind up the mountain for those preferring to climb on foot.

item.title: Murakami: Samurai Streets & Centuries-Old Salted Salmon — Guide
item.description: Murakami, a former castle town roughly an hour north of Niigata City, retains a well-preserved historic streetscape of samurai residences and merchant houses dating back to the Edo period. The town is equally famous for its centuries-old relationship with salmon, historically the first in Japan to practise sustainable salmon fishery management, and its distinctive salt-curing tradition, where whole salmon are hung to dry under the eaves of specialist shops each winter, creating an unmistakable seasonal streetscape.

item.title: Myoji Temple: A Historic Buddhist Complex Away From the Crowds — Guide
item.description: Myoji Temple is a quiet, well-preserved Buddhist temple complex in Fukui, offering traditional temple architecture and a peaceful, contemplative atmosphere considerably less visited than the region’s better-known sights like Eiheiji. The temple’s grounds provide a genuine, uncrowded look at Fukui’s Buddhist heritage, making it a rewarding stop for visitors seeking a quieter alternative or complement to the prefecture’s more famous temple destinations. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Fukui, Fukui Prefecture Hours ~9:00–16:30 Admission Small entry fee, typically ¥300–500 Time needed 45–75 min Best time Year-round; spring and autumn for pleasant weather What to See Traditional Buddhist temple architecture and grounds.

item.title: Myoko-Togakushi Renzan National Park: Volcanic Peaks & Alpine Trails — Guide
item.description: Myoko-Togakushi Renzan National Park, spanning the border between Niigata and Nagano prefectures, centres on the dramatic volcanic silhouette of Mount Myoko, one of Japan’s 100 famous mountains and a striking presence visible from a considerable distance. The park’s varied terrain includes alpine lakes, cedar forests and hot springs, with hiking trails ranging from gentle lakeside walks to demanding mountain ascents, while the region’s exceptional powder snow has made it a celebrated winter sports destination.

item.title: Naeba: World-Class Skiing & Home of Fuji Rock Festival — Guide
item.description: Naeba Ski Resort is one of Japan’s largest and most established ski areas, its expansive network of slopes and reliable snowfall drawing skiers and snowboarders of all levels each winter. Each July, the same mountain venue transforms entirely for Fuji Rock Festival, Japan’s largest and longest-running outdoor music festival, when tens of thousands of fans camp and hike across the resort’s forested slopes to see international and Japanese acts across multiple stages set amid the natural landscape.

item.title: Nasu Animal Kingdom: A Highland Wildlife Park for Families — Guide
item.description: Nasu Animal Kingdom is one of the largest and most popular family attractions in the Nasu Highlands, combining indoor and outdoor zones across a sprawling site that houses a wide range of animals from big cats to farmyard favourites. The park is known for its close-up encounter opportunities, including a petting zone with rabbits and small mammals, along with scheduled dog agility shows and bird-of-prey flight demonstrations that run throughout the day, making it a reliable full-day option for families visiting the highlands.

item.title: Nasu Highlands & Mount Chausu: A Volcanic Resort Above the Clouds — Guide
item.description: The Nasu Highlands, centred on the active volcanic peak of Mount Chausu (1,915 m), have been a favoured cool-climate retreat since the imperial family established a summer villa here in the early 20th century. A ropeway carries visitors partway up the still-steaming volcano for panoramic views and hiking trails across the crater rim, while the surrounding highland resort area hosts a changing calendar of seasonal events, from spring flower festivals to summer outdoor concerts and autumn foliage celebrations.

item.title: Niigata City: Port Waterfront & Sake Culture — Guide
item.description: Niigata City, capital of the prefecture, sits where the Shinano River — Japan’s longest — meets the Sea of Japan, its harbour long serving as a vital trading gateway that also made the city one of Japan’s foremost sake-producing centres, with more breweries per capita than anywhere else in the country. The revitalised waterfront around Bandai Bridge and Bandaijima blends modern buildings, riverside walking paths, and easy access to sake tasting venues and fresh seafood markets showcasing the Sea of Japan’s catch.

item.title: Niigata Matsuri: The Port City's Grand Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: Niigata Matsuri is the city’s largest annual festival, held each August and combining several older local celebrations into a single grand event that fills the streets around the Shinano River with parades, traditional dance performances and food stalls over several days. The festival culminates in a large-scale fireworks display over the river, drawing enormous crowds to the waterfront, and its energetic street parades feature elaborately decorated floats and thousands of participating dancers.

item.title: Niigata Sake: Japan's Highest Density of Breweries — Guide
item.description: Niigata has the highest concentration of sake breweries per capita of any prefecture in Japan, a heritage built on the combination of severely cold winters, exceptionally pure snowmelt water, and access to premium local rice varieties like koshihikari. The region’s sake is generally characterised by a crisp, dry, clean-tasting style known as ‘tanrei karakuchi,’ distinct from the sweeter styles found elsewhere in Japan, and each March the massive Sake no Jin festival gathers dozens of breweries under one roof for one of the country’s largest sake tasting events.

item.title: Nikko & Nasu Soba: Handmade Buckwheat Noodles from Tochigi's Highlands — Guide
item.description: Tochigi’s cool mountain climate and well-drained highland soil, particularly around Nikko and Nasu, are ideal for growing high-quality buckwheat, making the prefecture a respected soba noodle region. Specialist shops, some with dedicated buckwheat fields visible from the dining room, prepare noodles by hand from freshly milled flour, served either cold with a dipping sauce (zaru soba) or hot in broth, with a firm bite and pronounced buckwheat aroma that distinguishes handmade soba from mass-produced versions.

item.title: Nikko Autumn Foliage: Maple-Lined Roads and Waterfalls — Guide
item.description: Nikko is one of Japan’s premier autumn foliage destinations, its mountainous terrain and elevation range meaning colour changes progress gradually from the highlands down to the town over several weeks each October and November. The winding, hairpin-heavy Irohazaka road, connecting central Nikko to the Okunikko highlands, is famous for spectacular views of maple-covered valleys, while Kegon Falls and the grounds around Toshogu shrine offer equally striking, if more accessible, autumn scenery.

item.title: Nikko Cedar Avenue: The World's Longest Tree-Lined Approach — Guide
item.description: The Nikko Cedar Avenue (Suginamiki) is a Guinness World Record holder as the world’s longest tree-lined avenue, comprising roughly 12,000 towering Japanese cedars planted over a period of about 20 years starting in the early 1600s by a feudal retainer as an offering to the newly enshrined Tokugawa Ieyasu. The avenue stretches across three routes totalling roughly 37 km, with the most accessible and atmospheric sections near central Nikko offering a hushed, cathedral-like walk beneath centuries-old trees.

item.title: Nikko Onsen Town Kaiseki: A Multi-Course Feast After the Bath — Guide
item.description: Kaiseki, Japan’s traditional multi-course haute cuisine, is served each evening at ryokan across Nikko’s onsen towns, following a customary post-bath dinner tradition that transforms a simple hot spring stay into a full culinary experience. Nikko’s kaiseki menus typically showcase the region’s signature ingredients — delicate yuba tofu skin, foraged mountain vegetables (sansai), and river fish such as trout — presented across a carefully sequenced series of small, artfully arranged courses that change with the seasons.

item.title: Nikko Toshogu & Rinno-ji: Japan's Most Lavishly Decorated Shrine — Guide
item.description: Nikko Toshogu, the mausoleum of shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu who unified Japan and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, is the most lavishly decorated shrine in the country, its buildings covered in intricate gold leaf carvings, including the famous ‘see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil’ three wise monkeys. Together with the neighbouring Rinno-ji temple and Futarasan Shrine, it forms the ‘Shrines and Temples of Nikko’ UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the elaborate spring grand festival each May re-enacts a historic samurai procession honouring Ieyasu.

item.title: Nikko Woodcarving Workshop: Try the Craft Behind the Shrine's Carvings — Guide
item.description: Nikko’s tradition of fine woodcarving developed directly from the small army of skilled carpenters and carvers assembled to build Toshogu shrine in the early 1600s, whose techniques were passed down through generations and remain the foundation of the region’s celebrated craftsmanship, visible in the shrine’s famous carvings including the three wise monkeys. Several studios around Nikko now offer hands-on workshops where visitors can learn basic carving techniques under the guidance of trained artisans, working on a small wooden piece to take home.

item.title: Nikko Yuba: Delicate Tofu Skin, a Temple-Town Specialty — Guide
item.description: Yuba, the delicate skin that forms on the surface of simmering soy milk, has been a Nikko speciality since the town’s temples adopted it centuries ago as a protein-rich substitute within Buddhist vegetarian cuisine. Nikko’s exceptionally pure mountain water is credited with producing a particularly fine, flavourful yuba, and today dozens of restaurants and shops across the town serve it in countless preparations — as delicate sashimi-style slices, deep-fried, simmered in broth, or wrapped around other ingredients.

item.title: Nikko Yumoto Onsen: A Milky Sulfur Hot Spring in the Highlands — Guide
item.description: Nikko Yumoto Onsen sits at the far end of the Okunikko highland route, beside a small volcanic lake, with a history of hot spring use said to stretch back over 1,200 years to a Buddhist priest’s discovery of the sulfur waters. The distinctive milky white, sulfurous baths are believed to soothe skin ailments and fatigue, and the compact onsen town’s remote, mountain-ringed setting offers a genuinely quiet retreat, a marked contrast to the busier lower reaches of Nikko.

item.title: Ninja-dera (Myoryuji Temple): A Temple Full of Hidden Defensive Traps — Guide
item.description: Myoryuji Temple, nicknamed Ninja-dera or ‘Ninja Temple’ despite having no actual historical connection to ninjas, was built in the mid-17th century by the Maeda clan as a disguised defensive lookout post, its unassuming temple exterior concealing an interior riddled with hidden staircases, trapdoors, secret rooms and a lookout tower designed to detect approaching threats. The nickname comes from these deceptive architectural tricks rather than any ninja history, and the temple can only be visited on a guided tour, which must be booked in advance by phone or online.

item.title: Nishi Chaya & Kazuemachi: Kanazawa's Quieter Historic Districts — Guide
item.description: Nishi Chaya and neighbouring Kazuemachi are two of Kanazawa’s historic geisha districts, smaller and considerably quieter than the better-known Higashi Chaya across town, offering the same distinctive wooden latticed teahouse (chaya) architecture with far fewer crowds. Kazuemachi in particular sits along the Asano River, its narrow lantern-lit lanes and riverside setting giving it a particularly atmospheric feel, especially in the evening when the teahouse lanterns are lit. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kanazawa, Ishikawa Hours Streets always accessible; shop hours vary Admission Free to walk Time needed 45–90 min Best time Evening for lantern-lit atmosphere What to See Wooden latticed teahouse (chaya) architecture, quieter than Higashi Chaya.

item.title: Nodoguro: The Prized Blackthroat Seaperch of the Sea of Japan — Guide
item.description: Nodoguro, or blackthroat seaperch, is one of the most sought-after fish caught along the Sea of Japan coast near Ishikawa, prized among chefs and diners for its rich, buttery fat content and delicate flavour that intensifies when the fish is grilled. Because catches are limited and demand is high, nodoguro commands premium prices and is often featured as a highlight ingredient on kaiseki menus, though it’s also served more simply as sashimi or nigiri sushi at restaurants and market stalls throughout Kanazawa.

item.title: Noppe: Niigata's Comforting Root Vegetable Stew — Guide
item.description: Noppe (or noppei-jiru) is a traditional Niigata comfort dish, a gently simmered stew combining root vegetables like taro and carrot with mushrooms, konjac and often seafood such as salmon or scallop, bound in a light, slightly thickened broth. The dish varies considerably from household to household and season to season, but it holds a special place in Niigata’s New Year celebrations, when it’s traditionally prepared in larger batches and served slightly cool, its comforting simplicity representing a homely counterpoint to the region’s more elaborate seafood and sake specialities.

item.title: Noto Kiriko Festival: A Summer Tradition of Illuminated Lantern Floats — Guide
item.description: Kiriko festivals take place throughout the summer months across dozens of towns and villages on the Noto Peninsula, each community holding its own version of the tradition on a different date, carrying towering illuminated lantern floats called kiriko through the streets, often accompanied by drumming, chanting and a genuinely communal, participatory atmosphere. Unlike a single centralised event, the kiriko tradition is spread across the entire peninsula through the summer, giving visitors the chance to catch a smaller, more local festival experience beyond the larger, better-known Wajima Grand Festival.

item.title: Noto Peninsula: Rugged Coastlines and Rural Satoyama Landscapes — Guide
item.description: The Noto Peninsula juts into the Sea of Japan from Ishikawa’s northern coast, offering a considerably slower-paced counterpoint to Kanazawa’s city sights, with rugged coastal scenery, traditional fishing villages and terraced rice paddies that helped earn the region UNESCO recognition as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System for its traditional satoyama land management practices. The peninsula’s more remote, less-visited character rewards travellers with time to explore, offering an authentic look at rural coastal Japan increasingly rare elsewhere in the country.

item.title: Noto Satoyama Cycling: Pedalling Through Rural Coastal Ishikawa — Guide
item.description: The Noto Peninsula’s quiet roads, winding between terraced satoyama rice fields, small fishing villages and dramatic coastline, make it a rewarding cycling destination for visitors seeking a slower, less-touristed alternative to Japan’s busier cycling routes. Rental shops in the peninsula’s main towns offer bicycles for day trips or multi-day touring, and the light traffic and varied scenery, from coastal cliffs to inland farmland, give riders a genuine sense of rural Ishikawa’s satoyama landscape at a human pace.

item.title: Oarai Aquarium: One of Japan's Largest Shark Collections — Guide
item.description: Aqua World Oarai, the aquarium at Oarai, displays roughly 580 species of marine life across its exhibits, with a particular focus that has made it one of Japan’s leading facilities for shark and ocean sunfish (mola mola) displays. Large tanks recreate the Pacific and Kashima-nada ecosystems found just offshore, and the aquarium’s oceanfront location, a short distance from the iconic Oarai torii gate, makes it easy to combine with the area’s other coastal sights.

item.title: Oarai Coast: A Torii Gate Rising From the Sea — Guide
item.description: Oarai Coast is home to one of Ibaraki’s most photographed and instantly recognisable scenes — the Kamiiso torii gate, standing on a rock formation just offshore from Isosaki Shrine, appearing to rise directly from the Pacific Ocean. The dramatic composition is especially striking at sunrise, when the gate is silhouetted against the colours of the rising sun over open water, drawing photographers and shrine visitors alike to this rugged stretch of coastline north of Tokyo.

item.title: Ojiya: The Birthplace of Nishikigoi Ornamental Koi — Guide
item.description: Ojiya is recognised as the birthplace of nishikigoi, the vividly coloured ornamental koi carp prized by collectors worldwide as ‘swimming jewels,’ first developed by local rice farmers roughly 200 years ago who noticed and selectively bred colour mutations among their food-fish carp. Today the city’s mountain ponds continue to produce some of the world’s most prized koi bloodlines, and the Nishikigoi no Sato museum and viewing facility lets visitors learn the history and admire prize-winning specimens up close.

item.title: Omicho Market: Kanazawa's Kitchen for Nearly 300 Years — Guide
item.description: Omicho Market, nicknamed ‘Kanazawa’s Kitchen’, has supplied the city with fresh seafood, produce and local specialties for nearly 300 years, its narrow covered lanes lined with roughly 180 stalls selling everything from Kaga vegetables to premium crab and the region’s prized nodoguro fish. Beyond the stalls themselves, several small eateries within and around the market serve the day’s catch directly, making it a popular spot for a fresh seafood breakfast or lunch alongside its role as a working local market.

item.title: Oroshi Soba: Fukui's Signature Grated-Daikon Buckwheat Noodles — Guide
item.description: Oroshi soba is Fukui’s defining local noodle dish, topping firm, dark, coarsely-ground buckwheat soba with grated daikon radish (oroshi), bonito flakes, green onion and often a savoury dashi-based broth poured directly over the top, giving the dish a refreshing, gently sharp flavour from the radish. Typically served cold, the dish is a year-round staple across Fukui, with countless local restaurants each having their own balance of noodle firmness, broth strength and radish sharpness.

item.title: Owara Kaze no Bon: A Haunting Lantern-Lit Dance Festival in Yatsuo — Guide
item.description: Owara Kaze no Bon is a centuries-old festival held each September in the hillside town of Yatsuo, originally performed as a ritual to ward off the autumn winds that threatened the year’s rice harvest. Dancers, often wearing straw hats that partially obscure their faces or delicate masks, perform slow, elegant, flowing movements through the town’s lantern-lit streets late into the night, accompanied by melancholic shamisen and kokyu string music that gives the festival its distinctively haunting, wistful atmosphere.

item.title: Oze National Park: Skunk Cabbage & High-Altitude Wetlands from Gunma — Guide
item.description: Oze National Park, a vast high-altitude wetland straddling Gunma, Fukushima, Niigata and Tochigi prefectures, is accessible from Gunma’s Hinoemata trailheads and protected as a national park since 2007. Wooden boardwalks wind through the fragile marsh ecosystem, famous each June for spectacular blooms of white skunk cabbage (mizubasho) carpeting the wetland, followed by alpine wildflowers through summer, with Mt. Shibutsu rising above the plain and offering more demanding hiking for those wanting mountain views.

item.title: Ponshukan: Taste 95 Niigata Sakes in One Sitting — Guide
item.description: Ponshukan, located directly inside Niigata Station, offers one of the most efficient ways to explore Niigata’s celebrated sake diversity — visitors purchase tokens and use them at coin-operated tasting machines to sample small pours from nearly 100 different local sake varieties, ranging from crisp everyday brews to premium, award-winning labels. A companion salt-tasting bar lets visitors pair different types of salt with their sake, and a gift shop sells bottles of favourites to take home, making it an ideal introduction before or after exploring individual breweries.

item.title: Sabae Glasses: Japan's Eyewear Capital and Factory Tours — Guide
item.description: Sabae is Japan’s eyewear capital, producing the vast majority of the country’s domestically-made glasses frames and internationally recognised for pioneering the manufacture of lightweight, durable titanium frames in the early 1980s. Visitors can explore this precision craft industry through the Megane Museum (Glasses Museum), which combines exhibits, a shop selling locally-made frames and hands-on workshops, alongside factory tours at some manufacturers offering a look at the detailed process behind Sabae’s world-class eyewear.

item.title: Sado Earth Celebration: Kodo's Thunderous Taiko Drumming Festival — Guide
item.description: Earth Celebration is an annual world music festival held each August on Sado Island, organised by Kodo, one of the world’s most acclaimed taiko drumming ensembles, who have made the island their base since the 1980s. The festival combines Kodo’s own thunderous, athletic taiko performances with international world music acts and collaborative workshops, all staged against Sado’s natural coastal and mountain scenery, drawing music fans from Japan and abroad for a uniquely immersive island festival experience.

item.title: Sado Island Cycling: Coastal Roads Around Japan's Sixth Largest Island — Guide
item.description: Sado Island, Japan’s sixth largest island, offers rewarding cycling routes along its coastal roads, which wind past rice paddies, small fishing villages, dramatic sea cliffs and quiet beaches over a distance considerably more manageable than the island’s overall size might suggest, given the relatively flat terrain hugging much of the shoreline. Rental shops in the island’s main towns offer bicycles for day trips or multi-day touring, and the island’s slower pace and light traffic make it a genuinely relaxed cycling destination compared to busier tourist routes.

item.title: Sado Island Gold Mine: Japan's Historic Gold Rush & Noh Heritage — Guide
item.description: Sado Island’s gold mine, in operation for roughly 400 years until its 1989 closure, was once Japan’s largest source of gold and silver, producing wealth that helped fund the Tokugawa shogunate and shaping the island’s unique culture, including an unusually dense concentration of Noh theatre stages built by exiled aristocrats and miners seeking entertainment. Visitors can walk through preserved mining tunnels featuring animatronic displays of historical mining conditions, and the mine’s industrial heritage sites have been proposed for UNESCO World Heritage status.

item.title: Sado Taraibune: Paddle a Traditional Round Tub Boat — Guide
item.description: Taraibune, the distinctive round wooden ‘tub boats’ found on Sado Island, were originally developed by local fisherwomen in the late 19th century to navigate the narrow, rocky coves along the island’s southern coast, where conventional boat shapes struggled to manoeuvre while gathering shellfish and seaweed. Today, visitors can ride and even try paddling these unusual round vessels themselves, guided by experienced local boat handlers along calm, sheltered coastal waters, offering a genuinely unique hands-on maritime experience found nowhere else in Japan.

item.title: Sauce Katsu-don: Fukui's Worcestershire-Dipped Cutlet Rice Bowl — Guide
item.description: Sauce katsu-don is Fukui’s distinctive take on katsudon, diverging from the egg-simmered version common across most of Japan by instead dipping a freshly fried, crisp pork cutlet in a tangy, sweet-savoury Worcestershire-style sauce and laying it directly over a bed of rice, without egg. This approach keeps the cutlet’s crunchy exterior intact rather than softening it, and the dish is a local staple served at restaurants throughout Fukui, with some establishments claiming to be the original creators of the style.

item.title: Seisoji Temple & Mountain Trail: A Combined Temple Visit and Forest Hike — Guide
item.description: Seisoji Temple sits on a forested mountainside in Fukui, pairing a peaceful Buddhist temple complex with an accompanying hiking trail that winds through the surrounding forest, giving visitors the chance to combine spiritual sightseeing with light outdoor exercise in a single visit. The trail offers a genuinely rewarding forest walk beyond the temple grounds themselves, with the mountain setting providing a quiet, natural backdrop considerably removed from Fukui’s more urban sights.

item.title: Senjogahara Marshland: A High-Altitude Boardwalk Through Nikko's Wilderness — Guide
item.description: Senjogahara (‘battlefield plain’), named for a legend of a mythical battle between the deities of Mount Nantai and Mount Akagi, is a high-altitude marshland in the Okunikko highlands above Lake Chuzenji, sitting at roughly 1,400 m elevation. Wooden boardwalks wind through the wetland, protecting the fragile ecosystem while offering relatively easy hiking with views toward the surrounding mountains, wildflower meadows blooming through summer, and golden-brown grasses in autumn creating an atmospheric, open contrast to Nikko’s densely forested shrine areas.

item.title: Shima Onsen Valley: The Ryokan Said to Inspire Spirited Away — Guide
item.description: Shima Onsen is a tranquil, less-touristed hot spring valley scattered along a mountain river, home to numerous ryokan drawing on several distinct spring sources. Its most famous inn, Sekizenkan, dates back over 400 years and is widely believed among fans to have inspired the bathhouse setting of Studio Ghibli’s Spirited Away, its red arched bridge and lantern-lit wooden facade creating an atmospheric, almost magical scene especially striking at dusk. The valley’s quieter pace and forested setting offer a genuine escape from more crowded onsen towns.

item.title: Shinano River: Following Japan's Longest River to the Sea — Guide
item.description: The Shinano River, Japan’s longest at roughly 367 km, rises in the mountains of Nagano prefecture (where it’s known as the Chikuma River) before flowing north through Niigata and emptying into the Sea of Japan at Niigata City. The river and its extensive floodplain have shaped the region for centuries, its fertile silt deposits creating some of Japan’s most productive rice-growing plains, and its lower reaches near Niigata City offer pleasant riverside walking paths, historic bridges and views that shift with the seasons.

item.title: Shiraito Waterfall: Fukui's 'White Thread' Cascade — Guide
item.description: Shiraito Waterfall takes its name, meaning ‘white thread’, from the way its water spreads and separates into fine, thread-like strands as it cascades down a broad rock face, a gentler and more delicate sight than a single powerful drop of water. Set within a quiet forested valley, the falls are easily accessible via a short walk from nearby parking, making them a good stop for visitors seeking a peaceful natural spot without a demanding hike.

item.title: Shirakawa-go from Toyama: Visiting Japan's Famous Gassho-Zukuri Village — Guide
item.description: Shirakawa-go, Japan’s most famous UNESCO World Heritage gassho-zukuri village, is technically located just across the prefectural border in Gifu, but Toyama Station serves as one of the most convenient gateways for visiting, with direct highway buses running in around an hour. The village’s steep, thatched-roof farmhouses, some over 250 years old, are especially striking when illuminated during limited winter evening light-up events, and the surrounding rice paddies and mountain backdrop make it one of the most photographed rural landscapes in Japan.

item.title: Shiro-ebi: Toyama Bay's Delicate White Shrimp — Guide
item.description: Shiro-ebi, or white shrimp, are small, translucent shrimp caught almost exclusively in the deep waters of Toyama Bay, one of very few fishing grounds in the world where they occur in commercially viable numbers, earning them the nickname ‘jewel of Toyama Bay’. Prized for their sweet, delicate flavour and slightly firm texture, shiro-ebi are most commonly served raw as sushi or sashimi, though lightly fried tempura and dried kakiage fritters are also popular preparations found throughout Toyama’s restaurants and markets.

item.title: Shomyo Falls: Japan's Tallest Waterfall — Guide
item.description: Shomyo Falls, at 350 metres, is officially recognised as Japan’s tallest waterfall, dropping in four distinct stages down a sheer volcanic cliff face carved by ancient lava flows near the base of the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route. An easy walking trail from the car park leads to a viewing platform facing the falls, and in spring, snowmelt sometimes creates a seasonal fifth-stage cascade known as Hannoki Falls, briefly making the combined drop even more dramatic.

item.title: Takada Castle Ruins: 4,000 Cherry Trees & Japan's Great Night Blossoms — Guide
item.description: Takada Castle, once home to a feudal lord and later a military garrison, survives today primarily as a moated park rather than a standing keep, but its roughly 4,000 cherry trees have earned it a place among Japan’s three great night cherry blossom viewing spots. Each spring, the annual Takada Cherry Blossom Festival illuminates the trees and their reflections in the surrounding moat, drawing large crowds for an evening spectacle that ranks among the most photographed cherry blossom scenes in the country.

item.title: Takaoka Copperware: A Hands-On Metalworking Craft Experience — Guide
item.description: Takaoka has produced copperware and bronze casting for over 400 years, a tradition dating back to the early Edo period when the local feudal lord invited metalworking craftsmen to the area, and the industry remains active today, producing everything from temple bells to fine decorative objects. Visitors can try hands-on workshops in the city’s craft district, working under the guidance of local artisans to shape, polish or finish their own small copperware piece to take home as a souvenir of the experience.

item.title: Takaoka Great Buddha: One of Japan's Three Famous Daibutsu — Guide
item.description: The Takaoka Great Buddha, a seated bronze Buddha statue roughly 16 metres tall, was cast entirely by local craftsmen using Takaoka’s centuries-old bronze-casting tradition, and is often ranked by tourism guides among Japan’s three most celebrated Daibutsu, alongside the more famous statues in Nara and Kamakura. The current statue, completed in 1933 after earlier wooden versions were lost to fire, stands as a testament to Takaoka’s long-standing reputation as a centre of Japanese metalworking craftsmanship.

item.title: Takasaki Daruma: Japan's Daruma Doll Capital — Guide
item.description: Takasaki produces roughly 80% of all daruma dolls made in Japan, a craft tradition dating back over 200 years to a local temple priest who taught the technique to farmers as a winter income source. The round, hollow, red-and-white papier-mâché figures — purchased with blank eyes to set a wish or goal, with one eye painted in upon purchase and the second added once the goal is achieved — are produced at dozens of workshops around the city, some open for hands-on painting experiences, and each January the city hosts one of Japan’s largest daruma markets at Shorinzan Darumaji temple.

item.title: Takefu Hot Spring: A Quiet Local Onsen in Echizen City — Guide
item.description: Takefu Hot Spring, in the Takefu area of Echizen City, offers a quieter, more locally-oriented onsen experience than Fukui’s larger Awara resort, giving visitors a relaxed soak in a less touristy setting. Its location in central Echizen City makes it convenient to combine with the surrounding area’s rich craft traditions, including Echizen washi paper and Echizen pottery, as well as local cuisine, offering a restful stop within a fuller day of exploring the region’s makers and food.

item.title: Tarekatsu-don: Niigata's Sauce-Glazed Take on Katsudon — Guide
item.description: Tarekatsu-don is Niigata’s distinctive regional take on katsudon (pork cutlet rice bowl), diverging from the egg-simmered version common across most of Japan by instead dipping a freshly fried, crisp pork cutlet into a sweet-savoury soy-based sauce (tare) and laying it directly over a bed of plain rice, without egg. The result keeps the cutlet’s crispy exterior intact rather than softening it in simmered egg, giving Niigata’s version a satisfying textural contrast between the crunchy pork and soft rice beneath.

item.title: Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route: Cross the Japan Alps by Cable Car & Ropeway — Guide
item.description: The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route is a spectacular mountain-crossing transport route through the Northern Japan Alps, linking Toyama and Nagano prefectures via a chain of cable cars, ropeways, a trolleybus and highland buses that together climb over 2,400 metres above sea level. The route passes dramatic alpine scenery, including the famous Snow Corridor walls, and in winter and spring the surrounding slopes around Murodo also offer skiing and snowboarding for visitors wanting to combine alpine transport with time on the mountain itself.

item.title: Tateyama Snow Corridor (Yuki no Otani): Walk Between Towering Snow Walls — Guide
item.description: The Tateyama Snow Corridor, known in Japanese as Yuki no Otani, is created each spring when snow-clearing crews carve a road through drifts that can reach up to 20 metres deep near Murodo, on the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route. The result is a walkway flanked by towering walls of snow, often well above head height even in early summer, that opens to visitors from mid-April and remains a striking sight through late June as the walls gradually melt down over the following weeks.

item.title: Tobu World Square: 100+ World Landmarks in Miniature — Guide
item.description: Tobu World Square is a unique outdoor theme park displaying over 100 miniature reproductions of the world’s most famous landmarks and Japanese UNESCO World Heritage sites, each built at a precise 1/25 scale with astonishing architectural detail, down to tiny figurines populating the scenes. Visitors can walk past miniature versions of the Egyptian pyramids, the Taj Mahal, Tokyo Skytree and Nikko’s own Toshogu shrine in a single afternoon, making it a memorable and easily digestible stop for families and architecture enthusiasts alike.

item.title: Tochigi Strawberry Picking: Japan's Top Strawberry-Producing Prefecture — Guide
item.description: Tochigi has been Japan’s leading strawberry-producing prefecture for decades, its greenhouse cultivation techniques and mild winter climate ideal for growing premium varieties like Tochiotome and the newer, exceptionally sweet Tochiaika. Unlike the summer strawberry season found elsewhere in the world, Japanese strawberries peak in winter and early spring, and dozens of farms across Tochigi open to visitors from roughly November through May for all-you-can-eat picking sessions in heated greenhouses. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Various towns across Tochigi Hours Picking season roughly November–May Admission Around ¥1,500–2,500 for all-you-can-eat picking (30–40 min) Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Tojinbo Cliffs: Dramatic Basalt Formations Along the Sea of Japan — Guide
item.description: Tojinbo is a roughly 1-kilometre stretch of towering basalt cliffs along the Sea of Japan coast, designated a Natural Monument and considered one of only three such large-scale basalt cliff formations in the world, formed over millions of years by volcanic activity and subsequent erosion. Visitors can walk along clifftop paths for dramatic views down to the pounding surf below, or take a short pleasure boat tour that circles beneath the cliffs for a close-up perspective of the towering rock columns from sea level.

item.title: Tomioka Silk Mill: Japan's UNESCO-Listed Industrial Pioneer — Guide
item.description: Tomioka Silk Mill, established in 1872 as Japan’s first government-run modern silk-reeling factory, played a pivotal role in Japan’s rapid industrialisation during the Meiji era, employing French engineering expertise alongside traditional Japanese wooden-frame construction techniques. Remarkably well preserved, the mill’s brick-and-timber cocoon warehouses and reeling plant were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, and the site’s annual autumn Silk Festival celebrates the region’s silk-producing heritage with demonstrations and local crafts.

item.title: Tone River Wetlands: Reed Marshes on Japan's Second Longest River — Guide
item.description: The Tone River, Japan’s second-longest river, has played a vital historical role as a trade and transport artery for the Kanto region since the Edo period. Where it approaches the Pacific in Ibaraki, extensive reed marshes and wetlands line the lower river, supporting a range of birdlife and offering a quieter, more contemplative landscape than the region’s more visited attractions. The wetlands are especially atmospheric in late afternoon, when golden light catches the tall reeds along the waterway.

item.title: Toyama Bay Seafood Market (Shinminato): Fresh Catch Straight From the Port — Guide
item.description: The fishing port of Shinminato, on the eastern edge of Toyama Bay, hosts a lively seafood market where the day’s catch is unloaded, sorted and sold fresh each morning, offering visitors a direct look at the bay’s fishing industry alongside stalls selling seafood to take home or eat on the spot. Surrounding restaurants serve the market’s catch immediately, making it a good stop for a casual seafood meal that traces directly back to the boats docked just outside.

item.title: Toyama Bay Sushi: Where the Bay's Rich Waters Meet the Sushi Counter — Guide
item.description: Toyama Bay is known among Japanese sushi enthusiasts as a premier source of fresh seafood, fed by nutrient-rich currents and an unusually steep underwater topography that brings deep-water and shallow-water species into close proximity, yielding a wide variety of fish and shellfish landed daily at local ports. Sushi in Toyama ranges from affordable conveyor-belt kaiten-zushi restaurants, several of which are considered among the best of their kind in Japan, to high-end sushi counters showcasing the bay’s specialty catches, including shiro-ebi and hotaru-ika alongside more familiar seasonal fish.

item.title: Toyama Bay: Where the Northern Alps Meet the Sea — Guide
item.description: Toyama Bay is renowned for its dramatic geography, one of the few places in the world where mountains rising above 3,000 metres, the Northern Japan Alps, are visible directly across open water from the coastline, creating a striking contrast between sea and high peaks. The bay is also known for a rare spring mirage phenomenon, when atmospheric conditions bend light to distort the appearance of the far shore, and its unusually steep underwater topography feeds some of Japan’s richest coastal fishing grounds, source of specialties like shiro-ebi and hotaru-ika.

item.title: Toyama Black Ramen: A Salty, Soy-Dark Local Noodle Classic — Guide
item.description: Toyama Black Ramen is defined by its distinctively dark, intensely salty soy-based broth, a local noodle dish originally created in the postwar years as a hearty, high-sodium meal meant to replace salt lost by factory workers through sweat during physically demanding shifts. The broth’s dark colour comes from a generous amount of dark soy sauce, and the dish is typically topped with black pepper, chashu pork, bamboo shoots and scallions, remaining a defining local comfort food found in ramen shops throughout Toyama City today.

item.title: Toyama Castle: The City's Reconstructed Landmark Keep — Guide
item.description: Toyama Castle, originally built in the 16th century and reconstructed in concrete in 1954 after the original structure was lost, stands at the centre of Toyama City in a pleasant park setting surrounded by a moat lined with cherry trees. The keep houses a small local history museum with displays on the castle and city’s past, and an observation level offers views over central Toyama, making it an easy, low-commitment stop for visitors exploring the city on foot.

item.title: Toyama Glass Art Museum & Workshop: Contemporary Glass in a Kengo Kuma Building — Guide
item.description: The Toyama Glass Art Museum is housed within a striking building designed by renowned architect Kengo Kuma, part of the wider Toyama Kirari complex, and showcases contemporary glass art from Japanese and international artists across several gallery floors. Beyond the museum displays, visitors can also try a hands-on glassblowing workshop nearby, working under instructor guidance to shape molten glass into their own small piece to take home, reflecting Toyama’s modern reputation as a centre for contemporary glass art.

item.title: Toyama Matsuri: The City's Summer Festival Celebration — Guide
item.description: Toyama Matsuri is Toyama City’s summer festival, held each year and filling the streets around Toyama Castle Park with parades, traditional dance performances and food stalls that draw residents and visitors together for a lively celebration of local culture. The festival typically includes performances by local dance groups and marching bands, alongside stalls selling festival food and drinks, offering a good introduction to Toyama’s community spirit for visitors passing through the city.

item.title: Tsukuba Mineral Spa Resort: Hot Springs at the Foot of the Mountain — Guide
item.description: The mineral spa resorts clustered at the foot of Mount Tsukuba draw on naturally mineral-rich waters to offer a relaxing wellness experience for visitors who have spent the day hiking or sightseeing on the mountain. Several facilities offer day-use bathing (higaeri onsen) with views toward Tsukuba’s distinctive peaks, along with saunas, massage services and restaurants, making the area a comfortable base for combining outdoor activity with genuine relaxation. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Tsukuba, Ibaraki Hours Day baths typically 10:00–21:00, facility-dependent Admission Day bath from ~¥800–1,500 Time needed 1.

item.title: Tsukuba Space Center: Japan's Gateway to Space — Guide
item.description: Tsukuba Space Center, operated by JAXA (the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), is the country’s primary space development facility and one of the highlights of Tsukuba’s broader identity as a planned ‘science city.’ The centre’s free exhibition hall displays a full-size H-II rocket, mock-ups of the International Space Station’s Japanese Kibo module, satellite models and artefacts from Japan’s space history, while guided tours (some requiring advance reservation) take visitors past the mission control room used for real satellite and ISS operations.

item.title: Tsuruga Old Town: A Historic Port With a Railway and Maritime Legacy — Guide
item.description: Tsuruga is a historic port town on the Sea of Japan coast of southern Fukui, blending several strands of history, from the grand Kehi Jingu, one of the region’s most important Shinto shrines with a towering wooden torii gate, to a rich railway and maritime past that once made Tsuruga a gateway for international rail and ferry connections linking Japan with the Asian continent and beyond. The old town area preserves this layered heritage, with museums and historic streetscapes recalling its era as a bustling international port.

item.title: Uonuma Koshihikari: Japan's Most Prized Rice & Hands-On Rice Farming — Guide
item.description: Uonuma Koshihikari, grown in the mountain-ringed Uonuma region of southern Niigata, is widely regarded as Japan’s finest rice, its exceptional sweetness and texture attributed to the region’s cold, snowmelt-fed irrigation water, wide daily temperature swings, and mineral-rich soil. The rice commands premium prices nationwide, and local farms across the region offer hands-on seasonal experiences — transplanting seedlings by hand in spring and harvesting by sickle in autumn — that let visitors participate directly in the cultivation of Japan’s most celebrated rice.

item.title: Ushiku Daibutsu: One of the World's Tallest Bronze Statues — Guide
item.description: Ushiku Daibutsu, standing 120 metres tall including its pedestal and lotus platform, is one of the tallest bronze statues in the world, dwarfing landmarks like the Statue of Liberty. Completed in 1993, the colossal Amida Buddha rises dramatically above the flat Ibaraki countryside, visible from a considerable distance. Visitors can enter the statue itself, riding an elevator up to an observation deck around the chest level, which offers panoramic views across the surrounding plains, alongside a small museum and garden with seasonal flower displays at the base.

item.title: Utsunomiya Castle Ruins & City: A Reconstructed Earthwork Park — Guide
item.description: Utsunomiya Castle was once a strategically important stronghold along the old Oshu Kaido road connecting Edo to northern Japan, home to a succession of feudal lords over several centuries. Most of the original structure was dismantled after the Meiji Restoration and the site suffered further damage in WWII bombing, but a modern restoration project has rebuilt sections of the earthwork ramparts, moat and a small viewing tower within what is now a landscaped city park, offering a glimpse of the castle’s former layout alongside walking paths and open green space.

item.title: Utsunomiya Gyoza: Japan's Self-Proclaimed Gyoza Capital — Guide
item.description: Utsunomiya has branded itself Japan’s gyoza (pan-fried dumpling) capital, a claim rooted in soldiers returning from northeastern China after WWII who brought dumpling-making techniques back to the city, which then developed an unusually high concentration of specialist restaurants. Gyoza Street (Gyoza Dori) near the station is lined with competing shops, each with its own recipe and style, and the city’s annual Gyoza Festival each November draws large crowds sampling dozens of variations from vendors across the region.

item.title: Wajima Grand Festival: Giant Lantern Floats Through the Streets — Guide
item.description: Wajima Grand Festival, held each August, is the city’s largest annual celebration, featuring massive illuminated kiriko lantern floats, some standing over ten metres tall, carried and paraded through the streets by teams of local residents in a display of coordinated effort and community pride. The festival is part of the broader kiriko lantern tradition found throughout the Noto Peninsula, and Wajima’s version draws particularly large crowds given its status as the region’s biggest port town and the sheer scale of its illuminated floats.

item.title: Wajima Lacquerware: One of Japan's Most Prized Lacquer Traditions — Guide
item.description: Wajima-nuri, the lacquerware produced in and around Wajima on the Noto Peninsula, is considered one of Japan’s most prized lacquer traditions, renowned for its exceptional durability achieved through a painstaking application process that can involve well over 100 individual steps, including a distinctive undercoat reinforced with diatomaceous earth and cloth to strengthen the finished piece against daily wear. Visitors can try hands-on workshops in Wajima, working under artisan guidance to decorate or finish a small lacquerware piece, offering a hands-on introduction to a craft that traditionally takes years of apprenticeship to master.

item.title: Wajima Morning Market: One of Japan's Oldest Asaichi — Guide
item.description: Wajima Morning Market, or asaichi, has operated daily for over a thousand years, making it one of Japan’s oldest continuously running street markets, lining a stretch of central Wajima with dozens of small family-run stalls each morning. Vendors, many of them older women who have run the same stall for decades, sell fresh seafood caught along the Noto Peninsula coast, local produce and pickles, alongside Wajima’s famous lacquerware, offering visitors a genuine glimpse of daily life in this coastal fishing town.

item.title: Yamanaka Onsen: A Gorge-Side Hot Spring Town Praised by Basho — Guide
item.description: Yamanaka Onsen was praised by the famed 17th-century haiku poet Matsuo Basho for its restorative waters during his travels through the region, and the town retains a genuine literary and historical atmosphere alongside its traditional hot spring bathhouses. Beyond the baths, visitors can walk the scenic Kakusenkei Gorge trail along the Daishoji River, cross the striking red Korogi Bridge, and browse shops connected to Kutani porcelain, one of the Kaga region’s celebrated ceramic craft traditions.

item.title: Yamashiro Onsen: A 1,300-Year-Old Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Yamashiro Onsen is one of the Kaga region’s oldest hot spring towns, its waters discovered some 1,300 years ago according to local tradition, and the town today centres on Kosoyu, a beautifully restored public bathhouse rebuilt in the style of the Meiji-era original, alongside the still-functioning Soyu bathhouse next door. The town also has strong ties to Kutani porcelain, one of Japan’s most celebrated ceramic traditions, with a small museum and shops nearby offering a look at the distinctive, richly coloured pottery style associated with the region.

item.title: Yanagida Village Satoyama: Rural Life on the Noto Peninsula — Guide
item.description: Yanagida Village sits within the Noto Peninsula’s UNESCO-recognised satoyama farming landscape, its terraced rice fields, thatched farmhouses and small farming plots reflecting centuries of traditional land management practices that balance agriculture with the surrounding forest and coastal environment. The village offers visitors a genuinely slow-paced glimpse of rural Noto life, considerably quieter than the peninsula’s more visited towns, with scenery that shifts dramatically across the seasons, from bright green rice paddies in summer to golden terraces at harvest time.

item.title: Yuzawa Snow Country: Ski Resorts Reachable Direct from the Shinkansen — Guide
item.description: Yuzawa is Japan’s most accessible ski region for visitors without a car, thanks to GALA Yuzawa resort’s unique gondola station built directly into Echigo-Yuzawa Shinkansen Station, allowing skiers to travel from central Tokyo to the slopes in under 90 minutes with minimal transfers. The town, part of the ‘snow country’ immortalised in Nobel laureate Yasunari Kawabata’s novel of the same name, hosts numerous resorts of varying difficulty across the surrounding mountains, along with hot springs that make an ideal post-ski relaxation stop.

item.title: Zuiryuji Temple: A National Treasure Zen Complex in Takaoka — Guide
item.description: Zuiryuji Temple was built in the mid-17th century by Maeda Toshitsune, second lord of the powerful Kaga domain, to honour his father and predecessor, and today stands as one of the finest surviving examples of early Edo-period Zen temple architecture in Japan. Its main hall, sanmon gate and dharma hall are all designated National Treasures, connected by covered corridors in a symmetrical layout characteristic of formal Zen temple design, offering visitors a rare chance to walk through a complete, historically intact temple complex.

item.title: Aizu Autumn Festival: A Samurai Procession Through History — Guide
item.description: The Aizu Autumn Festival is one of Tohoku’s largest historical re-enactment events, held each September in Aizu-Wakamatsu. Its centrepiece is a spectacular samurai procession — hundreds of participants in authentic-style armour, including a portrayal of feudal lord Gamo Ujisato, march through the city streets toward Tsurugajo Castle, alongside performances honouring the tragic Byakkotai cadets. The three-day festival also features traditional music, dance and food stalls throughout the historic city centre.
