item.title: Aizu Lacquerware Painting Workshop: A 400-Year Craft Tradition — Guide
item.description: Aizu-nuri lacquerware is one of Japan’s foremost lacquerware traditions, dating back over 400 years to when a feudal lord invited lacquer artisans to Aizu to develop the local craft as an economic industry. The result is a distinctive style known for its warm gold and vermillion maki-e decoration, and today, workshops throughout Aizu-Wakamatsu let visitors try their hand at painting a small lacquerware piece — such as a bowl, chopsticks or small box — under the guidance of trained artisans, taking home a genuinely handmade souvenir.

item.title: Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival: A Summer Obon Tradition — Guide
item.description: The Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival takes place during the Obon season in August, when thousands of paper lanterns are lit along the city’s historic streets and around Tsurugajo Castle to honour ancestral spirits, a Buddhist tradition observed across Japan but given a particularly atmospheric setting here. As dusk falls, the warm glow of the lanterns against the castle backdrop and old townscape creates one of Fukushima’s most photogenic summer scenes, accompanied by traditional bon-odori folk dancing in the streets.

item.title: Aizu-Wakamatsu Sake: Brewery Tours & Tastings — Guide
item.description: Aizu-Wakamatsu has been one of Japan’s premier sake-brewing regions for centuries, its combination of pure mountain snowmelt water, rice-growing plains and bitterly cold winters creating ideal conditions for fermentation. Several historic breweries in and around the city, some dating back over 100 years, open their doors for tours explaining the brewing process, followed by tastings of a range of styles from dry (karakuchi) to fruity ginjo varieties, often in atmospheric wooden kura (storehouse) buildings.

item.title: Akiu Onsen: Sendai's Ancient Hot Spring Retreat — Guide
item.description: Akiu Onsen, ranked among Japan’s three oldest hot springs with a history stretching back some 1,500 years, sits in a wooded gorge just 30 minutes from central Sendai. Traditional ryokan inns line the Natori River, and the dramatic 55 m Akiu Great Falls thunders down nearby, framed by maple trees that blaze crimson each autumn — making this the easiest escape-to-nature option for Sendai-based travellers. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Taihaku-ku, Sendai, Miyagi Hours Day baths and falls always open (varies by inn) Admission Day bath from ~¥800; falls free Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Autumn (foliage); year-round for onsen What to See Akiu Great Falls, a dramatic 55 m cascade.

item.title: Aoba Castle Ruins & the Date Masamune Festival — Guide
item.description: Perched on the wooded Aoba Hill above Sendai, the ruins of Aoba Castle — built by the one-eyed warlord Date Masamune in 1600 — command sweeping views over the city grid Masamune himself designed. A dramatic bronze equestrian statue of Masamune in full armour stands at the ruined honmaru, his crescent-moon helmet unmistakable against the sky. Each June, the Date Masamune Festival recreates his triumphant entry into Sendai with a horseback procession in full 17th-century armour.

item.title: Azuma-Kofuji: A Perfect Volcanic Crater You Can Circle on Foot — Guide
item.description: Azuma-Kofuji (‘Little Mt. Fuji of Azuma’) is a strikingly symmetrical volcanic cone in the Azuma mountain range, its perfectly circular crater accessible via an easy walking trail around the rim, taking most visitors under an hour. Reached from a car park just off the scenic Bandai-Azuma Skyline drive, it’s one of the most accessible volcanic craters in Japan, offering sweeping views over the surrounding highlands and, on clear days, as far as Mount Bandai and Lake Inawashiro.

item.title: Bandai-Azuma Skyline & Nishi-Azuma Sky Valley: Fukushima's Great Scenic Drives — Guide
item.description: The Bandai-Azuma Skyline and the neighbouring Nishi-Azuma Sky Valley are two of Tohoku’s most celebrated scenic mountain drives, winding roughly 30 km combined through the volcanic Azuma range at elevations over 1,600 m. Each curve reveals a new lookout over jagged peaks, steaming volcanic vents and, come October, some of the region’s most vivid autumn foliage — a fiery tapestry of maple and beech that draws road-trippers from across Japan. Both routes are seasonal toll roads, closed by snow each winter.

item.title: Byakkotai Memorial, Mount Iimori: The Tragedy of the Teenage Samurai — Guide
item.description: The Byakkotai Memorial on Mount Iimori honours one of the most poignant episodes of the Boshin War — a unit of roughly 20 teenage samurai cadets, aged 16 to 17, who retreated to this hillside during the 1868 siege of Aizu-Wakamatsu and, seeing smoke rising from the castle town below, mistakenly believed Tsurugajo Castle had fallen. Rather than surrender, most took their own lives; one survivor’s account preserved their story. Their graves and a memorial statue now stand at the summit, alongside a curious gifted Roman column and Italian fascist-era monument.

item.title: Chichibu Night Festival: One of Japan's Three Great Float Festivals — Guide
item.description: The Chichibu Night Festival, held each December, is ranked among Japan’s three great float festivals and designated a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage. Six enormous, elaborately decorated floats — some weighing several tonnes and adorned with intricate wood carvings, lanterns and tapestries — are hauled through the streets by teams of local residents, accompanied by traditional flute and drum music, while a spectacular fireworks display lights the winter sky above. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Chichibu, Saitama Hours Evening, December 2–3 each year Admission Free to view Time needed 3–5 hours (evening parade + fireworks) Best time December 3 evening (main event) What to See Six enormous decorated floats, some weighing several tonnes.

item.title: Chichibu Plateau & Mount Buko: Hiking Above the Basin — Guide
item.description: The Chichibu Plateau, ringed by mountains including the distinctively quarried Mount Buko, offers some of the most rewarding hiking in the Kanto region within easy reach of Tokyo. Trails of varying difficulty wind across the plateau and its surrounding peaks, opening onto panoramic views over the Chichibu basin below, with cherry blossoms in spring and vivid maple foliage in autumn framing the mountain scenery. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Chichibu, Saitama Hours Trails always open Admission Free Time needed 2–5 hours depending on route Best time Spring (cherry blossoms); autumn (foliage) What to See Panoramic views over the Chichibu basin from plateau trails.

item.title: Chichibu Shrine & Old Town: A Mountain-Ringed Sacred Centre — Guide
item.description: Chichibu Shrine, with a history stretching back some 2,100 years, is one of the oldest and most revered shrines in the Kanto region, its vividly carved wooden gate and main hall set against the dramatic backdrop of the Chichibu mountains. The surrounding old town retains a quaint, small-city charm with traditional shops and eateries, serving as the spiritual and social heart of an area famous nationwide for its elaborate December night festival, one of Japan’s three great float festivals.

item.title: Chichibu Whisky & Craft Sake: A World-Renowned Distilling Region — Guide
item.description: The Chichibu Distillery, founded in 2008, has rapidly become one of the most acclaimed craft whisky producers in the world, its single malt expressions winning international awards and commanding premium prices among collectors. The distillery uses locally grown barley and traditional techniques, including its own cooperage for barrel-making, a rarity even in Scotland. Chichibu’s mountain water and cool climate have also long supported local sake breweries and craft beer producers, making the area a broader destination for spirits and brewing enthusiasts.

item.title: Fukushima Peaches: Japan's Finest Momo & Orchard Picking — Guide
item.description: Fukushima is widely regarded as producing some of Japan’s finest peaches (momo), a reputation built on the region’s ideal growing conditions — warm summer days, cool nights and mineral-rich volcanic soil around the Fukushima basin. Dozens of orchards across the prefecture open to visitors each summer for all-you-can-eat picking experiences, offering a range of varieties from early-season to late-season cultivars, each with its own balance of sweetness and juiciness. Neighbouring pear (nashi) orchards often extend the picking season into autumn.

item.title: Fukushima Waraji Matsuri: The Giant Straw Sandal Festival — Guide
item.description: The Fukushima Waraji Matsuri centres on one of Japan’s more eye-catching festival traditions — an enormous straw sandal (waraji), roughly 12 metres long and weighing around two tonnes, carried through the streets of Fukushima City by hundreds of participants each August. The giant sandal is dedicated to Haguro Shrine as a prayer for healthy legs and feet, echoing an old practice of offering oversized footwear to ward off illness, and is accompanied by energetic dance troupes and drumming through the city’s main avenues.

item.title: Goshiki-numa: The Five Colour Ponds of Urabandai — Guide
item.description: Goshiki-numa, the ‘Five Colour Ponds’, is a chain of volcanic lakes on the northern side of Mount Bandai, formed when the 1888 eruption dammed local rivers and created dozens of ponds across the Urabandai plateau. Mineral content and depth give each pond its own distinct hue — from cobalt blue to jade green to milky turquoise — best appreciated on the roughly 3.6 km walking trail that links the main ponds, part of the wider Bandai Highland Lakes region of forested trails and mountain scenery.

item.title: Higashiyama Onsen: Aizu's Historic Geisha Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Higashiyama Onsen, tucked into a wooded river gorge just outside Aizu-Wakamatsu, is one of Fukushima’s oldest hot spring towns, with a history stretching back some 1,300 years. Traditional ryokan line the Yugawa River, several of which retain a small community of working geisha who continue a centuries-old entertainment tradition once enjoyed by Aizu’s samurai elite. The mineral-rich waters and riverside setting make it a relaxing complement to a day exploring nearby Tsurugajo Castle.

item.title: Hitsujiyama Park Shibazakura: A Carpet of Pink Moss Phlox — Guide
item.description: Hitsujiyama Park in Chichibu is home to one of Japan’s most spectacular shibazakura (moss phlox) displays, where roughly 400,000 plants bloom across nine varieties into a vivid patchwork of pink, white and purple each April and May. The flower fields are arranged in undulating patterns across a hillside with Mount Buko rising in the background, and the annual Shibazakura Festival held during peak bloom draws large crowds with food stalls and local produce alongside the floral spectacle.

item.title: Jozenji Street Jazz Festival: Free Music on Every Corner — Guide
item.description: The Jozenji Street Jazz Festival is Japan’s largest street-level jazz festival, held every September when hundreds of amateur and semi-professional bands set up free outdoor stages across Sendai’s downtown streets, parks and plazas. Unlike ticketed festivals, the entire event is free — visitors simply wander between dozens of simultaneous performances along the tree-lined Jozenji-dori boulevard and surrounding streets, sampling everything from traditional jazz to fusion and Latin sounds. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Jozenji-dori & central Sendai, Miyagi Hours Weekend in mid-September, daytime Admission Free Time needed Half day to full day Best time Mid-September (festival weekend) What to See Hundreds of free outdoor performances across downtown Sendai.

item.title: Kawagoe (Little Edo): Storehouse Streets & Candy Alley — Guide
item.description: Kawagoe, nicknamed ‘Little Edo’ for its remarkably preserved streetscape, was a prosperous merchant town during the Edo period whose fireproof kurazukuri storehouses — thick-walled, black-tiled buildings — still line its main street today. A short walk away, Kashiya Yokocho (‘Candy Alley’) is a nostalgic lane of small shops selling traditional penny candies and rice crackers much as they did generations ago, making the combination one of the most complete slices of old Japan within easy reach of Tokyo.

item.title: Kawagoe Festival: A UNESCO-Listed October Float Procession — Guide
item.description: The Kawagoe Festival, held each October and designated a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, transforms Kawagoe’s historic Kurazukuri storehouse street into a stage for towering, elaborately carved floats (dashi), some dating back centuries and adorned with mechanical dolls, lanterns and tapestries. As floats pass one another in the narrow streets, musicians aboard sometimes engage in playful ‘hikkawase’ battles, competing to outplay each other’s traditional flute and drum music in a lively display of local pride.

item.title: Kawagoe Kimono Rental: Walk Little Edo in Period Costume — Guide
item.description: Kawagoe’s remarkably preserved Edo-period streetscape has made it one of the most popular destinations near Tokyo for kimono rental experiences, with dozens of shops offering a range of kimono and yukata styles, along with hair styling and accessories, for a half-day or full-day rental. Dressed visitors then wander the historic Kurazukuri storehouse street, Toki no Kane bell tower and Kashiya Yokocho candy alley, creating a genuinely photogenic sense of stepping back into old Japan.

item.title: Kawagoe Sweet Potato Snacks: Little Edo's Signature Treat — Guide
item.description: Kawagoe has been famous for its sweet potatoes (satsumaimo) since the Edo period, when the region’s rich volcanic ash soil proved ideal for cultivation, supplying the growing city of Edo with a reliable food source. Today the historic streets are lined with shops transforming the humble sweet potato into an astonishing variety of treats — roasted whole (yaki-imo), baked into tarts and cakes, blended into soft-serve ice cream, or fried into crisp chips, making it one of Kawagoe’s most recognisable culinary identities.

item.title: Kinkazan Island: Sacred Deer & Monkeys — Guide
item.description: Kinkazan — ‘Gold Flower Mountain’ — is one of Japan’s three great power spots, a sacred island off the Oshika Peninsula where hundreds of sika deer and wild macaque monkeys roam freely among the ancient shrine buildings. Koganeyama Shrine at the island’s centre has been a pilgrimage destination since the 8th century, and traditional belief holds that three consecutive January visits guarantee lifelong financial fortune. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ishinomaki (Oshika Peninsula), Miyagi Hours Ferry ~9:00–15:00 (seasonal) Admission Around ¥1,000 (island entry) Time needed About 2 hours Best time Year-round; January for the pilgrimage tradition What to See Hundreds of free-roaming sika deer and wild macaques.

item.title: Kitakata Ramen: One of Japan's Three Great Ramen Styles — Guide
item.description: Kitakata ramen is ranked among Japan’s three great regional ramen styles, distinguished by thick, wavy, hand-cut noodles in a light, clear soy-and-pork (shoyu) broth. The small city of Kitakata, with a population of roughly 30,000, is home to more than 100 ramen shops — reportedly the highest ramen-shop density per capita in Japan — many of them family-run for generations, and locals famously eat it for breakfast (asa-ramen) as often as lunch or dinner.

item.title: Kokubuncho: Sendai's Neon-Lit Nightlife District — Guide
item.description: Kokubuncho is Tohoku’s largest entertainment district, a dense grid of neon-lit streets packed with izakaya (Japanese gastropubs), bars, karaoke boxes and restaurants a short walk from Sendai Station. By day it looks like an ordinary commercial street; by night, thousands of illuminated signs turn it into one of northern Japan’s liveliest nightlife scenes, popular with both locals winding down after work and visitors seeking a lively evening out. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aoba-ku, Sendai, Miyagi Hours Evening onward, busiest after 19:00 Admission Free to walk; drinks/food extra Time needed 2+ hours Best time Friday and Saturday nights What to See A dense grid of neon-lit izakaya, bars and karaoke boxes.

item.title: Lake Inawashiro: Japan's Swan Lake Beneath Mount Bandai — Guide
item.description: Lake Inawashiro, Japan’s fourth-largest lake, sits in the shadow of Mount Bandai’s dramatic slopes, its clear waters earning it the nickname ‘Heaven’s Mirror’ for its reflections of the mountain. Each winter, thousands of migratory whooper swans arrive from Siberia to overwinter along the shoreline, particularly around Nagahama beach, creating one of the region’s most beloved wildlife spectacles. In summer, the lake’s beaches and water sports draw visitors, while the surrounding shoreline offers cycling routes with mountain views.

item.title: Mangoku-ura: A Ramsar Wetland for Migratory Birds — Guide
item.description: Mangoku-ura is a shallow coastal inlet near Ishinomaki designated as a Ramsar Wetland — twice daily the tide exposes vast tidal flats that host thousands of migratory shorebirds including dunlin, golden plover and rare spoonbill in spring and autumn. The surrounding pine forest and salt marsh ecosystem was heavily damaged in 2011 but has recovered remarkably, with bird populations now higher than pre-disaster counts. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ishinomaki, Miyagi Hours Always open; low tide for best flats viewing Admission Free Time needed About 1.

item.title: Matsushima Bay Kayaking: Paddle Among the Pine Islands — Guide
item.description: Sea kayaking through Matsushima Bay offers an entirely different perspective on one of Japan’s Three Great Views — paddling at water level between the bay’s roughly 260 pine-covered islets, gliding through narrow channels and sea caves the tour boats can’t reach. Guided tours suit all experience levels, with calm, sheltered waters ideal for first-time kayakers, and sunrise or sunset paddles offering especially striking light on the pines and rock formations.

item.title: Matsushima Bay's Moon-Viewing & Fireworks Festivals — Guide
item.description: Matsushima Bay hosts two of its most atmospheric seasonal events against the backdrop of its 260 pine-covered islands. The autumn Kangetsu-kai (moon-viewing festival) sees the bayfront lit only by candlelight and lanterns as visitors gather to admire the harvest moon reflected on calm water, a tradition rooted in centuries-old aristocratic moon-viewing customs. In summer, a spectacular fireworks display lights up the bay and its islets, with boats and shoreline viewing spots offering dramatic reflections on the water.

item.title: Matsushima Bay: One of Japan's Three Great Views — Guide
item.description: Matsushima is one of Japan’s three canonically great views — a calm bay scattered with over 260 pine-covered islands, each shaped by centuries of wave erosion into arches, caves and pinnacles draped in wind-twisted black pines. Viewed from the Saigyo Modoshi no Matsu hilltop at dusk, the islands recede in layers of blue-grey haze that seem more painting than reality. Boat cruises wind between the islands at water level, revealing hidden grottoes and cormorant colonies.

item.title: Miharu Takizakura: Japan's 1,000-Year Weeping Cherry Tree — Guide
item.description: Miharu Takizakura — the ‘Miharu Waterfall Cherry’ — is an estimated 1,000-year-old weeping cherry tree, designated a National Natural Monument and ranked among Japan’s three great cherry trees. Its massive, gnarled trunk supports cascading branches that, in full bloom each April, pour down like a pink waterfall, drawing photographers and pilgrims from across Japan. During the roughly two-week blossom festival, the tree is illuminated after dark, creating an especially dramatic sight against the night sky.

item.title: Mishima-machi Kouji Pickles: A Fermented Mountain Craft — Guide
item.description: Mishima-machi, a small mountain village in the Aizu region, is known for kouji-zuke — vegetables pickled and fermented using rice kouji (the mould culture also used in sake and miso production), a preservation tradition passed down through generations of local households to survive the region’s long, snowbound winters. The result is a mildly sweet, umami-rich pickle distinct from vinegar-based tsukemono, sold at farm stands, local markets and specialty shops throughout the village.

item.title: Miyagi Oyster Harvesting Experience — Guide
item.description: Miyagi’s coastal bays are among Japan’s premier oyster-growing waters, and several coastal towns offer hands-on harvesting experiences where visitors can pull up rafts of oysters, shuck them, and eat them on the spot at seaside oyster huts. The season runs through winter, when the oysters are plumpest and sweetest, and many venues offer all-you-can-eat grilling sessions alongside the harvesting activity. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Coastal Miyagi (various towns) Hours Winter season, typically 10:00–15:00 Admission Around ¥3,000–5,000 for harvest + eat sessions Time needed 2–3 hours Best time December–February What to Do Pull up rafts and hand-harvest fresh oysters.

item.title: Miyagi Tansu: Iron-Fitted Traditional Cabinetry — Guide
item.description: Miyagi tansu are traditional wooden chests renowned across Japan for their lustrous zelkova (keyaki) wood grain and elaborate hand-forged iron fittings, crafted using techniques passed down since the Edo period. Each piece can take months to complete, with the wood aged and polished to a deep reddish sheen and the iron hardware hand-hammered into intricate patterns — a genuine heirloom-quality craft still practised by a small number of Sendai-area workshops.

item.title: Musashi Ichinomiya Hikawa Shrine: A Grand Torii Avenue — Guide
item.description: Musashi Ichinomiya Hikawa Shrine holds the highest rank among the shrines of the old Musashi province, a region covering much of modern Tokyo and Saitama, with a history said to stretch back over 2,000 years. A remarkably long approach avenue, roughly 2 km and lined with towering stone and wooden torii gates, leads through a forested park to the vermillion main hall. The shrine’s grand festival each August draws large crowds with traditional rituals, food stalls and a distinctly local, community atmosphere.

item.title: Musashi Kyuryo National Government Park: A Vast Family Nature Park — Guide
item.description: Musashi Kyuryo National Government Park is one of only a handful of national government parks in Japan, a designation reflecting its scale and significance, spanning a vast area of forest, meadow and wetland. The park offers extensive cycling paths, large playground areas for children, seasonal flower fields, and quiet woodland trails, making it a popular destination for family outings and a peaceful contrast to Saitama’s more historic sightseeing spots. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Namegawa, Saitama Hours ~9:30–17:00 (seasonal variation) Admission Around ¥450 (adult) Time needed 2–4 hours Best time Spring (flowers); autumn (foliage); year-round for families What to See Extensive cycling paths through forest and meadow.

item.title: Musashino Udon: Firm, Dark-Broth Noodles of the Saitama Plain — Guide
item.description: Musashino udon is a distinctive regional noodle style native to the Musashino plateau spanning Saitama and western Tokyo, characterised by notably firm, chewy, hand-cut noodles served separately from a rich, dark, soy-based dipping broth (tsukejiru) often studded with pork and vegetables. The style developed from the region’s historical wheat cultivation, an alternative to rice farming on the plateau’s drier soil, and remains a point of local pride, with dedicated shops throughout Saitama each guarding their own broth recipe.

item.title: Nagatoro Gorge: Traditional Boat Rides Through Dramatic Rock Cliffs — Guide
item.description: Nagatoro Gorge, where the Arakawa River cuts through a series of distinctive layered rock formations known as Iwadatami (‘rock tatami mats’), is one of Saitama’s most scenic and photographed landscapes, designated a National Natural Monument for its striking crystalline schist cliffs. Traditional wooden boats, operated by local boatmen, carry visitors along a roughly 6 km stretch of the gorge, passing beneath towering rock walls and through gentle rapids, a tradition dating back over a century.

item.title: Nagatoro Outdoor Activities: White Water Rafting & River Adventure — Guide
item.description: Beyond its traditional wooden boat rides, Nagatoro’s stretch of the Arakawa River offers a range of more adventurous water sports, including white water rafting through rocky rapids, canoeing and river trekking. Guided tours run by local operators cater to various experience levels, from families seeking a mild rafting introduction to more experienced paddlers wanting a faster, technical run through the gorge’s rockier sections. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Nagatoro, Saitama Hours Tours typically 9:00–16:00 (seasonal, weather-dependent) Admission Around ¥5,000–7,000 per rafting tour Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Spring–autumn; higher water levels in early summer What to Do White water rafting through the gorge’s rocky rapids.

item.title: Narugo Gorge & Naruko Onsen: Autumn Colours & Kokeshi Dolls — Guide
item.description: Narugo Gorge erupts in some of Tohoku’s finest autumn colour each October and November — a 2 km ravine where the Narugo River has cut through volcanic rock to create vertical walls of deep red maple, yellow ginkgo and ochre oak reflected in the dark river below. The adjoining hot-spring town of Naruko is Japan’s kokeshi doll capital, with 11 different spring water types and dozens of craft workshops where visitors can watch masters turn painted wooden dolls on a lathe.

item.title: Ogose Plum Grove: One of Kanto's Great Plum Blossom Sites — Guide
item.description: Ogose Bairin, the plum grove of Ogose, is ranked among the finest plum blossom viewing sites in the Kanto region, with roughly 2,000 trees blooming across a hillside grove each February and March. Unlike the more famous cherry blossom season, plum viewing (ume-mi) draws a quieter, more contemplative crowd, and the annual Plum Festival held during peak bloom adds food stalls and local produce stands to the fragrant, pale pink and white scenery.

item.title: Omiya Bonsai Village: The Spiritual Home of Japanese Bonsai — Guide
item.description: Omiya Bonsai Village was founded in the 1920s when a group of Tokyo bonsai growers relocated here after the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, seeking clean water and open land suited to cultivation. Today the neighbourhood remains the recognised spiritual home of Japanese bonsai, with several working nurseries open to visitors displaying trees, some centuries old, alongside the Omiya Bonsai Art Museum, the world’s first public museum dedicated entirely to the art form.

item.title: Omurice at Urawa Retro Cafes: A Nostalgic Comfort Food Trail — Guide
item.description: Urawa’s cluster of old-fashioned kissaten (retro cafes) has made the neighbourhood a low-key pilgrimage site for fans of omurice — a soft, gently cooked omelette wrapped over ketchup-seasoned fried rice, a beloved Japanese comfort food dish with Western-influenced origins. These cafes, many decorated in a warm, unchanged 1970s-80s aesthetic of wood panelling and vintage furniture, serve the dish alongside strong drip coffee, offering an unhurried, nostalgic dining experience distinct from Tokyo’s trendier cafe scene.

item.title: Onagawa: A Modern Seafood Port Reborn — Guide
item.description: Onagawa is one of Tohoku’s most striking recovery stories — a fishing port devastated in 2011 that rebuilt not just its infrastructure but its entire town plan, creating a pedestrian-first centre with a modern seafood market, boutique shops and public art leading straight to the harbour. The market sells some of Miyagi’s freshest catch, including saury, salmon and the region’s famous silver salmon farmed in the bay. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Onagawa, Miyagi Hours Market ~9:00–15:00 (varies) Admission Free entry; seafood meals extra Time needed 1.

item.title: Osaki Hachimangu: Sendai's National Treasure Shrine — Guide
item.description: Built by Date Masamune in 1607, Osaki Hachimangu is one of Japan’s most elegant shrine buildings — a National Treasure clad in gold lacquer and vivid black urushi lacquerwork, blending Momoyama-period opulence with subdued Zen restraint. The long approach through an ancient cedar grove creates a quiet transition from the modern city outside. Every January the shrine hosts the Dontosai festival, and each November families bring children for Shichi-Go-San blessing ceremonies.

item.title: Ouchijuku: A Frozen-in-Time Edo Post Town & Negi Soba — Guide
item.description: Ouchijuku is a beautifully preserved Edo-period post town, its single main street lined with thatched-roof buildings that once served travellers on the old Aizu-Nishi Kaido route between Aizu and Nikko. Today the village is a living museum of traditional rural Japan, with shops selling crafts and local food. Its most famous quirk is negi-soba — buckwheat noodles eaten using a single whole green onion (negi) instead of chopsticks, a tradition unique to Ouchijuku.

item.title: Oze Marshland National Park: Japan's High-Altitude Wetland — Guide
item.description: Oze Marshland National Park is one of Japan’s great wilderness areas, a vast high-altitude wetland straddling Fukushima, Gunma, Niigata and Tochigi prefectures, protected as a national park since 2007. Wooden boardwalks wind through the marsh, letting hikers explore without disturbing the fragile peat-bog ecosystem, famous each May and June for spectacular blooms of white skunk cabbage (mizubasho) followed by alpine wildflowers through summer, with Mt. Shibutsu rising above the plain.

item.title: Railway Museum, Omiya: A Century of Japanese Trains — Guide
item.description: The Railway Museum in Omiya, operated by JR East, is one of Japan’s largest and most comprehensive train museums, home to dozens of historic locomotives and rolling stock spanning from Meiji-era steam engines to early Shinkansen bullet trains. Interactive exhibits, a large train diorama with model railways, a driving simulator and a panoramic observation deck overlooking the Tohoku Shinkansen line make it a favourite for train enthusiasts and families alike.

item.title: Ranzan Gorge: A Quiet Riverside Walk Named for Kyoto's Arashiyama — Guide
item.description: Ranzan Gorge takes its name from a Confucian scholar who, upon seeing the valley’s forested slopes along a tributary of the Arakawa River, was reminded of Kyoto’s celebrated Arashiyama district. The gorge offers a gentler, quieter alternative to Saitama’s more famous nature spots, with an easy riverside walking path through mixed forest that turns especially vivid during autumn foliage season, making it a relaxed half-day nature escape within reach of Tokyo.

item.title: Rinno-ji Temple Garden: Sendai's Refined Stroll Garden — Guide
item.description: Rinno-ji temple in the hills north of Sendai is home to one of Tohoku’s most refined stroll gardens — a mossy, intimate landscape of stone lanterns, koi ponds and maple trees that turns crimson in autumn and snow-white in winter. Founded in the 8th century and rebuilt multiple times, the temple exudes the quiet depth of a place long saturated with prayer. The garden’s spring display of azalea and camellia, unusual for Tohoku, makes it a distinctive stop.

item.title: Saitama Super Arena: Japan's Massive Multi-Purpose Venue — Guide
item.description: Saitama Super Arena is one of the largest multi-purpose indoor arenas in Asia, its distinctive design featuring a movable main stand that allows the venue to reconfigure between a compact arena setting and a massive stadium-style space seating up to roughly 37,000. Since opening in 2000, it has hosted major international concerts, world championship sporting events, conventions and the wrestling and basketball events of the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, making it a key stop for visitors attending large-scale events near Tokyo.

item.title: Saitama Unagi: Grilled Eel Over Rice, a Landlocked Speciality — Guide
item.description: Grilled eel over rice (unaju or unadon) is a beloved Saitama speciality, a somewhat unexpected tradition for a landlocked prefecture that developed thanks to the abundant rivers historically stocked with freshwater eel and the region’s role supplying Edo (old Tokyo) with food. Specialist unagi restaurants, some family-run for generations, prepare the eel with a meticulous process of steaming and charcoal-grilling with a sweet-savoury glaze, resulting in a dish that’s crisp outside and meltingly tender within.

item.title: Sasa Kamaboko: Sendai's Bamboo-Leaf-Shaped Fish Cake — Guide
item.description: Sasa kamaboko is a Sendai speciality — a grilled fish cake made from white fish paste, shaped like a bamboo leaf (sasa) and hand-fanned into its distinctive form before grilling over an open flame. It was created over a century ago as a way to preserve the abundant white fish catches of Miyagi’s coast, and remains a beloved snack and souvenir, with a smoky exterior and springy, delicately sweet interior.

item.title: Sendai City: Tohoku's Sophisticated 'City of Trees' — Guide
item.description: Sendai is Tohoku’s most sophisticated city — nicknamed the ‘City of Trees’ for its zelkova-lined boulevards, it blends the heritage of Date Masamune’s 17th-century castle town with a modern, cosmopolitan energy that sets it apart from other Tohoku cities. The city centre is compact and walkable, anchored by Aoba Castle ruins on the wooded hill above and the famous Kokubuncho nightlife district below. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sendai, Miyagi Hours City always open Admission Free (city); attractions vary Time needed Half day–full day Best time Year-round; August Tanabata, December illumination What to See The zelkova-lined boulevards that give Sendai its nickname.

item.title: Sendai Gyutan: Grilled Beef Tongue, Miyagi's Signature Dish — Guide
item.description: Grilled beef tongue (gyutan) is Sendai’s culinary trademark — thick slices of ox tongue, salted and aged, then char-grilled over binchotan charcoal until the edges crisp while the centre stays tender. The dish was invented after WWII by a Sendai restaurateur who didn’t want to waste tongue meat discarded by US military kitchens, and has since become the city’s signature, served in dozens of specialist restaurants around Sendai Station. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sendai, Miyagi Hours Lunch & dinner, most restaurants Admission Set meals from ~¥1,500 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to Try The classic gyutan teishoku (grilled tongue set with oxtail soup, barley rice, pickles).

item.title: Sendai Miso: A Bold Red Miso with Samurai Roots — Guide
item.description: Sendai miso is a distinctive dark red, unpasteurised soybean paste with a bold, slightly bitter depth of flavour, aged for over a year in wooden vats. Its origins trace to the early 1600s, when warlord Date Masamune established a dedicated miso brewery to supply his troops with long-lasting, nutritious rations — making it one of Japan’s oldest continuously produced regional misos. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sendai, Miyagi Hours Shop hours; some breweries offer tours Admission Free tasting at many shops; miso from ~¥500 Time needed 30–45 min Best time Year-round What to Try Rich miso soup made with Sendai miso at local restaurants.

item.title: SENDAI Pageant of Starlight: A Winter Tunnel of Light — Guide
item.description: The SENDAI Pageant of Starlight transforms the zelkova-lined boulevards of Jozenji-dori and Chuo-dori into a glittering tunnel of light each December, when hundreds of thousands of LED bulbs are strung through the bare winter branches overhead. First held in 1986, it has grown into one of Japan’s most beloved winter illuminations, drawing large crowds to walk beneath the golden-white canopy, especially in the evenings leading up to Christmas. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Jozenji-dori, Sendai, Miyagi Hours Lit nightly, roughly mid-Dec, evening onward Admission Free Time needed 30–60 min Best time Weeknight evenings (less crowded) What to See A glittering tunnel of LED-lit zelkova trees along Jozenji-dori.

item.title: Sendai Tanabata Festival: Japan's Largest Star Festival — Guide
item.description: Sendai Tanabata is Japan’s largest and most spectacular Star Festival, held each August (rather than the traditional July date) since a decision to preserve harvest-season timing centuries ago. Thousands of enormous, hand-crafted paper streamers — some reaching several metres long — hang from bamboo poles along the city’s covered shopping arcades, each one taking families and shopkeepers weeks to make, transforming central Sendai into a rustling forest of colour for three days.

item.title: Shiogama: Tuna Port, Sunday Market & National Treasure Shrine — Guide
item.description: Shiogama is one of Japan’s top tuna-landing ports, supplying much of Tokyo’s premium maguro market — the Sunday morning market at Uontana lets visitors buy directly from wholesalers at extraordinary prices, followed by kaisendon (seafood rice bowls) at restaurants that open at 7am. Above the port, Shiogama Shrine rises on a wooded hill with 202 stone steps, its main halls designated National Treasures. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Shiogama, Miyagi Hours Market Sun ~5:00–13:00; shrine always open Admission Free (market entry); meals extra Time needed 1.

item.title: Shiramizu Amidado: A Heian-Era National Treasure Temple — Guide
item.description: Shiramizu Amidado, built in 1160 by the widow of a regional lord to pray for her late husband’s soul, is a National Treasure and one of only a handful of surviving Heian-period Pure Land Buddhist temple gardens in Japan. The hall sits on an island in a lotus pond, meant to evoke the Buddhist paradise of the Pure Land, with the wooden structure and its seated Amida Buddha reflected serenely in the water — a rare, intact glimpse of 12th-century religious architecture.

item.title: Shizugawa Bay & Minami-Sanriku: Oysters and Recovery — Guide
item.description: Shizugawa Bay is Miyagi’s most productive marine farming zone — the cold Oyashio current and warm Kuroshio meet here, creating nutrient-rich water that produces some of Japan’s finest oysters, scallops and wakame seaweed. The coastal town of Minami-Sanriku was almost entirely destroyed by the 2011 tsunami; its remarkable recovery — rebuilt on elevated ground with a striking new market and memorial park — has made it one of Japan’s most visited recovery sites.

item.title: Soma Nomaoi: A 1,000-Year Samurai Horse Festival — Guide
item.description: Soma Nomaoi is one of Japan’s most extraordinary living traditions — a centuries-old cavalry festival in which several hundred horsemen, dressed in full samurai armour bearing family crests, gallop across open fields, compete to catch releasing flags, and parade through the streets of Soma and Minamisoma in a display rooted in real military horsemanship exercises once practised by the region’s samurai clans. Designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, the three-day festival each July remains a genuinely local event, run by the descendants of the samurai families it honours.

item.title: Tokorozawa Sakura Town: A Pop Culture & Architecture Complex — Guide
item.description: Tokorozawa Sakura Town is a large cultural complex developed by publishing giant Kadokawa, its centrepiece the striking Kadokawa Culture Museum — an angular, faceted stone building designed by architect Kengo Kuma that houses exhibitions spanning manga, anime, literature, and Japanese pop culture, alongside a vast bookshelf-lined library space. The complex also includes a shrine dedicated to anime and manga characters, event spaces and a hotel, making it a distinctive modern counterpoint to Saitama’s more traditional attractions.

item.title: Tsuchiyu Onsen: Fukushima's Mountain Hot Spring & Kokeshi Village — Guide
item.description: Tsuchiyu Onsen is a compact, historic hot spring town tucked into a river gorge on the edge of the Azuma mountains, just a short drive from Fukushima City. Traditional ryokan and free public foot baths line the Arakawa River, and the town is known nationally as a centre for traditional kokeshi wooden doll craftsmanship, with workshops where visitors can watch artisans at work. Tsuchiyu also pioneered small-scale hydroelectric power generation using its rushing mountain river, an innovative approach to disaster recovery after 2011.

item.title: Tsurugajo Castle, Aizu-Wakamatsu: A Samurai Stronghold Reborn — Guide
item.description: Tsurugajo Castle in Aizu-Wakamatsu is one of Japan’s most storied fortresses — the site of a month-long 1868 siege during the Boshin War, when Aizu samurai (including the teenage Byakkotai) made their last stand against imperial forces. The current five-storey keep, rebuilt in 1965 with a distinctive red-tile roof unique among Japanese castles, houses a museum on Aizu’s samurai history, and the surrounding park bursts into roughly 1,000 cherry trees each April.

item.title: Urawa Jukunichi Festival: A Daruma Doll New Year Market — Guide
item.description: Urawa Jukunichi is a traditional New Year market held each January, when the streets around Chōjuji Temple fill with stalls selling daruma dolls — round, hollow, red-and-white papier-mâché figures traditionally purchased to set an intention or wish for the coming year, with one eye painted in upon purchase and the second added once the goal is achieved. The festival’s name, meaning ‘19th day,’ reflects its traditional date, and the lively atmosphere of vendors, food stalls and crowds seeking fortune makes it a distinctly local slice of Japanese New Year culture.

item.title: Zao Snow Monsters (Juhyo): Miyagi's Frost Giants — Guide
item.description: Zao’s ‘snow monsters’ (juhyo) are one of Japan’s most surreal natural phenomena — fir trees on the Zao plateau above 1,400 m are encased in successive layers of freezing fog and blizzard snow from January through February, creating enormous white figures that fill the ski slopes like a silent army of frost giants. The Zao resort straddles the Miyagi-Yamagata border; the Miyagi side is less crowded and offers equally spectacular juhyo fields, best viewed from the ropeway gondola at dawn.

item.title: Zuiganji Temple: Tohoku's Great Zen Temple — Guide
item.description: Zuiganji is Tohoku’s most important Zen temple, founded in 828 and rebuilt in its current magnificent form by Date Masamune in 1609 — the gilded sliding-door paintings inside the main hall are among the finest surviving examples of Momoyama-period art. The approach from the main gate is one of Japan’s most atmospheric temple walks: a corridor of ancient cedar trees several hundred years old, their canopy blotting out the sky, lined with cliff-carved meditation caves.

item.title: Zunda Mochi: Sendai's Vivid Green Edamame Sweet — Guide
item.description: Zunda mochi is one of Sendai’s most distinctive sweets — soft rice cakes coated in a vividly green paste of mashed young soybeans (edamame), sweetened and lightly salted. The dish is said to date back to the samurai era, when warlord Date Masamune’s troops reportedly mashed beans with sword hilts during a campaign. Today it’s sold everywhere from department store basements to Sendai Station kiosks, as mochi, shakes, and even soft-serve ice cream.

item.title: A-FACTORY Aomori: Apple Cider & Food Souvenirs — Guide
item.description: A stylish market building right by Aomori Station, A-FACTORY is the essential one-stop for Aomori food culture. A glass-walled cider brewery makes Aomori’s famous apple cider on-site, while the market hall sells apple juice, local sake, dried scallops and the prefecture’s best-curated edible souvenirs. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City (by Aomori Station) Hours ~10:00–19:00 (varies) Admission Free entry Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to Do Taste Aomori apple cider from the on-site brewery.

item.title: Akita Inu: Meet Japan's National Dog — Odate, Akita Guide
item.description: The Akita is Japan’s most famous dog breed — designated a national natural monument in 1931 — and Odate City is its birthplace. The Akita Dog Museum (Akitainu Kaikan) lets visitors meet and pet purebred Akita Inu and learn the breed’s history, including the legendary loyal dog Hachiko, who was born nearby. Breeding farms offer guided meet-and-greets, and the city celebrates its dogs at an August festival. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Odate, Akita Hours Museum ~9:00–17:00 Admission Around ¥500–800 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round; festival August What to Do Meet and pet purebred Akita Inu dogs.

item.title: Akita Kanto Festival: Balancing 50 kg Lantern Poles — Guide
item.description: One of Tohoku’s four great festivals and a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage — the Akita Kanto Festival fills the city’s main boulevard for four evenings in early August with performers balancing towering bamboo poles hung with up to 46 lit paper lanterns on their palms, foreheads and shoulders. Each pole weighs 50 kg and stands 12 m tall. Daytime training sessions let visitors try a smaller practice pole. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Akita City, Akita Hours Evenings, early August (4 days) Admission Free to watch; paid seats available Time needed 2 hours Best time Early August (fixed dates) Highlights 50 kg, 12 m bamboo poles hung with 46 lanterns.

item.title: Akita Museum of Art: Foujita's Mural & Tadao Ando — Guide
item.description: The Akita Museum of Art, designed by Tadao Ando, is home to Tsuguharu Foujita’s monumental mural ‘Events in Akita’ — one of the largest canvases in Japan, depicting the prefecture’s festivals and daily life. Ando’s spiral staircase and a rooftop triangular water pool that frames Senshu Park make the building itself a work of art. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Akita City, Akita Hours ~10:00–18:00 (closed irregular) Admission Around ¥310 (collection) Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to See Foujita’s vast mural ‘Events in Akita’.

item.title: Akita Nairiku Line: A Scenic Ride Through Rural Akita — Guide
item.description: The Akita Nairiku Line is a scenic inland railway winding 94 km between Kakunodate and Takanosu, through rice valleys, mountains and the traditional Matagi hunting country of northern Akita. Passing rustic stations and river viaducts, it’s especially magical in October’s autumn colours and again under deep winter snow. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kitaakita–Senboku, Akita Hours Regular daily services Admission ~¥1,700 (full line) Time needed About 2.

item.title: Akita Sake: One of Japan's Finest Sake Regions — Guide
item.description: Akita is one of Japan’s most celebrated sake prefectures — pure snowmelt water, high-quality Akita rice and cold winters that allow slow fermentation produce sake of exceptional clarity and elegance. Over 40 breweries welcome visitors, and some offer toji (master brewer) experience days where you join actual brewing. The Yamamoto, Kariho and Dewatsuru labels are internationally known. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Akita City, Yuzawa & beyond Hours Brewery/bar hours Admission Tastings vary; experiences ~¥5,000 Time needed 1–2 hours (or full brewing day) Best time Year-round; brewing winter What to Try Clean, elegant Akita sake from 40+ breweries.

item.title: Aomori Apples: Orchards, Picking & Cider Tasting — Guide
item.description: Aomori produces around 60% of all Japan’s apples, and the orchards of the Tsugaru plain around Hirosaki are the source. From August to November you can pick your own from 50+ varieties, press fresh juice, and taste single-variety craft ciders that never reach city shops. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki & Tsugaru, Aomori Hours Orchards ~Aug–Nov, daytime Admission Picking ~¥300–1,500 Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Aug–Nov (harvest season) What to Do Pick your own from 50+ apple varieties, Aug–Nov.

item.title: Aomori Furukawa Market: Build Your Own Nokkedon — Guide
item.description: The Furukawa Fish Market near Aomori Station is home to the famous ‘Nokkedon’ — you buy a bowl of rice and a book of tickets, then wander the stalls exchanging tickets for slices of tuna, scallop, salmon roe and whatever the morning’s catch brings, building your own custom seafood bowl. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City (near Aomori Station) Hours ~7:00–15:00 (closed some Tue) Admission Nokkedon tickets ~¥1,500–2,000 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Morning; year-round What to Try The build-your-own Nokkedon seafood rice bowl.

item.title: Aomori Museum of Art: Yoshitomo Nara's Aomori Dog — Guide
item.description: The Aomori Museum of Art is home to Yoshitomo Nara’s colossal 8.5-metre ‘Aomori Dog’, the white puppy that has become the prefecture’s modern icon. Jun Aoki’s half-buried white architecture echoes the archaeological trenches of the neighbouring Jomon site. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City, Aomori Hours ~9:30–17:00 (closed some Mon) Admission Around ¥510 (more for shows) Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Aomori Nebuta Festival: Japan's Great Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: The Aomori Nebuta Festival is one of Japan’s three great festivals — and arguably its most spectacular. Each evening from August 2–7, giant illuminated warrior figures up to 9 m wide parade through Aomori City, accompanied by thousands of Haneto dancers chanting ‘Rassera!’ The final night sees floats carried out onto Aomori Bay with fireworks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City, Aomori Hours Evenings, Aug 2–7 Admission Free to watch; paid seats ~¥2,000+ Time needed 2–3 hours Best time August 2–7 (fixed dates) Highlights Giant illuminated warrior floats up to 9 m wide.

item.title: Appi Kogen Resort: Tohoku's Powder & Highland Playground — Guide
item.description: Appi Kogen is one of Tohoku’s largest ski resorts — famed for long, well-groomed runs of light powder snow in winter, drawing skiers from across Japan and abroad. In summer the highland turns green for golf, hiking and family activities, making it a year-round mountain playground in northern Iwate. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachimantai, Iwate Hours Winter ski season; summer activities Admission Lift passes / activity fees vary Time needed Half–full day Best time Winter (powder); summer (highland) What to Do Long, groomed powder-snow ski runs in winter.

item.title: Babahera Ice Cream: Akita's Rose-Shaped Roadside Treat — Guide
item.description: Babahera ice is a nostalgic Akita roadside treat — aproned ladies (baba) swirl pink and yellow sherbet with a spatula (hera) into a delicate rose shape on a cone. Light, refreshing and slightly retro, it’s an Akita summer icon found at roadsides, festivals and event grounds across the prefecture. The name simply blends ‘baba’ (auntie) and ‘hera’ (spatula). 🗓️ At a Glance Location Roadsides across Akita Hours Warm-season daytime Admission Cheap (per cone) Time needed About 10 min Best time Summer (warm months) What to Try Pink-and-yellow sherbet swirled into a rose shape.

item.title: Chagu-Chagu Umakko: Iwate's Decorated Horse Parade — Guide
item.description: One of Japan’s most colourful festivals — on the second Saturday of June, over 100 horses decorated with elaborate lacquerwork, embroidery and bells parade some 15 km from Onkoshi Shrine in Takizawa to Morioka Hachimangu Shrine. The gentle ‘chagu-chagu’ ringing of the horses' bells gives the festival its onomatopoeic name. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Takizawa → Morioka, Iwate Hours 2nd Saturday of June (morning–afternoon) Admission Free Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Second Saturday of June Highlights 100+ decorated horses in lacquer, embroidery and bells.

item.title: Chusonji Temple & the Golden Hall: Hiraizumi UNESCO — Guide
item.description: Chusonji in Hiraizumi is one of Tohoku’s greatest treasures. Its Konjikido (Golden Hall), built in 1124 and entirely sheathed in gold leaf, shelters the mummified remains of four Fujiwara lords — a dazzling survival of Heian Buddhist art and the centrepiece of a UNESCO World Heritage site. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hiraizumi, Iwate Hours ~8:30–17:00 (seasonal) Admission Around ¥800 Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Dakigaeri Gorge: Akita's Emerald Autumn Ravine — Guide
item.description: Dakigaeri Gorge near Kakunodate is a dramatic ravine of vivid emerald-blue water, spanned by the striking red Kami-no-Iwahashi suspension bridge. A riverside trail winds past clear pools and small waterfalls; in late October the surrounding maples and beeches blaze crimson and gold, making it one of Akita’s most beautiful autumn-foliage walks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Senboku, Akita Hours Trail daytime (best spring–autumn) Admission Free Time needed About 1.

item.title: Dewa Sanzan: Yamagata's Three Sacred Mountains — Guide
item.description: The three sacred peaks of Haguro, Gassan and Yudono have been a centre of Shugendo mountain asceticism for over 1,400 years, drawing yamabushi pilgrims in white robes who complete gruelling multi-day rituals combining Shinto, Buddhism and animist nature worship. Mt. Haguro’s five-storey pagoda at the base of a cedar-lined stone stairway is one of the most atmospheric approaches in all of Japan. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Haguro, Tsuruoka, Yamagata Hours Haguro grounds always open Admission Around ¥550 (Haguro) Time needed 2–3 hours (Haguro) Best time Summer (Gassan open); year-round Haguro What to See The five-storey pagoda at Mt.

item.title: Fujita Memorial Garden: Hirosaki's Taisho Garden — Guide
item.description: The Fujita Memorial Garden in Hirosaki is a refined two-level garden from the Taisho era. An upper garden with a Western villa and a lower garden with a pond and waterfall frame distant views of Mt. Iwaki — a peaceful stop away from the castle crowds. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours ~9:00–17:00 (seasonal) Admission Around ¥320 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Spring–autumn; fresh green & foliage What to See The elegant upper garden with a Taisho-era Western villa.

item.title: Furofushi Onsen: Aomori's Seaside Sunset Bath — Guide
item.description: Furofushi Onsen is a famed seaside hot spring in Fukaura where you soak in amber-coloured open-air baths at the very edge of the Sea of Japan, facing the sunset. Iron-rich water turns golden-brown on contact with the air, and waves break just metres away — a bucket-list bathing experience on the Gono Line coast. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Fukaura, Aomori Hours Day bathing ~8:00–16:00 (varies) Admission Day bath ~¥600 Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Geibikei Gorge: Iwate's Boatman-Song Ravine — Guide
item.description: Geibikei is one of Iwate’s most tranquil scenic spots — a gorge of towering 100-metre limestone cliffs explored by traditional flat-bottomed boat. The boatman poles slowly upstream and, at the turning point, sings a haunting folk song that echoes off the cliffs. A gentle, atmospheric ride quite unlike the wilder Genbikei nearby. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ichinoseki, Iwate Hours Boats ~8:30–16:00 (seasonal) Admission Boat ride ~¥1,800 Time needed About 1.

item.title: Genbikei Gorge & the Flying Dango: Iwate's Quirk — Guide
item.description: Genbikei is one of Japan’s most unusual scenic spots — a gorge where a rushing river and sculpted basalt walls have eroded into extraordinary forms. Its beloved novelty is the ‘flying dango’ (kakko dango): a wooden box pulled by rope across the gorge, delivering freshly made sweets to visitors on the far bank. A strange, delightful Iwate quirk. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ichinoseki, Iwate Hours Daytime; dango shop hours vary Admission Free (dango ~¥500) Time needed About 1 hour Best time Autumn foliage; spring & summer green What to See The famous ‘flying dango’ delivered by rope across the gorge.

item.title: Ginzan Onsen: Japan's Most Photogenic Hot-Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Ginzan Onsen is widely regarded as Japan’s most photogenic hot spring town — a handful of multi-storey Taisho-era timber ryokan line both banks of a narrow mountain stream in a tight valley, all preserved in immaculate 1920s style. After dark, traditional gas lanterns illuminate the buildings, reflected in the flowing water below — a scene so cinematic it reportedly inspired the bathhouse in Miyazaki’s ‘Spirited Away’. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ginzan, Obanazawa, Yamagata Hours Village always open; day bath varies Admission Free to visit; day bath ~¥500 Time needed 1.

item.title: Goishi Coast: Iwate's Pine-Shaded Rocky Shore — Guide
item.description: The Goishi Coast in Ofunato is a scenic stretch of the southern Sanriku shoreline — black pebble beaches (whose stones give the coast its ‘Go-stone’ name), wave-carved rock formations, and a pine-shaded coastal trail leading past thundering sea caves and blowholes. An easy, atmospheric walk on the recovering Sanriku coast. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ofunato, Iwate Hours Trail always open (daylight best) Admission Free Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Spring–summer; clear days What to See Black pebble beaches and wave-carved rocks.

item.title: Hachimantai & Yakehashiri Lava: Iwate's Volcanic Highland — Guide
item.description: Hachimantai is a serene volcanic highland straddling the Iwate–Akita border — a plateau of alpine marshes, ponds and hot springs. It holds the rare Yakehashiri lava flow (a national natural monument) and the famous ‘Dragon Eye’, a ring-shaped snowmelt pattern that appears on a highland pond in late spring. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachimantai, Iwate Hours Aspite Line road ~Apr–Nov Admission Free Time needed Half day Best time Late May (Dragon Eye); summer alpine What to See The ‘Dragon Eye’ ring-shaped snowmelt pond (late May).

item.title: Hachinohe Emburi: Aomori's Ancient Winter Rite — Guide
item.description: The Hachinohe Emburi is one of Japan’s most unusual major festivals — an ancient rice-planting ceremony held February 17–20, where farmers wearing magnificent horse-head headdresses (eboshi) dance to pray for a bountiful harvest. Over 800 years old, it feels genuinely archaic and remains almost unknown to foreign visitors. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachinohe, Aomori Hours Feb 17–20 (daytime performances) Admission Mostly free; some paid indoor shows Time needed 1–2 hours Best time February 17–20 (fixed) Highlights Dancers in dramatic horse-head headdresses (eboshi).

item.title: Hachinohe Morning Market: Japan's Largest Sunday Market — Guide
item.description: The Tatehana Wharf morning market in Hachinohe is one of Japan’s largest — over 300 stalls line the wharf from around 3am each Sunday (spring–autumn), selling fresh seafood, grilled fish, local snacks and handmade goods. Fishermen and farmers trade directly with the public in a wholly local, un-touristy atmosphere. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachinohe, Aomori (Tatehana Wharf) Hours Sun ~3:00–9:00 (Mar–Dec) Admission Free; pay per stall Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Sunday mornings, Mar–Dec What to Try 300+ stalls of seafood, produce and street food.

item.title: Hachinohe Sansha Taisai: UNESCO Float Festival — Guide
item.description: The Hachinohe Sansha Taisai is a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage festival held over five days in late July–early August. A grand procession of 27 towering, elaborately decorated floats bearing mythological tableaux rolls through the city, uniting three major Hachinohe shrines in a 290-year tradition of music, costume and pageantry. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachinohe, Aomori Hours Late Jul–early Aug (~Jul 31–Aug 4) Admission Free to watch; some paid seats Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Late July (annual) Highlights 27 towering decorated floats with mythological scenes.

item.title: Hakkoda Mountains: Snow Monsters, Ropeway & Skiing — Guide
item.description: The Hakkoda Mountains, a volcanic range 20 minutes from Aomori City, see some of Japan’s deepest snow. The year-round ropeway climbs to 1,324 m: summer brings alpine flowers and panoramas, while winter creates the famous ‘snow monsters’ (juhyo) and world-class powder skiing. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City area, Aomori Hours Ropeway ~9:00–16:20 Admission Ropeway ~¥1,900 (round trip) Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Summer (alpine); Jan–Mar (snow monsters) What to See The ropeway to 1,324 m with 360-degree views.

item.title: Hakkoda-maru Memorial Ship: Aomori's Ferry Museum — Guide
item.description: Moored in Aomori harbor beside the station, the Hakkoda-maru is a preserved Seikan railway ferry, now a floating museum. Before the Seikan Tunnel opened, these ships carried trains and passengers across the strait to Hokkaido — you can explore the bridge, engine room and nostalgic Showa-era passenger decks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City (Aomori harbor) Hours ~9:00–19:00 (seasonal; closed some days) Admission Around ¥510 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to See The preserved Seikan railway ferry on the water.

item.title: Hanamaki Onsen: Iwate's Rose-Garden Hot Spring Resort — Guide
item.description: Hanamaki Onsen is a classic hot-spring resort town in central Iwate — grand ryokan, a celebrated rose garden and quiet mountain baths gathered near the home of beloved poet Miyazawa Kenji. It’s an easy, comfortable onsen base for exploring the surrounding highlands and Hiraizumi to the south. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hanamaki, Iwate Hours Day bathing hours vary; stays overnight Admission Day bath ~¥800; stays vary Time needed Half day (or overnight) Best time Year-round; roses late May–Jun What to See Grand ryokan and mountain hot-spring baths.

item.title: Hinai-jidori: One of Japan's Three Great Chickens — Akita Guide
item.description: Hinai-jidori is one of Japan’s three designated premium chicken breeds, raised free-range in Akita’s Hinai region for around 150 days — twice as long as standard poultry. The meat is firmer, richer and far more intensely flavoured than supermarket chicken. Taste it in kiritanpo hot pot, grilled yakitori, an oyakodon rice bowl, or even as chicken sashimi at specialist restaurants. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Odate/Hinai & Akita City Hours Restaurant hours Admission Varies by dish Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to Try Firm, rich Hinai-jidori in kiritanpo hot pot.

item.title: Hiraizumi Cycling: Ride the UNESCO Landscape — Guide
item.description: Hiraizumi’s UNESCO World Heritage sites are connected by a flat, easy cycling route through rice paddies and old settlements. Rent a bike at Hiraizumi Station and link Chusonji, Motsuji, Kanjizaio-in and the Muryokoin ruins in a half-day loop that reveals the full scale of the Fujiwara capital — far more rewarding than the shuttle bus. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hiraizumi, Iwate Hours Rental shop hours (daytime) Admission Bike rental ~¥1,000/day Time needed Half day Best time Late spring–autumn What to Do Link the UNESCO sites on a flat cycling loop.

item.title: Hiraizumi Fireflies & Night Illumination: Summer Magic — Guide
item.description: In June and July, the rice paddies and streams around UNESCO World Heritage Hiraizumi come alive with thousands of fireflies, and evening firefly-viewing walks are organized. Seasonal night illuminations of Chusonji’s Golden Hall and Motsuji’s Pure Land garden add a contemplative beauty — heritage architecture glowing in the dark beside natural bioluminescence. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hiraizumi, Iwate Hours Evenings, Jun–Jul (seasonal) Admission Varies by event Time needed 1.

item.title: Hiraizumi Fujiwara Festivals: Heian Pageantry — Guide
item.description: Hiraizumi holds two Fujiwara festivals a year — in May and early November — recreating the glory of its 12th-century golden age. Processions in full Heian court costume, sacred kagura and the magnificent Ennen no Mai (longevity dance) performed by masked priests fill the UNESCO temple grounds, drawing visitors from across Japan. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hiraizumi, Iwate Hours Festival days (May 1–5; early Nov) Admission Grounds free; some events ticketed Time needed 2–3 hours Best time May & early November Highlights Processions in full Heian court costume.

item.title: Hirosaki Apple Pie Trail: 50+ Shops to Taste — Guide
item.description: Hirosaki turns its apple heritage into a delicious tasting trail: over 50 bakeries, cafés and restaurants around the city each bake their own distinctive apple pie, from buttery lattice to French-style tarte. An official guide map ranks the pies, making an afternoon of tastings around the castle park easy and fun. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Shop hours vary (roughly daytime) Admission Pies ~¥300–500 each Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Year-round; autumn apple season peaks What to Try Over 50 distinct apple pies across the city.

item.title: Hirosaki Castle & Cherry Blossoms: Japan's Best Hanami — Guide
item.description: Hirosaki Castle in western Aomori holds one of only twelve original Edo-period keeps left in Japan — but it is most famous as the country’s greatest cherry blossom site. In late April some 2,600 trees erupt in bloom, and fallen petals blanket the moat into the legendary pink ‘hanaikada’ flower raft. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Park always open; keep ~9:00–17:00 Admission Park free; castle areas ~¥320 Time needed 1.

item.title: Hirosaki Neputa Festival: Fan-Shaped Lantern Floats — Guide
item.description: Hirosaki’s Neputa Festival is the quieter, more painterly counterpart to Aomori’s Nebuta. From August 1–7, fan-shaped floats (ogi-neputa) painted with mythological warrior scenes and lit from within parade through Hirosaki to the beat of taiko. The effect is more refined and mysterious than Aomori’s three-dimensional warrior figures. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Evenings, Aug 1–7 Admission Free to watch; some paid seats Time needed 1.

item.title: Hittsumi: Iwate's Hand-Torn Dumpling Soup — Guide
item.description: Hittsumi is a beloved Iwate country soup — flat pieces of wheat dough are torn by hand and simmered with root vegetables, mushrooms and chicken or fish in a soy or miso broth. Hearty, humble and deeply warming, it’s classic rural home cooking, at its best in winter and served at local restaurants and inns across the prefecture. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Rural Iwate & Morioka Hours Restaurant hours Admission ~¥600–900 a bowl Time needed About 40 min Best time Winter (warming dish) What to Try Hand-torn wheat-dough dumplings in savory broth.

item.title: Hotokegaura: Aomori's Surreal Buddha Cliffs — Guide
item.description: Hotokegaura, the ‘Buddha Shore’, is one of Japan’s most extraordinary coastlines — white dolomite columns rising up to 100 m from the Sea of Japan along the Shimokita Peninsula, their shapes likened to Buddhist saints. Reachable only by seasonal boat, it stays almost unknown to foreign visitors. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sai Village, Shimokita, Aomori Hours Boat tours ~Apr–Oct, daytime Admission Boat tour ~¥2,000+ Time needed 1.

item.title: Iburigakko: Akita's Smoked Daikon Pickles — Guide
item.description: Iburigakko is a beloved Akita farmhouse specialty — daikon radish smoke-dried over wood fires, then pickled in rice bran, producing a crunchy, deeply smoky, gently sweet pickle. Traditionally made in snowbound winter farmhouses where radishes couldn’t sun-dry, it pairs superbly with sake and, in a modern twist, with cream cheese. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Inland Akita (Yokote etc.) Hours Shop hours Admission Cheap (packs) Time needed About 20 min Best time Year-round; made in winter What to Try Crunchy, smoky pickled daikon slices.

item.title: Ichigoni: Aomori's Luxurious Sea Urchin Soup — Guide
item.description: Ichigoni is a luxurious clear soup of sea urchin and abalone from the Hachinohe coast. Its name — ‘strawberry simmer’ — comes from the way the milky, poached sea urchin resembles wild strawberries floating in the broth. A summer delicacy, it’s one of Aomori’s most special regional dishes. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachinohe & Sanriku coast, Aomori Hours Restaurant hours (seasonal) Admission Premium; varies Time needed About 1 hour Best time Summer (urchin season) What to Try Clear, delicate sea urchin and abalone soup.

item.title: Ichinoseki Mochi Cuisine: Iwate's Multi-Course Rice Cake — Guide
item.description: Ichinoseki and neighbouring Hiraizumi are the heartland of Iwate’s extraordinary mochi food culture, where dozens of preparations of pounded rice cake are served as a full multi-course meal called mochi-zen. Each small dish presents mochi in a different guise — walnut sauce, sesame, sweet red bean, grated radish, or kinako soybean powder — a legacy of centuries of Buddhist feast-day traditions. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ichinoseki, Iwate Hours Restaurant hours Admission Mochi-zen sets ~¥1,500+ Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to Try A multi-course mochi-zen tasting meal.

item.title: Imoni: Yamagata's Riverside Taro Stew Tradition — Guide
item.description: Imoni is Yamagata’s most beloved seasonal dish — a hearty taro root and beef stew simmered with konnyaku, leek and a soy-based broth over an open fire on the riverbank in autumn. Imoni parties (imonikai), where friends gather to cook huge pots together, are a deeply embedded autumn ritual. The Yamagata Imoni Festival takes it to an extreme with a 6.5-metre iron pot feeding 30,000 people, stirred with a crane-mounted paddle.

item.title: Inaniwa Udon: Akita's Silky Handmade Noodles — Guide
item.description: Inaniwa udon, from Akita’s Yuzawa region, is one of Japan’s three great udon alongside Sanuki and Mizusawa — distinguished by its extraordinarily thin, silky-smooth strands made through a laborious multi-day hand-stretching process. Served cold in summer with dipping broth, or warm in a clear dashi, it is a study in refined simplicity. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Yuzawa (Inaniwa), Akita Hours Restaurant hours Admission ~¥900–1,500 a bowl Time needed About 45 min Best time Year-round; cold in summer What to Try Extraordinarily thin, silky-smooth udon strands.

item.title: Iwakiyama Shrine: the 'Nikko of the North' — Aomori Guide
item.description: At the foot of sacred Mt. Iwaki, the 1,200-year-old Iwakiyama Shrine is the spiritual heart of the Tsugaru region. Its ornately carved gates and halls, rich with colour and detail, have earned it the nickname the ‘Nikko of Oku’ — the Nikko of the far north. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Grounds always open Admission Free Time needed About 1 hour Best time Autumn; also summer climbing season What to See The lavishly carved main gate (romon) and halls.

item.title: Iwate Bank Red Brick Building: Morioka's Meiji Landmark — Guide
item.description: The Iwate Bank Red Brick Building is one of Morioka’s best-loved landmarks — a handsome 1911 former bank designed by Kingo Tatsuno, architect of Tokyo Station, and his partner. Its red brick and white stone facade anchors the historic city centre, and the beautifully restored interior is open to visitors. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Morioka, Iwate Hours ~10:00–16:30 (closed Tue) Admission Around ¥300 (interior) Time needed About 40 min Best time Year-round What to See The red brick and white stone Meiji facade (1911).

item.title: Jajamen: Morioka's Meat-Miso Noodle Dish — Guide
item.description: Jajamen is one of Morioka’s famous ‘three noodles’ — flat, udon-like noodles topped with a fragrant meat-miso sauce, cucumber and ginger. The local ritual is to crack a raw egg into the leftover sauce at the end, which the shop turns into a hot egg soup called ‘chitantan’. Mix, slurp, finish — a beloved Morioka comfort food. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Morioka, Iwate Hours Restaurant hours Admission ~¥600–900 a bowl Time needed About 45 min Best time Year-round What to Try Flat noodles with fragrant meat-miso sauce.

item.title: Jappa-jiru: Aomori's Cod & Miso Winter Hotpot — Guide
item.description: Jappa-jiru is a beloved Aomori fisherman’s soup — cod offcuts, miso, daikon, tofu and seasonal vegetables simmered into a deeply savory winter broth. Once a zero-waste dish made on fishing boats, it’s now cherished comfort food at izakayas along the Tsugaru coast from November to March. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City & Tsugaru coast Hours Izakaya/restaurant hours Admission ~¥600–1,000 a bowl Time needed About 1 hour Best time Winter (Nov–Mar) What to Try Rich cod-and-miso broth with daikon and tofu.

item.title: Joboji Urushi Lacquer: Japan's Lacquer Heartland — Iwate Guide
item.description: Joboji, in Ninohe in northern Iwate, produces the majority of Japan’s precious domestic urushi (natural lacquer) — the sap tapped from lacquer trees that coats the finest traditional crafts and restores national treasures. In this craft town you can try lacquer-coating or maki-e (gold-relief) decoration of a bowl, a hands-on encounter with a rare Japanese art. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ninohe (Joboji), Iwate Hours By reservation Admission Workshop ~¥3,000 Time needed About 1.

item.title: Jodogahama Beach: Sanriku's 'Pure Land' Shore — Guide
item.description: Named ‘Pure Land Beach’ by an 18th-century priest who found it too beautiful for this world, Jodogahama’s jagged white rhyolite columns rise from translucent blue water in the Rikuchu Kaigan National Park. Glass-bottomed boat tours reveal the underwater world, and swimming is possible in the sheltered cove. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Miyako, Iwate Hours Beach always open; boats daytime Admission Beach free; boat tours ~¥1,500 Time needed 1.

item.title: Junsai Water Shield: Akita's Silky Summer Delicacy — Guide
item.description: Junsai (water shield) is a delicate summer delicacy — a jelly-coated aquatic plant hand-harvested from ponds by wooden punt in Mitane, northern Akita, which produces most of Japan’s crop. Prized for its silky, slippery texture and clean taste, it’s served chilled with vinegar or dashi, in miso soup, or in hot pot. Some farms offer summer harvesting experiences by boat. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Mitane, Akita Hours Restaurant hours; harvest summer Admission Varies; harvest experiences extra Time needed About 30 min Best time Summer (May–Aug harvest) What to Try Silky, jelly-coated junsai chilled with vinegar or dashi.

item.title: Kabushima Shrine: Aomori's Seagull Island — Guide
item.description: Kabushima is a small shrine islet near Hachinohe that transforms each spring into a swirling home for some 30,000 black-tailed gulls — a designated Natural Monument. You can walk right among the nesting birds, a raucous, unforgettable wildlife spectacle rare in Japan. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachinohe, Aomori Hours Grounds always open Admission Free Time needed About 1 hour Best time Spring (Mar–Jul nesting season) What to See Around 30,000 black-tailed gulls nesting in spring.

item.title: Kakunodate Kabazaiku: 200-Year Cherry Bark Craft — Guide
item.description: Kakunodate’s 200-year-old craft tradition of kabazaiku uses cherry tree bark to create lustrous, durable containers, tea canisters and accessories. The bark is peeled, layered and polished to a warm honey-brown sheen — a uniquely Akita art form born from the samurai district’s need for a secondary income. Several workshops in the samurai quarter welcome visitors to watch artisans at work. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kakunodate, Senboku, Akita Hours Workshops ~9:00–17:00 Admission Free to browse; pieces vary Time needed 45 min–1.

item.title: Kakunodate Samurai District & Cherry Blossoms — Akita Guide
item.description: Kakunodate is one of Japan’s best-preserved samurai towns — a 400-year-old bukeyashiki (samurai residence) street lined with black-walled mansions and weeping cherry trees planted by samurai families. Six original residences are open to the public, and in late April the shidarezakura drape over the walls like pink waterfalls, one of Tohoku’s finest hanami. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kakunodate, Senboku, Akita Hours Street always open; residences ~9:00–17:00 Admission Some residences ~¥400 Time needed 1.

item.title: Kamaishi Rugby & Recovery Stadium: Iwate's Moving Story — Guide
item.description: Kamaishi is Japan’s most passionate rugby town — the Kamaishi Seawaves won the national championship eight times running in the 1970s–80s. Its rebuilt Unosumai Memorial Stadium hosted Rugby World Cup 2019 matches as a symbol of recovery from the 2011 tsunami, making it one of Japan’s most moving sporting venues. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kamaishi, Iwate Hours Match days & tours; check schedule Admission Varies (matches/tours) Time needed About 1.

item.title: Kaminoyama: Castle Town Onsen at the Foot of Zao — Guide
item.description: Kaminoyama is a graceful hot spring town at the foot of Mt. Zao with a 550-year history — legend holds it was discovered in 1458 by a sick crane bathing in a warm spring. The white-walled castle keep, rebuilt in 1982 on its Sengoku-era foundations, overlooks the town, while seven public bath houses (kyu-do-yu) let visitors hop between springs on a single pass, and casual foot baths dot the streets.

item.title: Kiritanpo Nabe: Akita's Iconic Rice Hot Pot — Guide
item.description: Kiritanpo is Akita’s most iconic dish — freshly pounded rice is moulded onto cedar skewers, grilled over charcoal, then simmered in a rich broth with Hinai-jidori chicken (one of Japan’s three great chickens), burdock, Japanese parsley and maitake mushrooms. The mochi-like kiritanpo soaks up the umami broth beautifully. Best from October to March. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Akita City & Odate, Akita Hours Restaurant hours Admission ~¥1,200–2,000 a set Time needed About 1 hour Best time Oct–Mar (winter) What to Try Grilled kiritanpo rice skewers in a rich hot pot.

item.title: Kitakami Tenshochi: Iwate's Riverside Cherry Tunnel — Guide
item.description: Stretching two kilometres along the Kitakami River, Tenshochi Park is lined with 10,000 Yoshino cherry trees that form a blossoming tunnel each April. Rent a rowboat to drift beneath the overhanging branches, or ride the little steam train through the park. Blossoms reflected in the river with the distant Kitakami mountains make this one of Tohoku’s most beloved spring walks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kitakami, Iwate Hours Park always open; festival late Apr Admission Free (boat/train extra) Time needed 1.

item.title: Kitayamazaki Cliffs: Iwate's 200 m Sea Walls — Guide
item.description: The Kitayamazaki Cliffs are one of the Sanriku coast’s grandest sights — eight kilometres of sheer 200-metre sea cliffs plunging into the Pacific. Clifftop lookouts give sweeping panoramas, while boat tours pass close to the sea caves and arches carved into the base. A raw, elemental landscape far from the crowds. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Tanohata, Iwate Hours Lookouts always open; boats seasonal Admission Free; boat tours extra Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Late spring–autumn What to See Sheer 200 m sea cliffs over 8 km of coast.

item.title: Kogin-zashi Embroidery: Tsugaru's Geometric Stitch — Guide
item.description: Kogin-zashi is Tsugaru’s centuries-old counted-thread embroidery — crisp white geometric patterns stitched onto indigo cloth, originally to reinforce and warm farmers' work clothes. Hirosaki workshops let you stitch a small coaster or accessory, a calming, hands-on encounter with a beautiful folk craft. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours By reservation Admission Workshop ~¥2,000 Time needed About 1.

item.title: Koiwai Farm's Lone Cherry Tree: Iwate's Iconic Spring Scene — Guide
item.description: A single wild cherry tree standing alone in the green meadows of Koiwai Farm, with snow-capped Mt.
